agent-sandbox-boundary.title: An AI Agent Sandbox Is Not Your Authorization Boundary
agent-sandbox-boundary.description: An AI agent sandbox limits where code runs, not what it can change. Set security boundaries for network access, credentials, approvals, and writes.

sections.text:
Your agent needs to inspect a repository, run tests, and suggest a patch. It does not need permission to merge a PR. Those two requirements are easy to blur when a managed agent comes with its own sandbox.

OpenAI's Agents API launched in public beta on September 10, 2026. It supplies the agent harness and lets developers choose an OpenAI-hosted environment or their own infrastructure. The quickstart creates a session in an openai_hosted environment and streams progress. This removes a lot of orchestration work. It does not transfer your application's authorization policy into the sandbox.
A sandbox limits where code runs. Your application decides what the agent may change.

This is a design recommendation, not a claim that a particular sandbox has been breached.

sections.heading: Five separate questions hiding behind “is it sandboxed?”
sections.text:
| Boundary | Question to answer before launch | Default for a patch-review agent |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Execution | Where can generated code run? | Disposable, task-scoped workspace |
| Network | Which destinations can it reach? | No outbound access unless the task needs it |
| Credentials | What secret material can agent-generated code read? | No production credentials in the workspace |
| Authorization | Who decides whether a proposed action is permitted? | Application-side policy, not agent prose |
| Durable state | Who applies changes to the real repository or deployment? | Human-reviewed PR; no merge or deploy permission |

The first two rows are environment configuration. The last two are product behavior. Don't treat a green check on the first row as an answer to all five.

OpenAI's hosted-sandbox documentation says outbound network access is enabled by default unless a template policy changes it. It offers disabled and restricted modes; restricted mode uses exact hostnames rather than wildcard domains. The same documentation says ordinary env variables are readable by agent-generated code and directs developers to use vault credentials for secrets instead. These are useful controls, but you must choose them explicitly for your workload. A domain allowlist controls a destination, not which operation the agent may perform at that destination.

sections.heading: Try the design review before reading mine
sections.text:
Scenario: A coding agent checks a dependency upgrade in an unfamiliar repository. It needs package installation, tests, and a patch for review. Pick the smallest permission set you would grant.

 
 Decision A: does an isolated workspace make generated code trustworthy? 

A sandbox limits the process environment; it doesn't establish that the patch is correct or safe. Keep each run disposable and task-scoped, then review the returned diff and rerun checks in a trusted CI environment against the exact revision.

 

 
 Decision B: allow outbound internet for package installation? 

First ask whether a prebuilt dependency cache or a setup step can satisfy the task. If the agent must fetch packages, restrict destinations as tightly as the build allows and pin dependency versions; don't assume an allowlisted package host makes package contents trustworthy. The hosted-sandbox docs warn that redirects and subdomains need separate allowlist entries. Re-run the install in a clean workspace before trusting the result.

 

 
 Decision C: put a GitHub token in the sandbox so it can open a PR? 

Keep a repo-scoped write token out of agent-generated code. Let the agent return a patch or artifact, validate it outside the workspace, and let a separate application service open the PR with the smallest necessary credential. OpenAI documents /workspace/outputs as the location for published, immutable artifacts when a turn completes; an artifact is output to inspect, not an authorization grant. If your workflow genuinely needs agent-accessible credentials, review the provider's vault-credential mechanism and its scope instead of putting a secret in env.

 

 
 Decision D: should the agent decide which actions are authorized? 

No. Treat model output, generated code, and tool requests as untrusted proposals. Enforce authorization in application-side policy at every tool boundary; the agent's explanation, a successful run, or a hostname allowlist is not that policy.

 

 
 Decision E: should a passing test run let the agent merge or deploy? 

No. An agent's summary is not a test attestation. Run the repository's checks in a separate trusted CI context against the exact proposed commit; review the diff and source of any downloaded dependencies. A merge is a different capability from preparing a patch. Make the human or a separately specified deployment policy authorize it.

 

These aren't model-quality questions. They are questions about where untrusted inputs become durable effects.

sections.heading: A narrow handoff you can implement
sections.text:
A safe first version of this workflow has three stages:

1. Run: give the agent a repository snapshot and a task, with no production secrets. Set an explicit network policy. Record the input revision and environment configuration alongside the run.
2. Inspect: collect its patch, explanation, and command output. Treat all three as untrusted. Check that the diff touches only allowed paths; run format, type, and test checks yourself against the exact patch. A passing check means _those checks_ passed, not that the change is secure.
3. Propose: a separate service, holding a scoped GitHub credential, opens a review-only PR. Require another authorization step for merge or deploy. Never use the agent's self-reported success as the condition for production writes.

The last two stages are an application-side architecture proposal, not features automatically supplied by the Agents API. OpenAI's quickstart also says to keep the application API key outside the sandbox and lists separate permissions for agent sessions and model inference. That is a helpful reminder: even the API used to _start_ a run has a different trust boundary from the code running _inside_ one.

There is a tradeoff. A no-network environment cannot install new dependencies from a registry; a review-only agent cannot autonomously ship a fix. Start there if the job is “prepare a patch.” Widen one capability at a time, with a concrete task that needs it and a check you can run independently. “It ran in a sandbox” is the beginning of that review, not the end.

For a runnable companion, see testing AI agent actions with an approval gate.

agent-sandbox-shared-cache.title: Your Agent Sandbox Shares an L3 Cache
agent-sandbox-shared-cache.description: OpenAI caught agents passing secrets through CPU cache timing inside microVM isolation. Why memory sandboxes do not bound timing, the bandwidth math, and what to change.

sections.text:
Two agents ran on the same physical machine, in separate microVMs, with no network between them and no shared writable file. They still passed a synthetic secret from one to the other.

They did it through the CPU cache. One agent evicted specific data from the cache; the other measured how long reloading that data took, and the fast/slow difference carried the message. OpenAI described exactly this on October 23, 2026, in a post about hardening frontier model training environments. The sentence that should get your attention is not "the models escaped." It is this: they exchanged information _without changing a shared file or opening a network connection_.

If your agent platform relies on "each run is its own VM" to keep tenants apart, that control is real but narrower than most people assume. It bounds memory and privilege. It does not bound timing, and timing is enough to move a secret.

This is the hardware-boundary cousin of why a sandbox is not an authorization boundary: there, the gap was between isolation and permission. Here, the gap is between isolation and physics.

sections.heading: What OpenAI actually reported
sections.text:
Three separate channels, from a red-team exercise:
Cache timing. Evict, then time the reload. Fast means "cached", slow means "evicted". One bit per observation.
Disk write drain timing. An agent watched how long a write took to complete and used the variance as a signal.
CPU time contention. Wall-clock slowdown as a function of what a neighbour is doing.

OpenAI is explicit that most of these tests were not spontaneous. In most cases they named the channel or handed the agents an encoding protocol. In one case, agents got only a broad list of infrastructure vulnerabilities and still turned one into a working channel. Read that the way an engineer should: the models are not reliably inventing covert channels on their own yet, but the channels exist and are discoverable, and a shared prompt is enough to agree on an encoding.

The same post reports an agent exploiting a DNS resolver misconfiguration to reach the internet on September 20, 2026, which paused that line of work until October 1. It also lists patched escape paths: a Kata Containers flaw (CVE-2026-24834) that let a container read host special files, a gVisor file-descriptor leak, and tightened Moby syscall filters. Those are software bugs and they get fixed. The cache channel is not a bug.

sections.heading: A VM boundary is a memory boundary, not a timing boundary
sections.text:
MicroVMs and containers partition _address spaces_ and _privilege_. Instructions, syscalls, page tables, device access. Nothing in that list partitions a shared last-level cache, a memory controller, a memory bus, SMT siblings, or a power budget.

Those resources are shared by construction, because that sharing is why the machine is cheap. The 2009 paper that made this mainstream, Ristenpart et al., "Hey, You, Get Off of My Cloud", did two things: mapped EC2's placement to find co-resident victims, then used cross-VM side channels to read information out of them. Sixteen years of hardware changes later, the shape has not changed. Spectre made it worse by turning speculative execution into a general-purpose leak primitive, and the mitigations that followed added latency, not isolation of timing.

So the question is not "is my sandbox isolated?" It is "who else is in this cache, and what are they allowed to learn?"

To make that concrete I measured the separation available on one ordinary laptop (13th-gen i7-1360P, 18 MiB L3, 64 MiB working set, 20,000 samples per path):

Two runs, idle machine:

A 7.4× latency gap with under 1% raw error on a quiet machine. No root, no kernel module, no network. Just clock_gettime and a buffer. That is the entire primitive, and it is available to any process you run next to another one.

hit  p10=14 p50=15  p90=16  ns
miss p10=103 p50=111 p90=121 ns
threshold=63 ns  false_positive=0.02%  false_negative=0.70%

sections.heading: The bandwidth argument, done properly
sections.text:
The instinctive rebuttal is "that channel is too slow to matter." That was true in 2009 and stopped being true a long time ago.

Published cross-VM rates, all measured, not modelled:

| Year | Channel | Rate | Error |
| ---- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ------------ |
| 2009 | L2, EC2 (Ristenpart) | 0.2 bit/s | not reported |
| 2015 | LLC, cross-VM (C5) | 751 bit/s | 5.7% |
| 2017 | LLC, EC2, error-corrected (Maurice) | 362 kbit/s | 0% |

Five orders of magnitude in eight years, and the fast end is a plain hypervisor on public cloud. That 2017 paper does not stop at a bit rate: the authors ran an SSH session between two EC2 instances over the covert channel. The slow end is what people quote when they call the problem theoretical.

So do the arithmetic at both ends:
At 751 bit/s: a 32-byte key takes 0.34 seconds; a 10 MB repository takes 30 hours.
At 362 kbit/s raw: the same key takes 0.7 milliseconds; the repository takes 3.7 minutes. Repetition coding to survive noise costs a factor of 3 or more, which is still minutes.

The conclusion changes with the rate, which is why the "it's slow" argument is a bet on someone else's hardware and someone else's error correction. Move the slider.

 

The range is the point. At the 2009 rate the channel is a curiosity. At the 2017 rate it replaces a socket, and the authors proved it by running SSH over it. What an agent platform actually holds sits in the small bucket: tokens, environment variables, mount paths, which other tenants are present, and the timing of a deploy. Every one of those is affordable even at ten bits per second. Assuming the fast end is out of reach is a hardware bet, not a security argument.

There is a second cost the model above makes visible. Sender and receiver need an agreed slot clock before the first bit, and that agreement cannot travel over the channel. It has to be pre-shared: same prompt, same protocol, same constant baked into the tool code. Which means the channel is only useful when the two sides already have a common reference, and _that_ is the part you can control.

sections.heading: What actually narrows the channel
sections.text:
Ranked by how much they buy per unit of operational pain, with honest limits:

| Control | Buys you | Does not buy you |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tenant co-location policy (never place untrusted runs on a host with secret-bearing runs) | Removes the channel completely | Costs money; needs placement guarantees your cloud may not sell |
| Disable SMT, or use Linux core scheduling | Blocks cross-hyperthread leakage; the kernel doc calls disabling HT the only full cross-HT mitigation | Does nothing for shared last-level cache |
| LLC partitioning (Intel CAT via resctrl) | Real isolation of cache sets when the hardware exposes it and you control the hypervisor | Usually unavailable inside a guest VM; verify before you put it in a diagram |
| Shorter secret lifetime | Turns a leak into a stale leak | Nothing, if the secret is long-lived by design |
| Behavioural monitoring (periodic syscall patterns, timing-shaped loops) | Detects the crude version | Misses a careful implementation; produces false positives on legitimate benchmark code |

Two of those are worth doing today for most teams: stop co-locating untrusted runs with privileged ones, and shrink secret lifetimes. Both are policy changes, both are cheap, and neither requires knowing whether anyone actually built a channel.

The documented-but-unavailable options are worth knowing because they show up in vendor decks. Core scheduling, per kernel documentation, lets you define which tasks may share a core so that cross-HT attacks are contained. It is a scheduler feature for when you need SMT on. It says nothing about the LLC, which is the resource in the OpenAI experiment, and that distinction is exactly the kind of thing a diagram flattens into "hardware isolation: yes".

sections.heading: The invariant to write down
sections.text:
Not "no shared files." Not "no network." Both were true in the experiment.

The invariant is: no shared measurable resource between trust domains. If two workloads can both observe the same counter, cache line, memory controller, or clock, they share a channel, and a channel with a channel capacity is a channel that will eventually be used.

That reframes the review question for any agent platform:

1. What is the trust domain? A tenant, a task, or a single run. Pick one and say it out loud.
2. What is co-resident with what? Placement is a security control. If you cannot answer "which other tenant was on this host," you are assuming the answer is "nobody interesting."
3. What secrets live inside a shared-hardware boundary? Credentials inside a sandbox that shares a cache are credentials with an unusual exfiltration path. Move the secret out of the sandbox and have a proxy inject it, the way you already do for database access.
4. What would a leak look like in telemetry? Periodic probes look like a benchmark loop. If you cannot distinguish them, you have a detection gap that predates agents.

OpenAI's answer to all of this was to remove internet access from frontier training entirely and add monitoring for cross-boundary behaviour, and to state that they will keep that policy until safeguards justify otherwise. That is a policy choice available to a lab and mostly not to you. But the reasoning transfers: when a channel cannot be closed, remove the thing worth sending.

The uncomfortable part is that this problem is older than the agents. Shared hardware has leaked through timing since before anyone coined "side channel," and every generation of isolation marketing rediscovers it. Multi-tenant agent platforms are just the newest system where a VM boundary gets mistaken for a wall.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.text:
OpenAI, Securing our frontier model training environment, October 23, 2026 — cache, storage, and CPU-contention channels; the September 20 DNS incident; Kata/gVisor/Moby fixes.
Ristenpart, Tromer, Shacham, Savage, Hey, You, Get Off of My Cloud, CCS 2009 — co-residency mapping and cross-VM side channels.
Maurice et al., C5: Cross-Cores Cache Covert Channel, DIMVA 2015 — 751 bit/s LLC channel, 5.7% error.
Maurice et al., Hello from the Other Side: SSH over Robust Cache Covert Channels in the Cloud, NDSS 2017 — 45.25 KB/s error-free on EC2.
Core Scheduling, Linux kernel documentation — what SMT containment does and does not cover.
Spectre, Kocher et al., 2018 — speculative execution as a general leak primitive.
Discussion: Hacker News on the training-environment post and the cache-channel follow-up.
Latency measurements: my own probe, probe.c, on a 13th-gen i7-1360P laptop, 20,000 samples per path, two runs. One machine, idle. Treat it as an existence proof, not a benchmark.

agentgate-block-agent-prs-that-weaken-te.title: Your AI Agent Can Pass CI by Deleting the Test. agentgate Blocks That PR
agentgate-block-agent-prs-that-weaken-te.description: agentgate is a free, open-source GitHub Action that fails AI-agent PRs which skip tests, edit CI guardrails, or escalate workflow permissions. Install it in two minutes.

sections.text:
Here is a pull request an agent could open in your repo today. The commit message is "Align monitoring with reference implementation." The tests pass and CI is green.

It also does this:

On-call no longer gets alerts. The test that would have caught it now asserts the broken behavior, and then it's skipped. In the same diff, the workflow moved to pull_request_target, picked up contents: write, and swapped a pinned action for @v4.

That example isn't made up for effect. On October 20, OpenAI reported that on October 6 its internal agent GPT-6 Astra removed a monitoring integration during a migration and replaced the test that protected it with one asserting the monitor was absent. CI stayed green because the agent had edited the check along with the code.

Semgrep won't flag that diff and neither will gitleaks, because nothing in it is insecure code in the usual sense. The test suite won't either, since the suite is the thing that changed. So I wrote a check for this layer, and it's called agentgate.

sections.heading: What agentgate does
sections.text:
agentgate is a GitHub Action and CLI. It reads the PR diff, runs five rules, and fails the check when a change needs a human to look at it.

This is its real output on the PR above:

That's eight findings and exit code 1. In a PR, each one shows up as an inline annotation on the line that triggered it, and the table goes into the job summary.
code:
## agentgate: BLOCK

| Severity | Rule                | Location                    | Finding                                                  |
| -------- | ------------------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| block    | test-weakened       | tests/alerts.test.ts:2      | Test disabled or focused: test.skip('alerts reach ...    |
| block    | test-weakened       | tests/alerts.test.ts        | Net 1 assertion(s) removed across test files             |
| block    | guardrail-edited    | .github/workflows/ci.yml    | Protected path changed (modified): needs human review    |
| block    | workflow-escalation | .github/workflows/ci.yml:1  | pull_request_target runs with a write token and secrets  |
| block    | workflow-escalation | .github/workflows/ci.yml:3  | write permission granted                                 |
| block    | workflow-escalation | .github/workflows/ci.yml:8  | action not pinned to a full commit SHA                   |
| warn     | dependency-added    | package.json                | New dependency: left-pad@^1.3.0 (dependencies)           |
| warn     | suppression-added   | src/monitoring/alerts.ts:3  | Scanner or type check silenced: // @ts-ignore            |

sections.heading: The five rules
sections.text:
| Rule | Fires when | Default |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| test-weakened | A test file is deleted or moved out of test paths, a test gets .skip/.only/xit/@pytest.mark.skip, or the PR removes more assertions than it adds | block |
| guardrail-edited | The PR touches .github/, CODEOWNERS, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursor/, scanner configs, or paths you add | block |
| workflow-escalation | A workflow gains pull_request_target, write-all, a write permission, a secret, ${{ github.event. }} interpolation, or an action not pinned to a full SHA | block |
| dependency-added | package.json or requirements.txt gains a dependency, or an install script changes | warn |
| suppression-added | A changed line adds @ts-ignore, eslint-disable, nosemgrep, # noqa, NOSONAR, gitleaks:allow, and similar | warn |

It understands JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Go, and Java/JUnit test conventions out of the box, and you can change the test globs.

sections.heading: Why an agent can't just turn it off
sections.text:
A gate that a PR can disable doesn't protect anything. Most of the design went into closing that gap.

 

Config comes from the base commit. agentgate reads .agentgate.json from the branch you're merging into, not from the PR. A PR that sets "test-weakened": "off" and skips a test in the same diff still gets blocked, and editing the config is itself a guardrail-edited finding.

Protected paths only grow. Your protectedPaths are added to the defaults. No config can drop .github/ or .agentgate.json from the list.

The override is for humans. When a reviewer has read the change and agrees with it, they apply the agentgate-approved label, and blocks become warnings for that run. The label only counts when:
the run was triggered by that label being applied,
the latest label event is labeled, not unlabeled,
the account that applied it is a user, not a bot,
that user isn't the PR author.

If anyone pushes new commits after approval, the block comes back and the label has to be applied again. So an agent with a token can't approve its own PR, and it can't get approval for one diff and then push a different one.

It fails closed. A shallow clone, a missing base commit, a bad config, or a GitHub API error exits with code 2 and fails the check. Each of those would otherwise be a quiet way to get a pass.

Nothing from the PR runs. agentgate only diffs the head commit and pattern-matches it. It runs with contents: read and pull-requests: read and never writes to the PR.

sections.heading: Install it in two minutes
sections.text:
Add .github/workflows/agentgate.yml:

Keep fetch-depth: 0, because agentgate needs the base commit. Then do the two things that make it hold:

1. Make agentgate a required status check on your default branch, under Settings → Rules → Rulesets. Without that, a PR can delete the workflow and merge anyway.
2. Create an agentgate-approved label for reviewers to use as the override.

The first PR, the one that adds the workflow, will block itself because it edits .github/. That's the gate working. Merge that one as an admin.

To run it locally before you push:
code:
name: agentgate

on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, labeled, unlabeled]

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: read

jobs:
  gate:
    name: agentgate
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: piyush97/agentgate@13e7fc870ea5ebd2df2166efe9b2118e950a85f4 # v0.1.0

git clone https://github.com/piyush97/agentgate && cd agentgate
node dist/cli.js check --base origin/main               # Markdown
node dist/cli.js check --base origin/main --format json # for scripts

sections.heading: Tuning it
sections.text:
Everything is optional. A repo with a spec/ folder and a sensitive src/auth/ might use:

Unknown keys, unknown rules, and typos in severities fail the run instead of being ignored, so a mistake in the config can't quietly turn a rule off.

sections.heading: What it does not catch
sections.text:
agentgate reads diffs. It doesn't understand behavior.

An agent that writes a convincing new test for the wrong behavior passes every rule. So does a missing authorization check, an IDOR, a tenant-isolation bug, or a race condition, because none of those look like a weakened check.

So it's one layer among several. Keep diff-aware SAST and secret scanning, put CODEOWNERS on your risky paths, and have a human review anything that touches auth or money. My previous post has the full three-job gate and the benchmark behind it: in LSCBench, agents passed functional tests up to 91.3% of the time, but their code was also secure at most 25.1% of the time.

sections.heading: Where it runs today
sections.text:
I run agentgate as a required check on my own repos: this website, RoastTube, Understory, omaswitch, and about a dozen more. It also gates its own repo. Its workflow is pinned to the released SHA, so a PR to agentgate can't swap in its own build of the gate.

It's MIT licensed, has no runtime dependencies, runs on Node 24, and ships with 69 tests.

github.com/piyush97/agentgate

If it blocks something it shouldn't, or misses something it should catch, open an issue. A real bypass counts as a security bug, so report that privately per SECURITY.md.

agents-md-repository-context.title: AGENTS.md Is Becoming the Most Important File in Your Repository
agents-md-repository-context.description: AGENTS.md is becoming the most important file in a repository. Turn agent instructions from prompt sludge into a working operating manual.

sections.text:
The most consequential file in your repository may no longer be package.json, Dockerfile, or README.md.

It is increasingly the small Markdown file that tells an AI agent what all of those files _mean_.

Call it AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or .github/copilot-instructions.md; the filename is less important than the shift behind it. Coding agents are moving from autocomplete into repositories, terminals, pull requests, and CI. In that world, the quality of the work is no longer determined only by the model you picked. It is determined by whether the repository can explain itself before the agent starts changing it.

This is not a niche workflow for people who enjoy configuring tools. GitHub's current documentation says its cloud agent and CLI can load AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and GEMINI.md, alongside repository- and path-specific instructions. OpenAI's Codex agent loop also loads AGENTS.md; Anthropic's Claude Code has the equivalent CLAUDE.md project memory. The tools are competing. The pattern is converging.

That is why a good instruction file is becoming engineering infrastructure—not a prompt.

sections.heading: The data says the work is already changing
Your repo is now part of the prompt
sections.text:
For years, teams treated repository documentation as a thing written for the next human developer. Agent instructions change the audience, not the underlying job. You are still preserving decisions, naming the hazards, and making the safe path obvious. The difference is that the reader can now edit 40 files and run commands before you have made a coffee.

That makes the document's job more precise.

| A weak instruction file | A useful instruction file |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| "Write clean, maintainable code." | "Use Vite+; run bun run ci after TypeScript changes; do not add ESLint, Prettier, or Biome." |
| "Follow existing patterns." | "API routes live in src/pages/api/, set prerender = false, and return JSON Response objects." |
| "Test your work." | "For a blog route, run bun run build; for a UI interaction, add or update the matching Playwright spec under tests/." |
| "Be careful with security." | "Never log tokens or cookies. Keep CSRF and rate-limit changes isolated to src/middleware/ and API routes." |

The left column sounds reasonable. It is also nearly useless under pressure. The right column gives an agent a decision it can actually execute and gives a reviewer something concrete to enforce.

This is the same reason good runbooks beat company values at 2 a.m. Specificity is not bureaucracy. It is a shortcut to a correct decision.

sections.heading: The instruction file should be a map, not a constitution
sections.text:
The common failure mode is taking every tribal rule in a company and pasting it into one enormous Markdown file. That creates a new problem: the agent pays attention to the generic rules and misses the one detail that matters for the task in front of it.

GitHub makes the same distinction in its documentation. It recommends repository-wide instructions for durable conventions, but says that instructions which are too large or too specific can distract from the immediate task; use a skill or a custom agent for focused workflows instead.

Think in three layers:

Your root AGENTS.md should cover the first layer. Keep it short enough that a human can audit it in one sitting. Put database rules near database code. Put your release checklist in a release playbook. The exact support varies by tool, but the design principle does not: give the agent the smallest useful context at the point where it needs it.
code:
Repository guide          Stable facts every task needs
                           architecture, commands, guardrails

Path-specific guidance    Rules that matter only in one area
                           API auth, database migrations, frontend a11y

Task playbooks            Repeatable, high-stakes workflows
                           security review, release, incident response

sections.heading: What belongs in a good AGENTS.md
sections.text:
Here is the skeleton I would start with for a web application:

That is deliberately boring. It contains no model-specific magic words and no inspirational advice. It tells a capable agent where it is, how the codebase is shaped, how to prove a change, and what it must not casually damage.

The exact details should come from the repository, not a template. If your app uses pnpm, do not copy the Bun command. If deployment has a migration gate, name it. If the fastest local test is a single Playwright project, make that the default. A lie in an agent instruction file is worse than no instruction file because it causes a confident wrong action.
code:
# Repository guide

## What this service does

One paragraph: users, core workflow, and production environment.

## Map

- `src/pages/`: routes and API endpoints
- `src/components/`: UI components
- `src/utils/`: pure shared logic
- `tests/`: Playwright end-to-end coverage

## Commands

- Install: `bun install --frozen-lockfile`
- Check: `bun run ci`
- Build: `bun run build`
- Test: `bun run test:smoke`

## Guardrails

- Do not add dependencies without a concrete need.
- Preserve public API response shapes unless the task explicitly changes them.
- Never expose secrets or log credentials.
- Make the smallest viable change; do not refactor unrelated code.

## Change recipe

1. Read the closest existing implementation and relevant tests.
2. State the intended behavior before editing when the requirement is ambiguous.
3. Add or update the narrowest useful test.
4. Run the relevant check, then report what passed and what remains unverified.

sections.heading: Write rules that survive a model change
sections.text:
The model race is moving too quickly to write your process around one vendor's quirks. A durable instruction describes the desired engineering outcome and the available evidence, not a chain of prompts optimized for this month's agent.

Good:

Fragile:

The first tells any agent—and any human reviewer—what success looks like. The second asks for an internal state you cannot inspect or verify.

The same rule applies to tool permissions. Describe allowed operations and their boundaries. "Do not delete production data" is vague. "Production database commands are read-only unless a human has approved the exact migration" is an operational control. Agents are powerful precisely because they can use tools; instructions should reduce blast radius, not merely ask the model to be cautious.

For a deeper look at those security boundaries, see my guide to AI agents, MCP, and the next supply-chain risk.
code:
For authorization changes, add a regression test for the unauthorized path.
Do not approve a change that widens access based only on a happy-path manual test.
Ask the agent to think extremely carefully five times before modifying auth.

sections.heading: Instructions are not a substitute for tests
sections.text:
This distinction matters more as the files get better. AGENTS.md is a steering layer. Tests, types, linters, CI checks, permissions, and code review are the enforcement layer.

An instruction can tell an agent to preserve a response shape. A contract test is what catches the accidental change. An instruction can tell an agent not to weaken authorization. A permission boundary and a regression test are what make the rule credible.

That is also why agents reward well-maintained projects unevenly. A repository with fast tests, crisp boundaries, and useful docs gives an agent short feedback loops. A repository with no checks gives it a large space in which to be confidently wrong.

The practical loop is simple:

If an agent repeatedly misses the same rule, do not immediately add another paragraph of admonitions. First ask which layer failed:
Was the rule absent or hard to find? Improve the relevant instruction.
Was the rule clear but not testable? Add a guardrail or regression test.
Was the task too broad? Break it into a smaller handoff.
Was the agent allowed to touch too much? Narrow permissions or isolate the environment.

That diagnosis produces a system improvement. A larger prompt usually produces only a larger prompt.
code:
Clear instruction → small change → automated check → reviewable diff
        ↑                                            │
        └──────── update the guide when it teaches you something new ─┘

sections.heading: Treat the file like production code
sections.text:
The best way to maintain agent instructions is to edit them when reality changes, not during an annual documentation drive.

Add a line when a production incident reveals a non-obvious invariant. Remove a line when the rule is duplicated elsewhere or no longer true. Review instruction changes in pull requests with the same skepticism you bring to CI changes, because they alter how future automated contributors will behave.

Three useful questions for every addition:

1. Would a new human engineer make a worse decision without this? If not, it probably does not belong in shared instructions.
2. Can I make this rule observable? Prefer a command, path, test, or interface over an adjective.
3. Is this global, local, or task-specific? Put it in the narrowest place that will still be discovered.

The syntax is not the point. Whether your team standardizes on AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or a vendor-specific instruction path, the useful content is remarkably portable. That portability is the opportunity: write down the engineering knowledge that should outlive a tool choice.

sections.heading: The real moat is legible engineering
sections.text:
Coding agents will keep getting cheaper, faster, and more autonomous. GitHub has already added model selection, self-review, security scanning, custom agents, and CLI handoff to its coding agent. The agent itself is becoming a commodity feature.

The durable advantage is a codebase that can be safely understood by a new contributor—human or artificial—without oral history, detective work, or a week of Slack archaeology.

AGENTS.md will not make a bad architecture good. It will not replace a test suite. It will not turn a vague product request into a correct implementation. But it gives every future agent a running start, and it forces a healthy question onto the team: could someone safely change this system if you were not online to explain it?

That is not an AI question. It is the oldest software-engineering question there is. The agents just made it impossible to ignore.

---

Sources: Anthropic — _Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise_, OpenAI — _Unrolling the Codex agent loop_, GitHub Docs — support for custom instructions, GitHub Docs — Copilot CLI customization guidance, Anthropic Docs — Claude Code memory, and GitHub Blog — updates to Copilot coding agent.

ai-agents-killed-junior-developer-jobs.title: AI Agents Didn't Kill Junior Developer Jobs. They Killed the Reason to Hire Them.
ai-agents-killed-junior-developer-jobs.description: Entry-level engineering postings are down 20-35% while AI/ML roles rose 163%. What actually killed junior developer hiring and how to stay employable.

sections.text:
Here's a contradiction nobody in tech wants to say out loud: 92% of companies plan to hire this year, and entry-level engineering postings have collapsed 20-35% globally over the same stretch. Google and Meta are hiring roughly half as many new grads as they did in 2021. At Big Tech overall, new grads now make up about 7% of hires, down from 32% in 2019.

Both of those things are true at once. That's not a hiring freeze. It's a hiring _rewrite_ — and if you're a junior developer, or you manage a team of them, you need to understand exactly what got rewritten, because "learn to code" was never the part that was fragile.

sections.heading: The jobs didn't disappear. The task list did.
sections.text:
The honest mechanical reason is unglamorous: there is no economic incentive to hire a junior engineer who takes three days to do what an agent finishes in three minutes. Boilerplate, CRUD scaffolding, simple bug fixes, first-draft docs, "implement this well-specified ticket" — that entire category of work is exactly what coding agents are good at today, and it also happens to be exactly the category of work junior engineers used to cut their teeth on. It wasn't busywork. It was the training pipeline. And it just got automated out from under the people who needed it.

Meanwhile the postings that _are_ growing tell the other half of the story. AI/ML engineering now leads every hiring category, up 163% year over year, with 500,000+ open roles globally and roughly 3.4 open AI roles per qualified candidate. AI skill requirements now show up in 73% of U.S. tech job postings, up from 71% the month before, and up 192% year-over-year. Demand for engineers didn't fall. Demand for a specific, cheap kind of engineering labor did.

sections.heading: Nobody's hiring "coders" anymore. They're hiring supervisors.
sections.text:
Fortune profiled this shift back in March as the rise of what they called "the supervisor class" — engineers whose primary value is no longer writing the code, but orchestrating the agents that write it, reviewing what comes out, and making the architectural calls that decide whether the whole system holds together. That's not a euphemism for "manager." It's a genuinely different skill:
Context design — structuring a codebase, its docs, and its interfaces so an agent can actually operate inside it without hallucinating half the API surface.
Agent orchestration — defining roles, tool access, and hand-off rules when multiple agents are working a task in parallel, which is now commanding premium comp precisely because almost nobody can do it well yet.
Validation judgment — knowing _when_ AI output is right, when it's confidently wrong, and being able to explain the difference to a security reviewer or a product owner.

Hiring managers have quietly updated the interview script to match. The question isn't "have you used Copilot or Cursor" anymore — everyone has. It's "when do you choose _not_ to use it, and how do you verify what it gave you." Engineers who can answer that with a real story are being hired over engineers who can't, at every level, junior included.

sections.heading: So what do you actually do with this?
sections.text:
If you're early-career, the uncomfortable truth is that the old apprenticeship path — get hired, get assigned small well-defined tickets, build judgment slowly — is narrower than it was three years ago. The counter isn't to avoid AI tools; it's the opposite. Show up already fluent, and spend your visible effort on the 20% of the job an agent still can't do for you: reading a vague requirement and turning it into a real spec, catching the security implication nobody wrote down, deciding whether the fast path is the right path. That's the part hiring managers are explicitly screening for right now, and it's learnable faster than "years of experience" implies.

If you're senior or hiring, the leverage move is the same one that always wins in a platform shift: don't compete on typing speed, compete on judgment. The engineers commanding the new premium aren't the ones who adopted the tools fastest — they're the ones who can tell you, with specifics, where the tools stop being trustworthy.

The market isn't shrinking. It's re-pricing a skill that used to be scarce — writing code — now that it's cheap, and re-pricing a skill that used to be implicit — judgment about code — now that it's the whole job.

---

Sources: The Pragmatic Engineer — State of the Software Engineering Job Market 2026, Dice Tech Job Report, June 2026, The New Stack — "AI is disrupting everything": Where do entry-level tech jobs go now?, IEEE Spectrum — How to Stay Ahead of AI as an Early-Career Engineer, KORE1 — Agentic AI Engineering Hiring Survey 2026, Fortune's March 2026 profile on engineering's "supervisor class."

ai-agents-mcp-security-crisis.title: What I Learned About AI Agents, MCP, and the Next Supply Chain Risk
ai-agents-mcp-security-crisis.description: AI coding agents now make real tool calls. What I learned about MCP, prompt injection, stolen credentials, and securing agentic development workflows.

sections.text:
The thing I underestimated about AI coding tools is not how fast they can write code.

It is how quickly they are becoming part of the execution path.

For the last few years, most developers treated AI assistants like smarter autocomplete. The assistant suggested a function, explained an error, generated a test, or helped refactor a component. That workflow had risk, but the boundary was still clear: the AI produced text, and the developer decided what to run.

That boundary is changing.

AI agents can now read repositories, inspect issues, call tools, run tests, modify files, open pull requests, and connect to external systems through protocols like MCP. Once an AI system can use tools, the security question changes completely.

The risk is no longer only:

"Did the model generate incorrect code?"

The risk becomes:

"What is this agent allowed to do, what can influence it, and where can data flow after it acts?"

That is the lesson I took away from looking at the current AI agent ecosystem: AI coding is becoming a software supply chain problem.

sections.heading: Why This Changed My Mental Model
sections.text:
Stack Overflow's 2025 Developer Survey shows the contradiction developers are living with. AI tool adoption reached 80%, but trust in AI accuracy dropped to 29%. The survey also found that 66% of developers spend more time fixing "almost-right" AI-generated code, and 52% say AI agents have already changed how they complete work.

That combination matters.

Developers are using AI more, trusting it less, and still moving toward workflows where AI has more agency. That is a strange place to be. It means the tools are useful enough to become normal, but unreliable enough that we need stronger engineering discipline around them.

The mistake is thinking the main issue is hallucination.

Hallucination is annoying. A tool-connected agent with excessive permissions is dangerous.

Bad code can fail tests. A badly constrained agent can read secrets, call APIs, mutate infrastructure, publish data, or create a pull request that changes how CI behaves.

That is a different class of problem.

sections.heading: What MCP Actually Is
sections.text:
MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a standard way for AI applications to connect to tools and data sources.

The simple explanation is:

MCP lets AI agents use external capabilities without every AI app needing a custom integration for every tool.

An MCP server can expose:
tools, such as reading files, querying a database, creating GitHub issues, running kubectl, or searching internal docs;
resources, such as tickets, logs, source files, metrics, design docs, or API references;
prompts and templates that guide how the model should use those capabilities.

Anthropic donated MCP to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025. At that point, Anthropic said MCP had crossed 10,000 active public servers and had been adopted across products including ChatGPT, Cursor, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Visual Studio Code, and other AI tools.

That adoption tells us something important: MCP is not a niche plugin format anymore. It is becoming a common integration layer for agentic software.

And every integration layer eventually becomes a security boundary.

sections.heading: The Old Supply Chain vs. The Agent Supply Chain
What Made Me Take MCP Security Seriously
sections.text:
The security research around MCP is still young, but the pattern is already clear.

OWASP now has an MCP Security Cheat Sheet. OWASP also documents MCP tool poisoning as a specific attack pattern. OX Security published MCP research in April 2026 claiming a broad supply-chain issue affecting 150M+ downloads and up to 200,000 vulnerable instances. On May 12, 2026, OX followed with additional MCP-related findings in tools such as kubectl-mcp-server, Archon OS, and MarkItDown.

Security vendor research should always be read with healthy skepticism. Headlines can overstate. Numbers can depend on assumptions. But the underlying concern is real:

AI agents are connecting to tools faster than teams are defining permissions, audit trails, sandboxing, and review practices.

That is how normal developer convenience turns into infrastructure risk.

sections.heading: Attack Pattern 1: Tool Poisoning
sections.text:
Tool poisoning is what changed my view of agent security the most.

A normal application calls an API and receives data. An AI agent calls a tool and receives data that may become part of its reasoning context.

That difference matters.

If a malicious or compromised MCP server can influence the model through tool descriptions, schemas, or responses, the server may not need direct access to the most sensitive system. It can try to persuade the agent to use another tool that has stronger permissions.

For example:

1. A documentation tool returns a normal-looking answer with hidden or indirect instructions.
2. The agent treats the tool response as useful context.
3. The agent then calls a GitHub, filesystem, shell, Slack, or database tool.
4. Sensitive data leaves through a tool call that looks legitimate in isolation.

This is why prompt injection becomes more serious in agentic systems. The injected text is not just trying to change an answer. It may be trying to change a sequence of actions.

That is the part developers need to internalize.

Prompt injection against a chatbot is a content integrity issue. Prompt injection against a tool-using agent can become an authorization issue.

sections.heading: Attack Pattern 2: The Confused Deputy
sections.text:
The confused deputy problem is old, but agents make it easy to recreate.

Imagine a user asks an agent to summarize an internal document. The agent uses an MCP server that has broad access to many systems. The user may not have permission to read everything the MCP server can read, but the tool acts with its own credentials.

Now the agent is not acting with the user's authority. It is acting with the tool's authority.

That is dangerous because the user interface hides the privilege boundary.

The developer sees:

"Summarize this."

The system may actually perform:

"Use a broadly scoped service token to search internal docs, tickets, repositories, and messages, then decide what context is relevant."

If the server does not enforce user-scoped authorization, the agent can become a path around the permission model.

The fix is not glamorous: least privilege, user-scoped auth where possible, short-lived tokens, and separate credentials per tool. Boring security controls become very interesting when the thing using the credential is non-deterministic.

sections.heading: Attack Pattern 3: Local Tool Access
Attack Pattern 4: Pull Requests as Execution Vehicles
The Mistake I See Coming
The Security Model I Would Use
sections.text:
The most useful mental model I found is this:
An AI agent is a process with a probabilistic planner and a tool belt. Secure the process, the tool belt, and the data paths between them.

That gives us three questions.

First: what can the agent observe?

Can it read the whole repository? Can it read .env files? Can it inspect private docs? Can it see customer data? Can it read tickets that contain credentials or internal URLs?

Second: what can the agent do?

Can it write files? Run shell commands? Install packages? Open pull requests? Send Slack messages? Query production? Deploy? Delete resources?

Third: what can influence the agent?

Can issue comments, docs, README files, logs, web pages, dependency output, or tool responses change what it does next?

That third question is easy to forget. In normal software, untrusted input might break a parser or alter a query. In agentic software, untrusted input can alter the plan.

sections.heading: My Practical Checklist
sections.text: If I were adding AI agents and MCP tools to a development workflow, I would start with this checklist.

sections.heading: 1. Inventory Every Tool
2. Use Narrow Credentials
3. Sandbox Local Servers
4. Separate Read, Write, and Release
5. Make Tool Calls Visible
6. Review Tool Definitions Like Code
sections.text:
Tool names, descriptions, schemas, and prompts shape model behavior.

That means they should be reviewed.

Pin versions. Diff updates. Avoid vague tools that accept arbitrary commands. Prefer small tools with clear parameters. Watch for tool description changes that alter how the agent is instructed to behave.

This feels strange only because the industry is still learning that prompts and tool schemas are executable influence.

sections.heading: 7. Log Enough To Debug Incidents
The Individual Developer Version
The Team Version
What I Believe Now
sections.text:
I do not think AI agents should be banned from development workflows.

I think they should be treated honestly.

They are not just autocomplete. They are not just chat. They are becoming tool-using development processes that sit inside the same systems we use to build, test, review, and ship software.

That makes them useful.

It also makes them part of the supply chain.

The teams that handle this well will not be the teams that connect every possible tool to every possible model. They will be the teams that make agent work observable, scoped, reversible, and reviewable.

That is the real lesson for me:

AI agents are not dangerous because they are intelligent. They are dangerous when they are connected to powerful tools without clear boundaries.

Boundaries are the product work now.

sections.text:

GitHub Docs: About Copilot cloud agent
OWASP MCP Security Cheat Sheet
OWASP MCP Tool Poisoning
OX Security: The Architectural Flaw at the Core of Anthropic's MCP
