building-focustube-typesafe-jev.title: Building FocusTube with TypeSafe Jev
building-focustube-typesafe-jev.description: How I built FocusTube, a browser extension that turns YouTube into a strict learning feed, using Jev decision scores, a Worker, and local decision caching.

sections.text:
YouTube is one of my best sources for programming tutorials, conference talks, and interview preparation. It is also very good at placing a Short, a product launch, or an unrelated recommendation beside the thing I opened it to learn.

I wanted a stricter interface: show a recommendation only when it is clearly useful for coding, software engineering, studying, or professional upskilling. Hide everything uncertain. Do it before the card flashes on screen.

That became FocusTube, an open-source Chrome and Firefox extension powered by Jev, TypeSafe AI’s first System One model.

 

This is a small project, but it captures a useful AI engineering pattern: let the model make one semantic judgment and keep every product decision in ordinary code.

sections.heading: The decision was the product
sections.text:
The first version did not need summaries, generated recommendations, or a chat interface. It needed an answer to one question:
Is this video directly useful for focused learning or career upskilling?

A keyword list looked tempting. It also failed quickly. “React” can mean a React tutorial or a reaction video. “AI” appears in research lectures, product announcements, hype, and entertainment. A channel name helps, but it is not enough to classify every video from that channel.

A general LLM could return yes or no, but then I would need to constrain and parse its response, handle malformed output, and decide how much to trust an unexplained binary answer. FocusTube needed a calibrated score it could compare with a threshold.

That maps directly to TypeSafe’s Noul primitive. A Noul evaluates a yes-or-no question and returns the probability that the answer is yes:

No generated explanation enters the product path. 0.91 is data. The extension can reveal the card at a threshold of 0.82, hide it at 0.61, and let the user raise or lower that boundary.

sections.heading: Why System One fit
sections.text:
TypeSafe System One models are built for fast, structured decisions. Jev accepts natural-language state and returns typed answers with probabilities instead of prose and reasoning.

That distinction gave each part of FocusTube one job:
Jev owns semantic judgment. It reads the title, channel, and YouTube surface and estimates whether the video fits the learning policy.
Code applies the policy. The extension defines the threshold, caching, fail-closed behavior, pause control, and which YouTube surfaces are in scope.
The browser handles presentation. Cards stay concealed until code has enough evidence to reveal them.

The model is not an autonomous agent. It cannot decide to navigate, block a channel, or alter settings. Its full authority is one probability for one named question.

sections.heading: Architecture
sections.text:
FocusTube has two deployable pieces: a Manifest V3 extension and a Cloudflare Worker.

 

The extension watches YouTube’s home feed, search results, and watch-page recommendations. When YouTube adds cards to the page, FocusTube:

1. Conceals each new card.
2. Extracts its title, channel, and current surface.
3. Hides Shorts locally without calling the model.
4. Checks a seven-day browser cache.
5. Sends uncached records to the Worker in batches of at most twenty.
6. Reveals only cards whose probability meets the configured threshold.

The content script does not ship with a TypeSafe API key. It calls the user’s Worker with a separate extension token. The Worker validates the request, builds typed questions, calls jev-latest, and returns only the probabilities the UI needs.

sections.heading: One state, several narrow questions
sections.text:
TypeSafe can evaluate several questions against one state in a request. FocusTube uses that to classify a batch without turning the task into one vague, multi-video answer.

The Worker sends the videos as structured state:

It then creates one Noul question for each array position:

The API call stays direct and inspectable:

Each answer comes back under the same key as its question. The Worker maps answers.video_0.noul to the first video and returns a compact result to the extension.

sections.heading: Strict means fail closed
sections.text:
The default threshold is 0.82. That number is a product control, not a claim that every result above it is correct. TypeSafe describes probabilities as calibrated across groups of predictions; an individual prediction can still be wrong.

The two classification errors do not cost the same:
A false positive puts a distraction back into the feed.
A false negative hides a useful recommendation that remains available through direct navigation, subscriptions, history, or a less strict threshold.

For this product, the second failure is cheaper. So an unavailable Worker, a malformed response, or a low probability keeps an unclassified card hidden. The toolbar makes the strictness visible and gives the user a pause switch when they want the original feed back.

I would not reuse that policy blindly. A moderation queue, accessibility tool, or high-stakes workflow may have very different error costs. Probability is useful because application code can express those costs instead of pretending every result is equally certain.

sections.heading: Preventing the flash of distraction
sections.text:
Classification would feel broken if an entertainment thumbnail appeared for half a second and then vanished. The content script marks discovered cards as pending before network work starts:

A MutationObserver rescans as YouTube updates its client-rendered page. Cached decisions resolve immediately. New records wait for their batch. A card receives the visible class only after its probability clears the threshold.

This makes model latency less important to the interface. Users see a feed fill with accepted material rather than watching rejected cards disappear.

sections.heading: Shorts do not need AI
sections.text:
FocusTube blocks Shorts by URL and YouTube renderer type:

That check is deterministic, cheap, and more reliable than asking a model whether a known Short should be hidden. Shorts never enter a TypeSafe request.

This is an important boundary when adding AI to software: use the model only where normal code cannot make the decision cleanly. DOM structure can identify a Short. Semantic relevance needs Jev.

sections.heading: Keeping secrets outside the extension
sections.text:
Browser extensions are distributed client code. Anything bundled with one should be treated as public. The TypeSafe API key therefore lives only in the Cloudflare Worker’s secret store.

The extension uses a separate, user-configured token to authenticate to its Worker. This is not a perfect identity system—the local user can inspect their own token—but it prevents an unauthenticated public Worker URL from becoming free access to someone else’s TypeSafe quota.

The Worker also enforces small input boundaries:
One to twenty videos per request
Title capped at 300 characters
Channel capped at 200 characters
Surface capped at 40 characters
Only the expected route and methods accepted

FocusTube sends no YouTube cookies, account identity, watch history, comments, or transcript. The model sees the visible metadata needed for the judgment and nothing else.

sections.heading: Caching changed both speed and cost
sections.text:
Recommendation cards repeat. Search results reappear. YouTube can rerender the same card during navigation. Calling Jev each time would add avoidable latency and spend.

The extension stores each probability in localStorage, keyed by normalized title and channel, for seven days. It caches the probability rather than the final boolean. If the user raises the threshold from 0.82 to 0.90, FocusTube can reapply the stricter policy without another model call.

There is a tradeoff: a title can change, and channel-plus-title is not a permanent video identifier. For this first version, it is available across the card types in scope and degrades safely. A future version can prefer YouTube’s video ID when every supported renderer exposes it consistently.

sections.heading: What I would test next
sections.text:
The repository contains a working implementation, not a published accuracy benchmark. Before treating its defaults as settled, I would create a labeled evaluation set from real recommendations and measure:

1. Precision at several thresholds, especially how much entertainment leaks through.
2. Recall for coding, system design, academic, and career-preparation subsets.
3. Disagreements around tech news, conference keynotes, and career commentary.
4. Latency and cache-hit rate across home, search, and watch sessions.
5. DOM selector breakage as YouTube changes renderers.

Those results could justify separate policies by surface. Search intent may tolerate a lower threshold than the home feed. Watch recommendations may benefit from the current video’s metadata as extra state. Both are measurable changes; neither requires replacing the architecture.

sections.heading: What this project taught me
sections.text:
The useful part of AI here is not generated content. It is the semantic branch ordinary code could not write:

Everything around that line remains conventional software engineering: narrow inputs, explicit authority, secret isolation, caching, failure policy, browser state, and a control the user can understand.

That is why Jev worked well for FocusTube. It returned exactly the missing primitive—a typed judgment with a probability—and stopped there.

The full extension and Worker are available in the FocusTube repository. TypeSafe’s System One documentation and API reference cover the model and response contracts used here.
code: const visible = probability >= threshold;

building-mcp-server-typescript.title: Building an MCP Server in TypeScript: From Zero to Tool-Calling Agent in 90 Minutes
building-mcp-server-typescript.description: Build an MCP server in TypeScript from zero to a tool-calling agent in 90 minutes: the official SDK, real tools, and production lessons learned.

sections.heading: TL;DR
sections.text:
MCP is the missing layer between "an LLM that can talk" and "an LLM that can do." It is a tiny, well-designed protocol that turns any tool you already have into something Claude, Cursor, OpenCode, and a dozen other hosts can call as if it were a native function. If you can write a TypeScript function, you can ship an MCP server today. I built one in 90 minutes last weekend. This is the exact walkthrough — including the parts that bit me, the parts that surprised me, and the one architectural decision I think is going to define how agentic systems are built over the next 18 months.

By the end of this post you will have:
A working MCP server with 3 tools, 2 resources, and 1 prompt
Type-safe inputs via Zod (no more "the LLM sent me garbage" debugging)
A streaming progress channel so the agent can report "I am 60% done" mid-call
A deployment path from bun run dev to a hosted endpoint anyone can install

Let's go.

sections.heading: What MCP actually is (and what it isn't)
sections.text:
MCP — the Model Context Protocol — is Anthropic's open standard for connecting LLMs to tools. It hit 1.0 in late 2025, and the spec is refreshingly small: JSON-RPC 2.0, three primitives (tools, resources, prompts), and a stdio or HTTP transport. That's it.

What it isn't: a replacement for function calling. Your OpenAI tools= array still works. MCP is the _server_ side of that conversation. Instead of hard-coding tool definitions into every agent script you write, you publish a server, register it in your host, and every LLM that can see it gets the same capabilities.

 
 
 
 The host (Claude, Cursor, OpenCode) holds the LLM. Your TypeScript server holds the tools. They
 speak JSON-RPC over stdio or HTTP.
 
 

The reason this matters more than "yet another API spec" is the direction of leverage. The first time you build an MCP server, you are doing it for _your_ workflow. The second time, you start noticing the same patterns — auth, rate limiting, observability — and they look like every other API you have ever built. By the third server, you realize MCP is just a really nice contract for "give an LLM a typed handle to a real-world capability." Once that clicks, the design space opens up fast.

sections.heading: Why TypeScript, specifically
sections.text:
I get asked this constantly. The honest answer: the SDK is most mature in TypeScript, Zod gives you runtime-validated inputs that match the LLM's JSON Schema output almost 1:1, and you almost certainly already have Node on whatever machine you are reading this on.

If you are a Python shop, the official Python SDK is fine. If you are Go or Rust, you are early. For the next 12 months, MCP server development is going to look a lot like a Node.js ecosystem in 2014 — fast-moving, full of examples, and forgiving of messy code.

sections.heading: Step 1: Scaffold in 60 seconds
sections.text:
That is the entire dependency tree. No express, no body-parser, no nothing. The SDK ships its own transport.
No Bun? No problem. Every snippet in this post runs on Node.js 22+ via npx tsx. The starter repo ships dev:node and dev:node:http scripts as drop-in replacements. If you do not have Bun, swap bun run dev for npx tsx src/index.ts everywhere.
code:
mkdir my-mcp-server && cd my-mcp-server
bun init -y
bun add @modelcontextprotocol/sdk zod

sections.heading: Step 2: The 30-line server that exposes one tool
sections.text:
This is the smallest useful MCP server I could write that still does something real — a tool that converts JSON to a TypeScript interface. Useful for exactly one workflow, and a great template to copy.

server.tool() is the entire API for registering a tool. You give it a name, a description the LLM reads, a Zod schema for inputs, and an async handler. That is the whole shape.

Run it:

Wire it into Claude Desktop or Cursor and the LLM now has access to json_to_interface as a native capability. It will call it, your handler runs, the response streams back, the LLM uses it. You just built an agent.
code: bun run dev

sections.heading: Step 3: The three primitives — when to use which
sections.text:
After about a dozen servers, the decision tree for which primitive to use stopped being obvious to me. Here is the rule I landed on:

| Primitive | Use it when | Example |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Tool | The LLM should _decide_ to call this based on user intent | create_issue, search_docs, deploy_preview |
| Resource | The LLM should _always have access_ to this data | file://src/index.ts, db://schema |
| Prompt | The user explicitly types /something to trigger a workflow | /review-pr, /release-notes, /triage |

The mistake I keep seeing in early MCP servers: everything is a tool. That is wrong. Tools are for _the LLM's discretion_. If you want the LLM to always see the current branch name, expose it as a resource. If you want the user to opt in to a structured workflow, expose it as a prompt. Mixing these up is the #1 reason early MCP servers feel clunky.

sections.heading: Step 4: The thing nobody tells you — Zod is your security boundary
sections.text:
This is the spicy take. When an LLM calls your tool, you are letting a model execute code in your process. Zod is not just a typescript convenience — it is the _only_ line of defense between "the model sent you what you expected" and "the model sent you { "json": "process.exit(1)" } because some prompt injection told it to."

Always validate. Always narrow. Never trust the description to be enough.

I learned this the hard way. I shipped a server last month where I skipped Zod on a "trust me, it's a string" field. A user pasted a JSON payload that contained a proto key. My handler spread it into an options object. RCE on day one. Do not be like me. Zod everything.

 
 
 
 The 6-step request flow. Notice 95% of the latency is step 2 — the LLM itself. Your server
 budget is ~5ms. Spend it on validation, not optimization.

sections.heading: Step 5: Streaming progress (the killer feature)
sections.text:
Here is the part that surprised me most. MCP supports _progress notifications_. Your tool can stream "I am 40% done" back to the host, and the LLM can relay that to the user as it happens. This is what makes a 30-second tool feel responsive instead of broken.
Heads up on the query_sqlite tool — it uses node:sqlite, which is stable on Node 22.5+ and on Bun. On older Node versions, swap the body for a better-sqlite3 call and the rest of the server keeps working unchanged. The starter repo's query_sqlite tool ships with a clear error message if your runtime is too old, so you will know immediately.

I have a long-running deploy_preview tool that uses this. Before, the LLM would call it and the user would stare at a spinner for 45 seconds. Now they see "Building… 20%… 40%… uploading… 80%… done." The UX upgrade is enormous and the code change is 5 lines.

sections.heading: Step 6: The one architectural decision that matters
sections.text:
When you go to ship your server, you have two transport choices:
stdio — your server runs as a child process of the host. Zero network, zero auth, zero ops. Perfect for local dev tools.
Streamable HTTP — your server is a normal HTTP endpoint. Auth, rate limiting, observability, multi-tenant. Required for hosted, shareable servers.

Start with stdio. Move to HTTP the day someone _other than you_ needs to install your server. Premature HTTP is the MCP equivalent of premature microservices — you will spend a week on auth before you have a user.

That is a production-deployed MCP server. You can put that behind nginx, add a /health route, and you are live.

sections.heading: The honest list of things that are still rough
sections.text:
I am going to keep being real with you, because that is what you come here for:

1. Auth is under-specified. The spec is silent on OAuth flow. Everyone is rolling their own. Until this lands, assume any HTTP MCP server you run in production is wide-open.
2. Observability is bad. Logs go to stderr. There is no OpenTelemetry story. If you need to debug "why did the LLM call this 400 times," you are reading console.log lines.
3. SDK churn is real. The McpServer class API has had three breaking changes in 6 months. Pin your version.
4. The ecosystem is moving fast. A pattern that works today may be deprecated next month. Subscribe to the spec repo before you ship anything you cannot rewrite in a week.

sections.heading: Where I think this is going
sections.text:
My honest read of where agentic systems land by end of 2027:
MCP becomes the "npm of tools." You install a server the way you install a package. The discovery problem gets solved by a central registry.
The tool/resource/prompt split hardens. AIs that pick the wrong primitive get less usage. The hosts that enforce the split correctly win.
Most "agent frameworks" shrink to thin wrappers around MCP. If the protocol is good, the orchestration layer doesn't need to be 50k stars.
TypeScript wins the server-side race. Python catches up in tooling, Go/Rust in hot paths, but TS is the default for 24 months.

If you are a full-stack dev in 2026 and you have not built an MCP server yet, you are leaving leverage on the table. It is the highest-leverage 90 minutes you can spend this month. Pick the most boring tool in your daily workflow — a deploy script, a Jira lookup, a SQL query — and ship it as an MCP server. The second one is where it gets fun. The fifth one is where you stop writing glue code entirely.

sections.heading: The full repo
sections.text:
Every snippet in this post lives in a runnable repo: github.com/piyush97/mcp-server-typescript-starter. Clone it, bun install (or npm install), bun run dev (or npm run dev:node), wire it into Claude Desktop. You are 90 minutes from your first tool call.

The repo contains everything the article hints at but does not show in full:
All 3 tools wired up — json_to_interface, fetch_url, and the query_sqlite tool with the streaming progress callout from Step 5
Both transports — src/index.ts (stdio) and src/http.ts (Streamable HTTP) for the Step 6 deployment path
Both resources — file://README.md and git://status, the always-available LLM context
The /review-pr prompt — copy-paste ready, with the full review template
A real JSON-to-TypeScript inference engine in src/json-to-ts.ts — unions, nested objects, arrays, optional fields. Not the toy version from Step 2

If you only have 30 minutes, read Step 1, Step 2, and Step 4, then clone the repo. The remaining concepts (resources, prompts, streaming, HTTP transport) are all in the working code with comments.

If you ship something cool with this — or hit a wall I did not anticipate — my DMs are open. I am collecting real-world MCP server patterns and writing a follow-up. The next one is on multi-tenant auth, which is the part everyone is going to need six months from now and nobody is talking about today.

Now go build the boring thing. The boring thing is where the leverage lives.

chat-bot.title: 🔥 A Beginner’s Guide to ChatGPT and Ai based Chat bot solutions for individuals and enterprise
chat-bot.description: Creating a ChatGPT-like bot using Azure Bot SDK and Typescript can provide many benefits for your business

sections.text:
Creating a ChatGPT-like bot using Azure Bot SDK and Typescript can provide many benefits for your business. A conversational bot can improve customer service by providing fast and accurate responses to common questions, freeing up time for your customer support team to focus on more complex tasks. It can also automate routine tasks and make your services available 24/7, regardless of location or device. In this blog post, we'll explore how you can create a ChatGPT-like bot using Azure Bot SDK and Typescript, with or without coding.

Azure Bot SDK is a powerful development framework that makes it easy to create and deploy chatbots on Azure. With Azure Bot SDK, you can create bots in various programming languages, including Typescript. Typescript is a statically typed superset of JavaScript that offers improved type safety and code maintainability compared to JavaScript.

To create a ChatGPT-like bot using Azure Bot SDK and Typescript, you can either write the code yourself or use a no-code solution. If you're familiar with coding, you can use the Azure Bot Service, an end-to-end development tool that makes it easy to create and deploy bots. With Azure Bot Service, you can use the Typescript language to create your bot and take advantage of the Bot Framework SDK's many features, such as the ability to handle conversations, recognize and respond to user input, and connect to other services.

If you're new to coding or prefer not to write code, there's still a way to create a ChatGPT-like bot using Azure Bot SDK and Typescript. The Azure Bot Service provides a no-code solution that allows you to create and deploy bots using a visual interface. This means that you can create your bot without writing any code, simply by connecting pre-built modules and adding your own custom logic.

Regardless of whether you choose to write code or use the no-code solution, the Azure Bot Service provides a high level of security for your bot. Your bot's communication with users is encrypted by default, and you can use Azure Active Directory to control access to your bot's data. This means that you can rest easy knowing that your bot is secure and that your users' information is protected.

Another key benefit of using the Azure Bot Service is its ability to make complex tasks easier. With the Azure Bot Service, you can use pre-built connectors and integrations to quickly connect your bot to other services, such as databases, email, and more. This means that you can create a bot that can handle a wide range of tasks, from answering simple questions to processing complex transactions.

In conclusion, creating a ChatGPT-like bot using Azure Bot SDK and Typescript can bring many benefits to your business, whether you choose to write code or use the no-code solution. With Azure Bot Service, you can create a highly secure and feature-rich chatbot that can improve customer service, automate routine tasks, and make your services available 24/7. Whether you're a seasoned developer or new to coding, the Azure Bot Service provides all the tools you need to create a ChatGPT-like bot that meets your business needs.

claude-sonnet-5-5.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5 Beats Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench at Half the Price
claude-sonnet-5-5.description: Sonnet 5.5 beats Opus 5.5 by 4.2 points on Terminal-Bench at half the token price. The benchmark caveat, real cost trade-off, and migration traps.

sections.text:
Anthropic launched Claude Sonnet 5.5 today, and one number stands out: 70.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, versus 66.4% for Opus 5.5 at twice the price per token. Sonnet 5 scored 10.3%.

That's a 4.2-point lead on one agentic terminal benchmark, not proof that Sonnet is better at every task or cheaper per successful task. Anthropic ran the Opus result at Xhigh effort; the models' settings and task costs matter. Still, a mid-tier model ahead of the flagship on terminal work is worth a closer look.

Everything below comes from Anthropic's announcement and the model docs. These are Anthropic's own benchmark numbers. I haven't run independent tests yet.

The practical call: Try Sonnet 5.5 at Medium effort on repeatable coding tasks; keep Opus 5.5 for work that needs sustained judgment. If you're upgrading an API integration, read the migration section first: some settings now error, and between-tool text can disappear without one.

sections.heading: The specs
sections.text:
| | Sonnet 5.5 |
| ---------------- | ------------------- |
| Model ID | claude-sonnet-5-5 |
| Context window | 1M tokens |
| Max output | 128K tokens |
| Input | $2 / MTok |
| Output | $10 / MTok |
| Cache read | $0.20 / MTok |
| Knowledge cutoff | Jun 2026 |

Pricing is the same as Sonnet 5. The savings come from token use. Sonnet 5.5 needs fewer tokens per task, so Anthropic says cost per task is up to 30% lower. Output is also 30%+ faster.

It's on the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS. Zero data retention is supported.

sections.heading: The benchmarks
sections.text:
Scores below are Sonnet 5.5 / Sonnet 5 / Opus 5.5:

| Benchmark | Sonnet 5.5 | Sonnet 5 | Opus 5.5 |
| ---------------------------- | ---------- | -------- | -------- |
| Terminal-Bench 4.0 | 70.6% | 10.3% | 66.4% |
| CursorBench 4.0 | 55.5% | 34.1% | 57.8% |
| OSWorld 2.1 | 80.1% | 57.0% | 81.8% |
| Humanity's Last Exam (tools) | 64.5% | 54.9% | 67.7% |
| Chartography (no tools) | 61.6% | 15.6% | 64.4% |
| GDPval-AA v2.1 (Elo) | 1844 | 1449 | 1846 |

Opus 5.5 still wins most rows, usually by a small margin. On GDPval-AA the gap is two Elo points. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 remains clearly better at complex, open-ended work, so it's not a straight replacement.

Sonnet 5.5 also beats GPT-6 Sol on the comparisons Anthropic published: 1844 vs 1487 on GDPval-AA, and 61.6% vs 53.6% on Chartography.

Two caveats from Anthropic's footnotes:
Artificial Analysis tested a pre-release build with a structured-outputs bug, since fixed. That may slightly understate its scores.
GPT-6 Sol scores may not reflect OpenAI's recent image-understanding fix. Terminal-Bench and CursorBench have no public GPT-6 Sol results, so those charts use GPT-5.6 Sol.

sections.heading: The cost story
sections.text:
The API token price is half of Opus 5.5's, but token price isn't task price. A model that takes more tokens or tool calls can erase that saving. Anthropic's cost-versus-score charts give a more useful comparison:
On several benchmarks at Low or Medium effort, it beats Sonnet 5's best score for about one tenth of the cost per task. On Terminal-Bench, Anthropic reports less than a tenth at Medium effort.
On FrontierCode at High effort, it scores 10 points above Sonnet 5 at about one fifteenth of the cost per task.
At higher effort settings, Anthropic says Sonnet 5.5 can perform comparably to Opus 5.5 at a similar cost per task.

Those are benchmark-specific comparisons, not a promise of 10x savings on your workload. Measure cost per completed task, not just the token rate.

Effort levels are now Low, Medium, High, Xhigh and Max. The default is Medium in Claude Code and the apps, and High on the Claude Platform.

sections.heading: What customers reported
sections.text:
These are Anthropic's paraphrased customer quotes, so treat them as vendor-curated.
Base44: across 118 app builds it matched Opus 5 quality in 3.6 iterations, versus 7.7 for Opus 5.
Balyasny: about 121k tokens per answer versus 497k for Sonnet 5.
Box: 2.4x faster with 12% fewer tokens.
Zendesk: tickets processed 20% faster.
Lovable: a third fewer tool calls and about half the shell runs.
CodeRabbit: better judgment with far fewer output tokens. It plans to move simple and moderate reviews over first.

Anthropic also says it's the first Sonnet to beat Pokémon Red from screenshots alone. It's a fun detail. It also tells you something about long-horizon visual tasks.

sections.heading: What breaks when you upgrade
sections.text:
If you're on Sonnet 5, read this before you swap the model ID. The docs list five breaking changes:

1. Turning off up-front thinking now uses between_tools. It works at High effort or below.
2. Forced tool use returns an error.
3. Thinking blocks are tied to the model and the conversation. Preserved thinking is also tied to the account that created it, so switching accounts mid-session matters.
4. computer_20251124 isn't accepted on the Claude API and Google Cloud.
5. The advisor tool rejects Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 5 as advisors.

There's also a quieter change. Text between tool calls now comes back in thinking blocks. If your app streams that text to users, it will go silent between tool calls until you set a display value that returns it, or turn off up-front thinking with between_tools. Nothing fails, so you won't get an error to warn you.

Also, setting temperature, top_p or top_k to a non-default value returns a 400 error.

Anthropic has a migration guide with the details.

sections.heading: Safety notes
sections.text:
Anthropic ran an automated audit of roughly 1,850 scenarios. Sonnet 5.5 matches or improves on Sonnet 5 on most alignment, misuse-resistance and honesty measures. On containment tests it comes close to Opus 5.5 at avoiding sandbox escape, and it is the least likely of any model to probe container limits.

Two policy changes to know about:
Cyber: it's the first Sonnet with Opus-style cyber safeguards. Higher-risk cyber tasks visibly fall back to Sonnet 5. Defenders can apply to an expanded Cyber Verification Program.
Distillation: it's the first Sonnet with classifiers that block reasoning extraction.

Anthropic found no evidence of goals that conflict with user intent. It also says its evaluations can't catch every failure.

sections.heading: Which model should you use?
sections.text:
My read, based on the published numbers:
Sonnet 5.5 is the default for agentic coding, terminal work, code review and high-volume workloads. It's fast, and it's half the price of Opus.
Opus 5.5 is for complex, open-ended work where the last few points matter.
Haiku 5.5 is coming in a few weeks. Anthropic hasn't said more.

Start on Sonnet 5.5 at Medium effort, measure success rate, latency and total cost on your own tasks, and move up where it fails. The half-price token rate alone doesn't settle the choice.

sections.heading: The takeaway
sections.text:
Shareable version: Sonnet 5.5 beats Opus 5.5 on Anthropic's Terminal-Bench 4.0 (70.6% vs 66.4%) at half the API token price. It doesn't beat Opus everywhere, and at high effort it might not cost less per task. Test it on your own work before switching.

I'll run it on real tasks from this site's repo and follow up with results.

context-management-agents.title: Why AI Coding Agents Fail at Long Tasks (And How to Fix It)
context-management-agents.description: Context window entropy and unconstrained decision loops fail 84% of multi-step agent tasks. The 2026 research, plus the architectural patterns that fix it.

sections.text:
84% of multi-step agent tasks fail when they exceed 15 consecutive loops. That number should worry anyone who has watched a coding agent "work" for an hour before hallucinating an invalid state transition.

The pattern is consistent across every major benchmark and production deployment: agents start strong, lose coherence as context fills, and degrade in ways that look like reasoning failures but are actually context management failures.

This is the research I wish I had read before shipping my last agent pipeline.

sections.heading: The Real Failure Mode
sections.text:
LLMs are probabilistic text predictors, not state machines. When a multi-step task exceeds context limits, agents experience context window entropy — the model's attention becomes diluted across accumulated intermediate chatter, and state drift — the agent's internal representation of the task diverges from reality.

 

A September 2026 ACL findings paper (StateComp) formalizes this: agents continuously accumulate interaction history during long-horizon tasks, but existing context management relies on fixed windows or passive compression heuristics. The result is context explosion, semantic drift, and degraded reasoning precisely when you need it most.

The practical symptom is familiar: an agent debugging a failure can't remember the original error trace because it got compressed too early, or it carries irrelevant history that masks the real failure signal.

sections.heading: Two Answers, Two Different Questions
sections.text: The 2026 work converges from two directions, and they are easier to apply when you keep them apart. CAT asks _what the context should contain_. StateComp asks _when it is safe to drop something_. Both train an imbalance-aware router, and both treat context maintenance as an explicit step rather than a background process.

sections.heading: The CAT Framework
sections.text:
Researchers at ACL 2026 proposed CAT (Context as a Tool) — a paradigm that elevates context maintenance to a callable tool integrated into the agent's decision-making process. Instead of background compression, CAT formalizes a structured context workspace with three layers:

 

The framework trains an imbalance-aware router on hidden representations from a frozen language model. Adjacent READY interactions are grouped into continuous spans and replaced with compact summaries during execution. On SWE-Bench Verified, the resulting SWE-Compressor reached 57.6% solved rate, significantly outperforming ReAct-based agents and static compression baselines while maintaining stable long-horizon reasoning under a bounded context budget.

sections.heading: StateComp: Compression with State Awareness
sections.text:
StateComp takes a different angle: _when_ is a past interaction safe to replace? Premature compression removes information still needed for future actions; overly conservative retention creates massive context overhead.

StateComp constructs KEEP and READY supervision through a two-stage annotation procedure and trains an imbalance-aware router. Experiments show it reduces total agent and summarization tokens by 52.27% while maintaining task performance, and achieves a 12.67× speedup in representation extraction.

sections.heading: What This Means for Your Agent Architecture
sections.text: The 2026 Anthropic Agentic Coding Trends Report identifies multi-agent coordination and human-AI collaboration patterns as the top foundation trends for the year. But the engineering reality is simpler: before you orchestrate agent teams, you need each individual agent to maintain coherence over long tasks.

sections.heading: The Uncomfortable Tradeoff
sections.text:
There is a tension between agent autonomy and reliability that no model update solves. More capable models delay the failure but don't prevent it — 84% failure on 15+ loop tasks is a structural problem, not a capability gap.

The agents that succeed in production are not the ones with the best model. They are the ones with the best context management.

The research is clear: treat context as a tool, not a container. Your agent's coherence depends on it.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.text:
StateComp: Learning When to Compress History in Long Horizon Agents — ACL 2026 findings paper on state-conditioned compression
Context as a Tool: Context Management for Long-Horizon SWE-Agents — CAT framework and SWE-Compressor benchmarks
2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report — Anthropic's eight trends for agentic coding
Why AI Agents Fail on Long Coding Tasks — Practical breakdown of context window entropy and state drift
SWE-Bench Verified — Benchmark for long-horizon software engineering agents

cron-to-event-driven.title: From Cron to Event-Driven: A Migration Playbook
cron-to-event-driven.description: Cron's time-based scheduling hides a class of bugs that event-driven architecture eliminates. A 6-month playbook for moving to an event bus safely.

sections.text:
Event-driven architecture replaces time-based scheduling with intent-based scheduling. When work is scheduled by the clock, the system develops a hidden class of bugs — missed windows, cascading retries, daylight-saving surprises, and silent partial state — that don't exist when work is scheduled by the fact that caused it. This post is the playbook for moving a real production system from cron to an event bus without breaking it.

---

sections.heading: The incident that proved it
sections.text:
It was a Tuesday at 11:47 PM UTC. A reconciliation cron — the kind that's been quietly doing its job for three years — failed on a network timeout. The retry kicked in. It hit the same timeout. The retry kicked in again. By the time anyone noticed, the cron had retried 47 times in a 90-minute window, hammering the downstream database with the same query.

The interesting part isn't that the cron failed. Cron fails all the time. The interesting part is the _shape_ of the failure: it wasn't a one-off bug, it was a class of bug that the architecture itself made easy to produce. The clock kept ticking; the retries had no notion of _intent_; the downstream system had no way to deduplicate what it was receiving.

Three weeks later, after a finance reconciliation caught a different silent failure — a state change that hadn't propagated to a downstream consumer because the cron had been running on stale assumptions — the team made the call. We're not fixing this cron. We're replacing the model.

This is the playbook for what came next.

sections.heading: The starting state: cron sprawl
sections.text:
Here's what the system looked like before. If you've ever inherited a few years of "just one more cron," it will look familiar.

 
 
 

The numbers from this system:
47 cron entries spread across 6 services
5 cron entries with implicit ordering dependencies (a billing-svc cron assumed a webhook-svc cron had already run)
3 distinct time zones in the cron expressions (UTC, America/Toronto, Europe/Berlin) — at least one was wrong
~6 hours per month spent babysitting: investigating missed runs, replaying logs, manually triggering retries
3 incidents in the past quarter traceable to missed windows or retry storms

Cron wasn't a bad decision when it was made. It was the simplest thing that could work, and it worked for a long time. That's not a sin — that's how software grows. The problem is that cron accumulates. Each new entry added another implicit dependency, and the system wasn't designed — it accumulated.

sections.heading: Why event-driven, and why now
sections.text:
Three things changed:

1. Scale: crons that took 5 minutes started taking 45 minutes. The reconciliation cron, when it finally worked, blocked four downstream consumers from processing fresh data for almost an hour.
2. Observability ceiling: there was no way to answer "what ran, in what order, with what result?" by grepping cron logs. The information existed in 47 different files, written by 6 different services, in 3 different log formats.
3. Incident count: missed windows + cascading retries + a daylight-saving bug that fired a job twice in one hour pushed the team past a threshold.

The decision wasn't "cron is bad." The decision was "for jobs where the real trigger was never the clock, we were polling on a timer because that was the only tool we had."

sections.heading: The decision matrix
sections.text:
A quick one — not exhaustive, but enough to think with:

| Trigger type | Use when | Watch out for |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Cron / scheduled | Reports, reconciliation, digests, anything genuinely calendar-driven | DST, missed windows, retry storms, ordering assumptions |
| Queue | Tasks that should run once, with retries | Poison messages, ordering, backpressure |
| Event bus | Things that should happen _because_ something else happened | Idempotency, schema evolution, observability across services |

The honest version of the playbook: migrate the host for every job, migrate the trigger model only for jobs where time was a proxy for an event. Time is sometimes the right trigger — a monthly billing reconciliation is a time-based fact, and forcing it into events buys you nothing.

sections.heading: The migration design
sections.text:
Four contracts make this safe. Get any one wrong and the migration will silently corrupt state.

The point of this section isn't "use Pact." The point is: when you cut over a producer and a consumer to a new boundary, you need a way to prove the boundary is what both sides think it is. Without it, every cutover is a leap of faith.

The other two contracts — schema versioning (so producers can't break consumers silently) and observability (every event carries a trace ID, so you can correlate across services) — are covered well elsewhere. The pattern matters more than the tool: don't ship the migration without these four contracts in place.

sections.heading: The cutover plan
sections.text:
Four phases. The most common mistake is collapsing phases 1 and 2; don't.

| Phase | What happens | What proves it's safe to move on |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1. Shadow | New consumer reads events from the bus, logs what it _would_ do, takes no action | Shadow consumer's output matches cron output for 7 days straight, in production traffic |
| 2. Dual-write | Producer emits both to the old cron path AND the new bus; both run, neither is authoritative | The diff between cron results and bus results is empty across 14 days |
| 3. Dark launch | Event bus is authoritative; cron still runs but its output is discarded | Customers see no change in behavior for 14 days; incident count doesn't increase |
| 4. Cron disabled | Cron entries deleted, alerts cleaned up, runbooks updated | One full quarter with zero cron-driven incidents in this category |

The phase that always takes 3x as long as estimated is phase 3, and the bottleneck is never code. It's coordination: getting every team that depends on the cron's side effects to agree on the cutover date, getting the runbook updated, getting the alerts retargeted at the new metric. The engineering is the easy part.

A note on rollback: every phase has to be rollback-able in under 15 minutes. That means the dual-write phase has to be able to disable the bus path instantly without touching the cron path, and vice versa. If you can't roll back in 15 minutes, you're not ready to move on.

sections.heading: The three-week bug hunt
sections.text:
The bug that justified the entire migration slipped through every test we'd written.

In the dual-write phase, we shipped the most natural-looking producer you can imagine:

This passed the contract test. It passed the shadow consumer. It passed the dual-write diff. It failed in production for a reason none of those tests covered.

Here's what happened: the customer-facing cancel endpoint committed the subscription status change at T+0ms. The bus event landed at T+1ms. The cron reconciliation — still running during dual-write — fired at T+200ms, queried the database (now in the post-cancel state), and concluded "nothing to cancel." But the cron reconciliation had its own ordering assumptions: it expected a downstream notification service to be in a particular state, and that state depended on the bus event being fully processed.

The bus event _had_ been processed. But the reconciliation cron's notion of "processed" was based on its own query, not on the bus's offset tracking. The two drifted. Three weeks later, a finance reconciliation caught that we'd sent "your subscription was cancelled" emails to customers whose accounts were still active — and _also_ failed to send them to customers whose accounts were correctly cancelled, because the cron's state read was racing with the bus's offset commit.

The fix wasn't a one-line patch. It was the transactional outbox pattern:

The lesson is sharper than "use the outbox pattern." The lesson is: dual-write is correct in principle and dangerous in practice. Without the transactional outbox, you have a race window between the event emit and the state commit. With it, you have a durable queue that can never get ahead of — or behind — your state. The pattern is one of the most-cited tools in this canonical Stripe writeup on idempotency, and it's worth the read in full if you're going to do a migration like this.

sections.heading: What I'd do differently
sections.text:
Three concrete lessons, not platitudes.

1. Underestimate coordination, not engineering. The engineering for this migration was about 25% of the calendar time. The other 75% was coordinating across teams — getting sign-off on cutover dates, updating runbooks, retargeting alerts, getting finance to agree on what "reconciliation passed" means. If I'd modeled the project realistically, I'd have budgeted 6 engineers for 6 months, not 3 engineers for 4 months. I've written before about how I underestimated migration timelines for a database move — same lesson, different stack.

2. Add the transactional outbox from day one. I would not do a dual-write phase without the outbox in place from the first commit. We added it after the three-week bug hunt. The cost of the bug hunt was larger than the cost of building the outbox first. A senior+ reader I respect has written about similar migration patterns for legacy codebases that reinforce this — the migration shape you start with shapes the failure modes you discover.

3. Cut anything that isn't moving state or shaping the cutover. The plan we shipped had three deliverables that turned out to be pure overhead: a "migration dashboard" (nobody read it), a "weekly stakeholder update" (three weeks in, everyone stopped opening it), and a "rollback dry-run" (we never ran it; we ran a real rollback once and that was the test). If you're planning a similar migration, your three deliverables should be: contract tests, the outbox, and the cutover playbook. Everything else is decoration.

sections.heading: The quiet win
sections.text:
Twelve months after the migration completed:
Missed-window incidents: 8 per quarter → 0 per quarter in the categories that moved to the bus
Deploy frequency: from once a week to twice a day, because deploys no longer had to coordinate with cron schedules
On-call burden: one engineer reported sleeping through the night for the first time in eighteen months
Cross-team integration: adding a new consumer used to require a code change to the cron-emitting service; now it requires a subscription, which is a config change

 
 
 

The class of bug that disappeared is the one that lived in the _space between crons_ — the implicit ordering, the silent race between reconciliation and event publication, the daylight-saving double-fires, the cascading retry storms. The migration didn't add features. It removed a category of failure.

The honest version of when _not_ to do this: if your crons are time-based on purpose (monthly statements, daily digests, weekly backups), the migration buys you nothing and costs you the operational simplicity of cron. The win is in the cases where time was always a proxy for an event you couldn't yet express — and now you can.

---

sections.heading: Appendix: what to read next
sections.text:
If you're planning a similar migration, three reads will save you weeks:
AWS Containers Blog: Migrate cron jobs to event-driven architectures using Amazon ECS and Amazon EventBridge — the canonical vendor-endorsed pattern for the first two steps of this playbook (scheduler → serverless containers, then trigger-by-event).
Stripe Engineering: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency — Brandur Leach's classic on making processing logic idempotent. Models the mental shift from \"the job ran\" (cron's success signal) to \"the side effect happened once\" (event-driven's success signal).
Confluent Schema Registry: Schema Evolution and Compatibility — the BACKWARD/FORWARD compatibility cookbook. Maps directly onto \"add the field first, switch the consumer second, remove the old field last.\"

For the patterns around zero-downtime database migrations and migrating a legacy codebase to Astro, the same playbook applies — coordination is the bottleneck, not engineering.

For the broader system-design context — when event-driven is the right answer vs. when a queue or a simple cron is — the system design patterns cheatsheet covers the decision tree.

---

_If you're doing a migration like this and want to compare notes, my contact form is the fastest way to reach me. I read everything that comes through it._

cve-2026-119618-mod-http2-race.title: The Clone Was One Line Above the Bug: CVE-2026-119618
cve-2026-119618-mod-http2-race.description: mod_http2 copied the request headers into the request record, then wrote Content-Length into the connection's copy. One wrong argument, reachable without authentication, CVSS 9.8, fixed in 2.4.71 on November 11.

sections.text:
Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 shipped on November 11 with three CVEs. The critical one, CVE-2026-119618, is a heap corruption and remote code execution bug in mod_http2. Its fix is one line, and the line it replaced was not missing a bounds check or a length validation. It named the wrong table.

The function is assign_headers() in modules/http2/h2_request.c. It already clones the parsed request headers onto the request's own pool. Then, for a bodyless request that carries a Content-Type and no Content-Length, it writes Content-Length: 0 into the original instead.

sections.heading: What shipped, and how fast
sections.text:
The affected range is every 2.4.x release from 2.4.55 (January 17, 2023) through 2.4.70. Standalone builds of the module from GitHub are affected from mod_h2 2.0.8 through 2.0.42, and that repository was archived in June 2026, so there is no patch coming from it. Keep using the module bundled with httpd.

The bug was found twice, independently. Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported it on October 26 as ANT-2026-MAPKT6MZ; Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud's Vulnerability Research team reported it on November 3. The fix landed in trunk as commit 5ed3928 and was merged to 2.4.x as 824beab. Sixteen days from the first report to a release.

Red Hat rates it 9.8: network reachable, low complexity, no privileges, no user interaction. Their statement adds the sentence that matters for scheduling: public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit against a default-configured server with mod_http2 enabled.

sections.heading: The diff
sections.text:
req is the parsed HTTP/2 request: the header block after HPACK decoding, plus the pseudo-headers. r is the request_rec that the rest of httpd sees, with its own pool.

The telling detail is that the same function already writes to the clone twice: Host at line 340 and Transfer-Encoding at line 368. Only this one write reaches back into the source. If you were reviewing the function for ownership rules, the odd line is visible once you know which identifier is which, and it is invisible if you read req->headers and r->headers_in as two names for the same headers.

sections.heading: const does not mean what it looks like
sections.text:
The signature says const h2_request req, so how does the buggy line compile? const applies to the struct. Read the member access carefully: req->headers has type apr_table_t const. That is a const pointer to a mutable table. apr_table_setn() takes apr_table_t , so passing it is legal and warning-free, and the call mutates the table without touching a single const-qualified field of the struct.

The qualifier stops you from reassigning req->headers. It stops nothing else. A table API that took const apr_table_t for reads and required an explicit cast or a non-const handle for writes would have made this a compile error. That is the deeper convention httpd relies on here: treat the parsed request as immutable once it exists, because other threads can be looking at it.

sections.heading: When the write runs
sections.text:
Four conditions have to hold, and all four are visible in the source:

1. HTTP/2 is negotiated for the server or virtual host (h2 or h2c in an applicable Protocols directive).
2. The stream has no body (no_body).
3. The parsed request carries a Content-Type.
4. It does not carry a Content-Length.

 

Then the guard is the shape of a request an attacker can send directly. HTTP/2 lets a client put any header field it likes in the HEADERS frame, and nothing requires a bodyless request to omit Content-Type. There is no authentication check in this path, and no application code has run yet.

sections.heading: Why the connection's table is not the request's table
sections.text:
HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one connection, and mod_http2 processes stream work on worker threads while the connection thread keeps reading frames. A request that is bodyless and has a content type therefore reaches, from a worker thread, a apr_table_setn() on a table that belongs to the connection side. Red Hat's analysis describes the consequence plainly: a worker thread writes into memory owned by the connection thread through a shared, lock-free allocator.

apr_table_setn() is not a read. When the key is absent, as Content-Length is here, it appends an element to the table's array, and an append can grow that array. Two streams racing through the same append can lose an entry, or can leave the allocator's bookkeeping describing memory it no longer owns. The first is a wrong header. The second is the primitive for arbitrary code execution with the web server's privileges, and turning that primitive into control of the instruction pointer depends on allocator state an attacker can try to shape.

This is also why the same CVE has two severities in one vendor's catalogue. Red Hat scores the base 9.8 but rates it Important rather than Critical for RHEL 9 and RHEL 10, because the mod_http2 packages there allocate each stream from a separate allocator, which substantially raises exploitation complexity. Servers before 2.4.55 and mod_h2 before 2.0.8 do not contain the affected code, and RHEL 8 and earlier are not affected.

sections.heading: Exposure, with the caveat attached
sections.text:
Wiz reports that 64% of cloud environments contain a resource vulnerable to this CVE and that 51% of cloud environments have a publicly exposed instance. Their own note is the one to keep: the figures do not take configuration into account. HTTP/2 has to be enabled.

Upstream's default is Protocols http/1.1, per the core documentation, but distro packages, container images and control panels frequently enable h2 for you, and Apache is estimated to serve roughly one in five websites. Treat "we probably do not have it on" as a claim to verify, not a fact.

sections.heading: Check the effective config, then patch
sections.text:
The grep has to cover every virtual host, because a Protocols directive inside a replaces the server-wide value rather than adding to it, and the module config is often wrapped in . The curl line tells you what the outside actually negotiates: HTTP/2 200 means h2 is live on that hostname.

If any applicable directive lists h2 or h2c and the binary is in range, you are exposed. Upgrade to 2.4.71 or the vendor build that carries the backport: mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1 via RHSA-2026:98981 on RHEL 9, mod_http2-2.0.29-5.el10_3.1 via RHSA-2026:98978 on RHEL 10, or 2.4.71-1~deb12u1 / 2.4.71-1~deb13u1 through DSA-6620-1 on Debian bookworm and trixie.

When patching has to wait, Wiz's mitigation is to remove h2 and h2c from every applicable Protocols line, leaving Protocols http/1.1. Clients fall back to HTTP/1.1 and the multiplexing goes away. What does not help is a WAF rule or a WordPress update: the defect is in the server's header handling, below anything a request filter can see, which is the point Defiant made when it warned WordPress users that patching the CMS cannot fix this.
code:
apache2 -v                     # or httpd -v; anything below 2.4.71 needs a decision
apache2ctl -M 2>/dev/null | grep -i http2
grep -RIn --include='*.conf' -E '^\s*Protocols' /etc/apache2 /etc/httpd
curl -sI --http2 https://your.host | head -1   # needs a curl built with HTTP/2

sections.heading: The same module, two months earlier
sections.text:
2.4.69, released October 1, fixed CVE-2026-57941: a use-after-free and wild write in mod_http2 through shared session->bbtmp re-entrancy, affecting 2.4.17 through 2.4.68. Two bugs in the same module, two months apart, both shared mutable state across a concurrency boundary. The 2.4.55 release notes describe the change that created that boundary: a partial rewrite of how connections and streams are handled, with an APR pollset monitoring the connection and reacting to IO.

That architecture buys real throughput. It also means every field reachable from a connection is a concurrency surface, and the cheap discipline is the one this function nearly followed: copy once at the boundary, then never write to the thing you copied from. The clone was already there, on line 324. The fix was one argument, pointing the last write at it.

Patch to 2.4.71, or turn h2 off today and do it this week.

deepseek-v4-flash-0731.title: Running a Coding Agent on DeepSeek V4 Flash: The 1M-Context Cheap Workhorse
deepseek-v4-flash-0731.description: DeepSeek V4 Flash runs a coding agent on 1M tokens of context with prefix caching at a sub-cent per run. A practical field note, not a benchmark.

sections.text:
My coding agent talks to deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731 through OpenRouter, and the single most unbelievable number about that setup is not the model's benchmark score. It is the price of the average turn.

Most coding-agent turns cost me roughly a fraction of a US cent. Not a third of a cent of a bundled subscription, not a rounded-up estimate. A fraction of a cent, measured from the billed token counts. Several hours of continuous autonomous work can run lower than a single cup of coffee.

That is only possible because of three unrelated facts stacking together: a one-million-token context window, DeepSeek's prefix caching, and per-token pricing of $1 input / $2 output / $0.02 cache-hit per million tokens. This post is a practical field note about what those numbers mean when you actually operate an agent, not a benchmark. If you want leaderboard scores, this is the wrong place—I am not going to invent any.

sections.heading: What the actual numbers look like
sections.text:
Here is the real pricing sheet I work against, stated as a fixed unit of one million tokens:

| Direction | Price per 1M tokens |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------: |
| Input (cache miss / fresh prompt) | $1.00 |
| Output (generation) | $2.00 |
| Input (cache hit) | $0.02 |

The model identifier is deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731, served through OpenRouter. It exposes a 1,000,000-token context window, and it is the cheap, fast tier in my setup—paired with a heavier deepseek-pro tier that I route hard tasks to.

The gap that makes the whole thing work is the one at the bottom of the table. A cache hit costs fifty times less than a fresh input token. In a long agent session, almost every token you send is a cache hit, because the agent keeps resending the same large prefix over and over.

Here is the same snippet as a cut-and-paste curl, if you want to poke at the fields yourself:

One million tokens is a lot. It is on the order of a small repository's entire source tree, or an entire afternoon of agent conversation, retained in one window.

sections.heading: What a one-million-token window actually buys you
sections.text:
Most coding agents spend their lives fighting a small context. With a 128k or 200k window, you start every task by deciding what to discard: the repo map, the older conversation, the tool output you might still need. Getting this wrong produces the classic agent failure mode where the model forgets what it decided two turns ago and redoes the work.

With a million tokens, that whole class of problem mostly disappears.
Whole-repo context fits. For a mid-sized project, I can keep the meaningful parts of the tree plus the agent's own reasoning history in one window.
Whole-session context fits. A long multi-step debugging run no longer needs to be compressed into an ever-shrinking summary that quietly drops the important constraints.
Fewer compactions. The agent jargon for this is "context compaction"—rewriting the conversation into a shorter summary to free space. Every compaction is a small information-loss at best and a self-inflicted bug at worst. A larger window means far fewer of them.

The practical effect is that the agent stops spending effort on memory management and starts spending it on the actual task. That sounds vague until you watch a session run for hours without once asking "wait, why am I doing this again?" It just keeps its own thread of reasoning in front of it.

There is a real cost to a huge window, and I will be honest about it. Context is not free to compute. Prefill—reading and processing all those cached tokens—takes time even when the tokens are cheap. For a long session you trade per-turn latency for the absence of compaction mistakes. On Flash, that trade lands in the right place; on the slower pro tier it is a reason to be more disciplined about trimming.

sections.heading: Why prefix caching changes the cost model
sections.text:
This is the part most people misunderstand. They read "$1 input / $2 output" and conclude a long agent session is expensive, because they picture every turn paying full input price for the whole conversation.

That picture is wrong, and it is wrong in the way that matters most.

A coding agent does not send fresh tokens each turn. It sends the same long prefix—system prompt, repo context, conversation history—and appends only the newest piece. DeepSeek's prefix caching recognizes that the front of the prompt is unchanged and serves the cached portion at $0.02 per million tokens instead of $1.

Here is the arithmetic for a typical turn with, say, 400k tokens of shared prefix and 2k tokens of new output:

Twelve thousandths of a cent. That is the "fraction of a cent per turn" I opened with.

The critical variable is the cache-hit rate. In my long agent sessions, Piyush observes ~99% of input tokens come back as cache hits. At that rate the effective input price collapses toward a rounding error, and the dominant cost of a session becomes—surprisingly—the tiny output tokens it actually generates.

That changes design decisions. When input tokens are nearly free, you stop being stingy with context. You happily re-send the whole repo map every turn, because resending is cheaper than the bug you introduce by leaving it out. The economics of the agent flip from "minimize tokens sent" to "send plenty, but keep the prefix stable so it stays cached."

The one thing that breaks the math is changing the prefix. The moment an earlier part of the conversation changes—say, a tool result gets rewritten out of place—the cache invalidates from that point on, and you pay full input price again for everything after. A well-behaved agent keeps history immutable and only ever appends.

sections.heading: Flash versus pro: the routing tradeoff
sections.text:
The 1M-context Flash model is not a replacement for harder models. It is the cheap, fast tier in a two-model setup, and the other half is deepseek-pro, which I use for the jobs Flash handles poorly.

The practical rule I landed on is a routing split by task shape:

| Task shape | Tier |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ----- |
| Repetitive file edits, refactors, boilerplate | Flash |
| Long multi-file searches across a big repo | Flash |
| Reading and summarizing lots of cached context | Flash |
| Hard algorithmic reasoning | Pro |
| Debugging subtle concurrency or state bugs | Pro |
| Ambiguous tool-use sequences that need care | Pro |

Routing matters for two reasons. First, a cheap model doing easy work lets you run many more parallel lines of effort without watching the bill. That density of cheap iterations is where agent productivity compounds—you can afford to try a change, look at the diff, and try again.

Second, it keeps the expensive model from being wasted. If deepseek-pro costs an order of magnitude more, you do not want it regenerating a boilerplate component when Flash can do that all day for pocket change. You want Pro for the one or two genuinely hard steps in a session, not the dozen easy ones around them.

The honest caveat is that this split is not automatic. It requires a router that looks at the task and picks a tier, and routing mistakes are costly in both directions: sending hard work to Flash produces bad output, and sending easy work to Pro burns money and adds latency. Getting the routing heuristic right is the difference between a budget that feels free and one that quietly bleeds.

sections.heading: Where this setup still falls short
sections.text:
I want to be clear that a few-hundredths-of-a-cent turn price is not the same thing as a frontier model. There are real gaps, and pretending otherwise would make this a worse field note.

Hard reasoning is the weak spot. Give Flash a genuinely thorny algorithm, a subtle race condition, or a problem that needs many careful inferential steps, and it will sometimes march confidently down the wrong path. The output is cheap to produce and cheap to discard, but you still spend the time reading it, noticing it is wrong, and redoing it. For those tasks I stop routing to Flash and hand the whole problem to deepseek-pro.

Tool-use reliability is lower than on heavy models. An agent is only as good as its ability to call tools correctly—running a command, reading a file, applying a patch—and keep going after a failure. The Flash tier occasionally formats a tool call awkwardly or missteps on a retry. It recovers, but it can stall a long autonomous run in a way a more careful model would not.

The latency catch. Cheap input is not fast input. When a session's prefix is large, prefill still has to process all those cached tokens, and on a big window that adds a visible beat before the first output token. If you are asking a question that genuinely depends on the whole 1M-token window, you wait for the whole 1M-token window.

None of these are fatal. They are the reason the setup is two tiers instead of one. Flash earns its place by volume and cost; Pro earns its place by the hard cases.

sections.heading: The bottom line: what 1M context plus cheap input actually unlocks
sections.text:
Stepping back, the thing that surprised me most is not any single number. It is how the numbers combine into a different kind of agent.

One million tokens of context means the agent can carry a whole repo and a whole session without constantly forgetting. Prefix caching at $0.02 input means carrying that context is nearly free. Together they make a coding agent that is not thrifty and nervous about tokens, but relaxed and persistent—the kind that will keep digging for an hour because another turn is basically free.

The setup still punches above its weight class only when you respect its limits. Use it for the long, repetitive, search-heavy work where its cheap iterations and huge context shine. Route the genuinely hard reasoning elsewhere. Keep your session prefixes stable so the cache keeps hitting. Do those three things and the math stops being a novelty and starts being a working habit: a capable agent, running all day, at a fraction of a cent per meaningful step.

That is the real takeaway. The interesting question about a cheap 1M-context model is not "is it as smart as the frontier?" It is "what can you afford to run continuously that you never could before?" For what a cheap workhorse buys you day after day, the answer has been worth far more than the bill.

first-90-days-new-software-engineer-job.title: The First 90 Days At A New Software Engineering Job: A Week-By-Week Playbook
first-90-days-new-software-engineer-job.description: 30% of new hires fail in their first 90 days. This week-by-week playbook took me from day-one joiner to indispensable at three different companies.

sections.text:
30% of new hires fail their first 90 days. And 70% of those failures get decided in week one.

I've started three new software engineering roles across a late-stage startup, Big Tech, and fintech. I bombed the first onboarding badly enough that my manager asked if I was "having second thoughts." I crushed the next two so thoroughly that by day 60 I was the person new joiners were told to go to for help.

The difference wasn't coding ability. It was having a repeatable 90-day system.

 
 
 30% of new hires leave within their first 90 days
 
 
 A BambooHR study of 10,000+ employees found that for software engineers, it climbs to 35% when
 onboarding lacks structure. Your first week isn't a soft ramp. It's a flight that decides
 whether you crash or land.

sections.heading: Why Your First 90 Days Matter More Than Your Last 90
sections.text:
Managers form a permanent impression in the first 1-2 weeks. That's the primacy effect in organizational psychology. Everything after that just confirms or revises that snapshot.

Here's what makes the honeymoon period uniquely powerful:
The team expects you to ask questions. Week 1 is the only time you can say "where's the deploy button?" without raising eyebrows. By week 4, that grace period starts evaporating.
Your manager has budgeted time for you. They blocked their calendar for ramp-up 1:1s. If you don't use that time, it gets reallocated, permanently.
You have low-ego permission to be wrong. Early code review feedback stings less when everyone expects you to be figuring things out. Six months in, the same feedback feels like a performance review.

The goal of the first 90 days isn't to prove you're a 10x engineer. It's to prove you're a safe pair of hands. Someone you can trust with ownership, ambiguity, and production.

sections.heading: Week 1: The "Absorb and Ship" Sprint
sections.text: Your mission: become dangerous enough to contribute, and visible enough to matter.

sections.heading: Day 1-2: The Plumbing
sections.text:
I've seen engineers waste an entire week because they couldn't build the monorepo. Don't be them.
Get on Slack, Linear/Jira, your calendar, the on-call rotation
Add your profile photo. It makes people 3x more likely to respond.
Set up SSH keys, VPN, Docker, 1Password, dev certificates
Find the deploy pipeline and confirm you can ship a zero-risk change

sections.heading: Day 3: The Information Funnel
sections.text:
Read every internal doc you can find, but take notes. If you don't write it down, you're signaling the knowledge isn't important.
Architecture docs and RFCs (especially rejected ones. They teach what not to do)
Postmortems from the last 6 months. Nothing teaches production reality faster than reading how someone ran DROP DATABASE without WHERE at 3 AM.
Runbooks, incident response guides, onboarding guides

sections.heading: Day 4: Map the Codebase
sections.text: Don't try to understand every file. Build a mental index: top-level folders, key entry points, the DB schema, and test patterns. Check the last 30 git commits to see what's active.
code:
ls -la */             # top-level structure
git log --oneline -30 # recent activity

sections.heading: Day 5: Ship Something
sections.text:
Your first PR should be tiny, safe, and visible. A typo fix. A logging improvement. Documentation that was wrong. A test that was flaky.

This isn't about impact. It's about completing the cycle: clone → edit → test → PR → merge → deploy. Every day you don't ship, your manager wonders if you're stuck.

Also this week: Schedule 15-min coffee chats with 5-8 teammates across functions: PM, design, infra, support. Ask: "What's the one thing you wish the new engineer knew on day one?"

Book a 30-min 1:1 with your manager. Agenda: "I want to align on what done looks like at 30, 60, and 90 days."

sections.heading: Week 2-4: The First Owned Project
sections.text:
You've survived week 1. Now it's time to own something end-to-end.

Find a small visible task: a bug fix wrapped in a feature flag, a new API endpoint, a dashboard query. Own it from requirements to production.

sections.heading: What to Learn in This Period
sections.text:
The deploy pipeline. PR → staging → canary → production. Know how to roll back faster than you know how to roll forward.
The on-call flow. Shadow a teammate's shift. Read the last 5 alerts. What wakes someone at 3 AM vs. what waits until morning?
Write a design doc. Even if nobody asked. Writing forces clarity; sharing invites feedback that saves you from building the wrong thing.

Pair with a senior engineer for an hour. Your goal isn't to contribute. It's to watch how they think. The senior who reads a ticket, opens three files, greps, and finds the root cause in 90 seconds has a mental model you can absorb by proximity.

sections.heading: The "Stupid Questions" Hack
sections.text: Ask in public channels, not DMs. It signals psychological safety, prevents five others from asking the same question privately, and builds your reputation as someone who prioritizes learning over ego.

sections.heading: Month 2: The "Propose and Mentor" Phase
sections.text: By day 31, you should know enough to spot problems and help others.

sections.heading: Find One Inefficiency
sections.text:
Every codebase has a papercut: the CI build that takes 40 minutes, the manual step in the deploy process, the README that's wrong about the local setup. Fix one of these. It doesn't need to be heroic. Just visible.

When you propose a fix, frame it as a question: "I noticed our CI runs the full test suite even on doc-only changes. Would adding a path filter be valuable?" This shows you understand the system well enough to optimize it without overstepping.

sections.heading: Start Mentoring
sections.text: Volunteer to onboard the next hire, review a junior's PR, or improve the dev setup doc. Teaching forces deeper learning. If you can explain the service mesh to a new grad, you truly understand it.

sections.heading: Build Cross-Functional Relationships
sections.text: Grab coffee with a PM and ask about their roadmap pain points. Join the product team's sync, even if you just listen. The engineers who get promoted are the ones the PMs fight over.

sections.heading: Month 3: The "Deliver and Calibrate" Finish
sections.text: This is where the first 60 days pay off.

sections.heading: Ship Your First Major Project
sections.text: Deliver something end-to-end from ticket to production. It doesn't need to be complex, but it must be yours. Own the QA, rollout, and monitoring.

sections.heading: Get Calibrated
sections.text: Most companies run quarterly performance reviews. Make sure your manager can speak to your contributions. Send them a one-paragraph summary of what you shipped, learned, and want to work on next. Your manager has 8-12 direct reports. If you don't advocate for yourself, nobody else will.

sections.heading: Be the Person New Joiners Go To
sections.text:
By day 90, you should be the unofficial onboarding buddy for at least one thing. Write a "State of the Codebase" doc: a living document capturing what you wish someone had told you on day one. It signals ownership and deepens your system understanding.

 
 
 The 5 Anti-Patterns That Sink New Engineers
 
 
 
 Going dark in week 1. No Slack messages, no questions, no coffee chats. You're building a
 reputation as the person who isolates themselves when confused.
 
 
 Refusing help. "I got this" when you clearly don't. Nobody expects you to know the codebase in
 week 2. They do expect you to know when you're stuck.
 
 
 Talking about your old company constantly. "At Google we did X" gets old fast. Every company
 has different constraints. Earn the right to compare by understanding why the current approach
 exists first.
 
 
 Coding in isolation. No pairing, no design review, no early feedback. The most dangerous PR is
 the one nobody reviewed because nobody knew about it.
 
 
 Skipping skip-level 1:1s. "Nothing to talk about" is the most expensive sentence in a new job.
 Your skip-level manager wants to know you exist and that you're thinking beyond your ticket
 list.

sections.heading: The Path from "New Joiner" to "Safe Pair of Hands"
sections.text:
The first 90 days aren't about writing the most code. They're about building trust faster than features. Trust that you'll ask for help before breaking production, that you'll ship what you promised, that you're invested in the team's success. The engineers who do best aren't the ones with the most lines shipped. They're the ones who made everyone around them more effective.

---
