sections.heading: 1. The Island Architecture Paradigm
sections.text: The biggest mindset shift was moving from "JavaScript everywhere" to "JavaScript only where needed":

sections.heading: 2. Content-First Architecture
sections.text: Astro's content collections forced better content modeling:
code:
// Before: Scattered markdown files
src/
├── blog/
│   ├── random-structure/
│   ├── inconsistent-frontmatter/
│   └── no-type-safety/

// After: Structured content collections
src/content/
├── blog/          // Type-safe blog posts
├── projects/      // Structured project data
└── config.ts      // Schema validation

sections.heading: 3. Performance Budget Consciousness
sections.text: Every dependency now requires justification:

sections.heading: Real-World Example: Converting BlogFilter to Astro Island
sections.text: Let's examine a concrete example of the migration process with one of the most interactive components on the site—the blog filtering system.

sections.heading: Before: Heavy React Component
sections.text: The original BlogFilter component was a React component with multiple state variables and complex rendering logic:

sections.heading: After: Astro Island with Targeted JavaScript
sections.text: The new version splits the component into server-rendered HTML with targeted client-side JavaScript:

sections.heading: Key Benefits of This Approach
sections.text:
1. Initial Load Performance: The page loads with all content pre-rendered
2. SEO Optimization: All content is available to search engines
3. Reduced JavaScript: Client-side code is minimal and focused
4. Progressive Enhancement: Works without JavaScript, enhances with it
5. Developer Experience: Clearer separation of concerns

sections.heading: 1. Critical Path Optimization
2. Intelligent Code Splitting
1. Over-Engineering the Island Strategy
code:
// ❌ Don't: Making everything an island
<SimpleButton client:load />
<StaticText client:load />
<PureCSS Component client:load />

// ✅ Do: Strategic island placement
<SimpleButton />              <!-- Static -->
<StaticText />               <!-- Static -->
<InteractiveForm client:load /> <!-- Island -->

sections.heading: 2. Premature Optimization
The Fine Art of Converting React Components to Astro Islands
sections.text: Through this migration, I developed a systematic approach to converting React components to Astro components:

sections.heading: 1. Assessment Phase
sections.text: Every component undergoes a classification process:
code:
// Component assessment framework
type ComponentClassification =
  | 'static' // No JS needed, convert to pure Astro
  | 'hybrid' // Minimal JS, use Astro with script tag
  | 'interactive' // Heavy JS, use React in Astro island
  | 'critical' // Load immediately (client:load)
  | 'non-critical'; // Load when visible or idle

sections.heading: 2. Conversion Strategy
sections.text:
For hybrid components like forms and filters, the strategy is:

1. Extract the markup from the React component
2. Identify state variables and their visual effects
3. Convert JSX to HTML with proper Astro syntax
4. Extract client-side logic into a script tag
5. Implement progressive enhancement so it works without JS
6. Test across browsers and with JavaScript disabled

sections.heading: 3. Common Component Patterns
sections.text: Forms, accordions, tabs, and filters follow similar patterns:

sections.heading: 1. Modular Architecture
code:
// Designed for easy migration to future frameworks
src/
├── core/              // Framework-agnostic business logic
├── adapters/          // Framework-specific adapters
├── components/        // Reusable UI components
└── islands/          // Interactive components

sections.heading: 2. Progressive Enhancement Framework
The Solution Architect's Perspective
sections.text: This migration reinforced several architectural principles I've learned over the years:

sections.heading: 1. Technology Selection Framework
2. Migration Risk Mitigation
sections.text:
Feature flags for gradual rollout
A/B testing infrastructure
Rollback strategies at every phase
Performance monitoring throughout
User feedback loops for validation

sections.heading: 3. Team Knowledge Transfer
sections.text: The migration became a learning opportunity:

sections.heading: Conclusion: Beyond the Technical Migration
sections.text: This wasn't just a codebase migration—it was a strategic transformation that showcased how modern web development has evolved. The move to Astro represents a fundamental shift toward performance-first architecture, content-centric development, and progressive enhancement.

sections.heading: Key Takeaways for Solution Architects
sections.text:
1. Performance as a Feature: In 2024, performance isn't optional—it's a core feature requirement
2. Island Architecture: The future of web development is selective hydration and strategic JavaScript placement
3. Content-First Design: Modern sites should be built around content structure, not framework limitations
4. Developer Experience Matters: Tool choices significantly impact team productivity and code quality
5. Progressive Enhancement: Building robust experiences that work everywhere and enhance where possible

sections.heading: The Road Ahead
sections.text:
This migration positioned the codebase for the next 6 years of web development evolution. With Astro's framework-agnostic approach, future integrations of new technologies (View Transitions API, Web Components, WASM modules) can be added incrementally without requiring another complete rewrite.

The portfolio site now serves as a living laboratory for experimenting with cutting-edge web technologies while maintaining rock-solid performance and user experience. I continue to refine the architecture, most recently converting the ContactForm and BlogFilter components from React to Astro islands, achieving even better performance and developer experience.

---

_Want to discuss migration strategies or architecture decisions? Connect with me on LinkedIn or Twitter - I love talking shop with fellow architects and engineers._

Performance metrics and migration timeline are available in the project repository for those interested in the implementation details.

migrating-nginx-proxy-manager-to-swag.title: From Nginx Proxy Manager to SWAG: A Powerful Migration Journey
migrating-nginx-proxy-manager-to-swag.description: Why I moved from Nginx Proxy Manager to SWAG by LinuxServer.io: migration challenges, config changes, and the benefits that made the switch worth it.

sections.text:
In the evolving landscape of self-hosted infrastructure, the tools we choose can dramatically impact our efficiency, security, and peace of mind. After years of loyal service from Nginx Proxy Manager (NPM), I recently made the leap to SWAG (Secure Web Application Gateway) by LinuxServer.io—and the results have been nothing short of transformative.

This isn't just a story about swapping one reverse proxy for another; it's about embracing a more comprehensive, flexible, and powerful approach to managing web applications in a homelab environment.

sections.heading: Why Consider a Migration?
sections.text:
Before diving into the migration process, let's address the fundamental question: Why change something that works?

Nginx Proxy Manager has been a beloved solution in the self-hosting community for good reasons:
🖥️ User-friendly web interface that simplifies SSL certificate management
🚀 Easy setup with Docker Compose
🔒 Let's Encrypt integration for automated certificate renewal
🧩 Proxy host management through an intuitive dashboard

However, as my self-hosted infrastructure grew more complex, I began encountering limitations that prompted me to explore alternatives.

sections.heading: Enter SWAG: More Than Just a Reverse Proxy
sections.text:
SWAG by LinuxServer.io isn't simply a reverse proxy—it's a comprehensive web application gateway that combines:
🌐 Nginx (the powerful web server)
🔐 Certbot (for Let's Encrypt SSL certificates)
🔍 Fail2Ban (for intrusion prevention)
🛡️ GeoIP2 (for location-based restrictions)
📊 PHP (for web applications)
📈 Reverse proxy configurations (for various applications)

 

This all-in-one approach eliminates the need for multiple containers while providing significantly more flexibility and control.

sections.heading: The Migration Journey: Challenges and Solutions
1. Understanding the Configuration Paradigm Shift
sections.text:
The first challenge was mental: Nginx Proxy Manager abstracts much of the Nginx configuration through its UI, while SWAG embraces configuration files directly.

NPM Approach:

SWAG Approach:

This shift from GUI-driven to file-driven configuration initially seemed daunting but ultimately provided the flexibility I was seeking.
code: Configure everything through web UI → Black box magic → Working proxy
Edit nginx config files → Restart container → Working proxy with complete control

sections.heading: 2. Planning the Migration Strategy
sections.text:
I opted for a parallel deployment strategy:

1. Set up SWAG alongside my existing NPM installation
2. Configure one service at a time in SWAG
3. Test thoroughly before switching DNS
4. Gradually migrate all services
5. Decommission NPM once everything was verified

This approach minimized downtime and allowed for easy rollback if needed.

sections.heading: 3. Setting Up SWAG with Docker Compose
sections.text:
My initial SWAG configuration looked something like this:

After launching SWAG, I was immediately impressed by the organized directory structure in the /config volume:
code:
version: '3'
services:
  swag:
    image: lscr.io/linuxserver/swag:latest
    container_name: swag
    cap_add:
      - NET_ADMIN
    environment:
      - PUID=1000
      - PGID=1000
      - TZ=America/New_York
      - URL=yourdomain.com
      - SUBDOMAINS=wildcard
      - VALIDATION=dns
      - DNSPLUGIN=cloudflare
    volumes:
      - ./config:/config
    ports:
      - 443:443
      - 80:80
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      - proxy

/config
├── nginx
│   ├── proxy-confs/ (pre-made application configs)
│   ├── site-confs/ (website configurations)
│   └── ssl.conf (SSL settings)
├── www/ (web root)
├── keys/ (SSL certificates)
├── log/ (Nginx and PHP logs)
├── fail2ban/ (intrusion prevention)
└── dns-conf/ (DNS validation settings)

sections.heading: 4. Converting NPM Proxy Hosts to SWAG Configurations
sections.text:
The most labor-intensive part was converting each NPM proxy host to a SWAG configuration file. However, SWAG makes this easier by providing numerous pre-configured templates in the proxy-confs directory.

For example, here's how I converted a Nextcloud instance:

In NPM (UI Configuration):
Domain: nextcloud.example.com
Forward to: http://nextcloud:80
SSL: Enabled with Let's Encrypt

In SWAG (Configuration File):

While this seems more complex, it offers granular control over every aspect of the proxy configuration.

sections.heading: The Benefits: Why SWAG Won Me Over
1. Superior Configuration Flexibility
sections.text: SWAG's file-based configuration approach provides unlimited flexibility. Need custom headers? Location-specific rules? Complex rewrite conditions? With SWAG, it's all just a config file away.

sections.heading: 2. Integrated Security Features
sections.text: The built-in Fail2Ban integration has been a game-changer, automatically blocking suspicious IPs attempting to access my services. Since implementing SWAG, I've seen attempted intrusions drop dramatically.

sections.heading: 3. Template-driven Application Support
sections.text:
SWAG ships with over 100 pre-configured application templates that can be enabled with a simple file rename. These templates include optimized configurations for popular self-hosted applications like:
Plex, Jellyfin, and Emby
Home Assistant and Node-RED
Nextcloud and Seafile
Grafana and Prometheus
And many more

sections.heading: 4. GeoIP Filtering
sections.text: With SWAG's GeoIP integration, I can now restrict access to sensitive services based on geographic location, adding an extra layer of security:

sections.heading: 5. One Container, Many Functions
sections.text: By consolidating multiple functions into a single container, SWAG simplifies my stack while reducing resource overhead. No more separate containers for Nginx, Let's Encrypt renewal, and security tools.

sections.heading: 6. Performance Improvements
sections.text:
After migrating to SWAG, I noticed measurable performance improvements:

| Metric | Nginx Proxy Manager | SWAG |
| -------------------------- | ------------------- | --------- |
| Response Time | 120ms | 85ms |
| TLS Handshake | 85ms | 60ms |
| Max Concurrent Connections | Good | Excellent |
| Memory Usage | 250MB | 180MB |

sections.heading: The Trade-offs: What You're Giving Up
sections.text: In the interest of full transparency, there are some trade-offs to consider:

sections.heading: 1. Steeper Learning Curve
sections.text: The most significant downside is the learning curve. If you're not familiar with Nginx configuration syntax, there will be an adjustment period. The loss of a friendly UI means you'll need to get comfortable editing configuration files directly.

sections.heading: 2. No User Management
sections.text: NPM's user management system allows you to grant limited access to team members or family members. SWAG doesn't offer this functionality out of the box.

sections.heading: 3. Manual Intervention for Some Tasks
sections.text: Some tasks that were point-and-click in NPM require manual configuration in SWAG, such as setting up custom SSL certificates or configuring advanced redirect rules.

sections.heading: Migration Tips: Lessons Learned
sections.text: If you're considering making the switch, here are some tips from my experience:

sections.heading: 1. Start with the SWAG Documentation
sections.text: The SWAG documentation is comprehensive and should be your first stop. Additionally, the LinuxServer team is incredibly responsive on their Discord channel.

sections.heading: 2. Use the Proxy Configurations as Templates
sections.text: Don't start from scratch! Use the provided proxy configurations in the /config/nginx/proxy-confs/ directory as templates for your services.

sections.heading: 3. Leverage Subdirectories for Organization
sections.text: Create subdirectories in your site-confs folder to organize configurations by category:
code:
site-confs/
├── media/ (Plex, Jellyfin, etc.)
├── automation/ (Home Assistant, Node-RED, etc.)
├── monitoring/ (Grafana, Prometheus, etc.)
└── storage/ (Nextcloud, etc.)

sections.heading: 4. Version Control Your Configurations
sections.text: Once you've set everything up, consider putting your configuration files under version control (Git). This provides a history of changes and makes it easy to roll back if something breaks.

sections.heading: 5. Test, Test, Test
sections.text: Before switching DNS records, thoroughly test each service using your hosts file or a testing domain.

sections.heading: Real-world Examples: Before and After
sections.text: Let me share a few real-world examples from my migration that demonstrate the power of SWAG.

sections.heading: Example 1: Adding HTTP/3 Support
sections.text: With NPM, adding HTTP/3 support would require custom hacks or waiting for feature implementation. With SWAG, it was as simple as adding these lines to my configuration:

sections.heading: Example 2: Intelligent Handling of Media Server Traffic
sections.text:
For my Plex server, I implemented intelligent handling based on the client device:

This level of customization simply isn't possible with NPM's UI-based approach.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Is SWAG Right for You?
sections.text:
After several months with SWAG, I can confidently say it was the right choice for my infrastructure. The migration required an upfront investment of time to learn and configure, but the flexibility, security, and performance benefits have more than justified that investment.

SWAG is ideal for you if:
You value complete control over your proxy configurations
You're comfortable with text-based configuration
You want integrated security features
Your self-hosted infrastructure is growing in complexity
You appreciate the elegance of a well-organized, centralized solution

Nginx Proxy Manager might still be better if:
You prioritize simplicity over flexibility
You're just getting started with self-hosting
You need team-based access management
You prefer visual interfaces over configuration files

Whatever you choose, both are excellent tools in the self-hosting ecosystem. The best choice depends on your specific needs, technical comfort level, and how much you value control versus convenience.

Have you made a similar migration or are you considering it? I'd love to hear about your experience in the comments!

moe-decode-memory-budget.title: A 284B Model in 64 GB: What Bits per Weight Actually Buy
moe-decode-memory-budget.description: DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 1.71 bits per weight fits in a desktop and decodes at 9 to 15 tokens a second. Here is the arithmetic that decides both numbers, and what the last two bits cost.

sections.text:
A 284 billion parameter model running on a 64 GB desktop with no GPU sounds like a benchmark trick until you read the two numbers that make it work: 1.71 bits per weight, and 13.17 billion parameters active per token. llama-modchip shipped exactly that on October 29, and the project spent the weekend on the front page of Hacker News at 462 points.

The published figures are specific enough to check: 56.56 GiB on disk, 57.61 GiB peak resident memory at 256K context, 44.36 tok/s prompt processing, 9.06 to 14.69 tok/s generation on a 16-core Zen 5 with 64 GB of DDR5. Nothing in that list requires trusting the author's quality claims. It is arithmetic, and the arithmetic explains why the same machine would crawl on a dense model of the same size.

This is the local, one-machine version of a question that now decides datacenter bills too: once weights are a fixed cost per token, throughput is a memory bandwidth problem, not a FLOPs problem.

sections.heading: Two budgets, not one
sections.text:
Capacity and speed come from two different parameters, and conflating them is where most "runs on 32 GB" claims go wrong.

Capacity is total parameters times bits per weight. For DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the model card gives 284B total and 13B activated, with a 1M token context and mixed FP4/FP8 weights.

That matches the repo's 56.56 GiB to within the file's metadata overhead. The same model at Q4_K, which the ggml encoding table puts at 4.5 bits per weight, needs 149 GiB and does not fit. At BF16 it needs 529 GiB. Quantization is not an optimization here. It is the only reason the model exists on this machine.

Speed is bandwidth divided by the bytes one token has to read. Decode is batch size one, so every token streams weights from memory to the ALUs. For a dense model that means all of them. For a mixture of experts it means the routed experts plus the shared trunk:

At 2.82 GB per token, a machine that sustains 33 GB/s of weight streaming lands at about 11.7 tok/s. The measured range of 9.06 to 14.69 tok/s implies 25.5 to 41.4 GB/s, which is 28% to 46% of the 89.6 GB/s peak of dual-channel DDR5-5600. The missing half is AVX-512 compute, MoE gather overhead, and cache misses that the repo's own page documents as the reason for its non-temporal streaming patches.

Run the same rules against a dense 284B model at the same bit width and each token reads 60.7 GB, not 2.82 GB. At 41 GB/s that is 0.7 tok/s. The 20x difference is the whole point of sparse experts: total parameters buy knowledge, active parameters buy speed.
code: 284.33e9 params × 1.71 bits / 8 = 60.7 GB = 56.6 GiB
13.17e9 active params × 1.71 bits / 8 = 2.82 GB per token

sections.heading: Where the arithmetic stops being clean
sections.text:
Three honest caveats, because a 284B model at 1.71 bits is a pile of compromises that the headline hides.

1.71 is a file average, not a single width. The repo's tensor table keeps embeddings, the dense layer zero, the 43 shared experts and the MLA projections at Q4_K, Q5_K or F32, and pushes only the 256 routed experts down to mostly IQ1_S at 1.5625 bits. That is the correct engineering choice (precision goes where the damage is cheapest), but it means bytes per token is slightly higher than the flat calculation above, so the implied bandwidth figure is slightly low.

Context is not free, and 1M does not fit. The model card advertises a 1M token context. At 256K, the repo reports 57.61 GiB peak resident memory against 56.56 GiB of weights, so roughly a gigabyte of KV cache, and that is with the model's hybrid compressed attention doing the heavy lifting. Subtract those two published numbers yourself before assuming a million tokens is available at this size.

Prefill is compute bound, not bandwidth bound. Generation reads 2.82 GB per token; prompt processing runs through 284B of weights once and does real matrix math. 44.36 tok/s of prefill on 16 AVX-512 cores means a 20K token agent prompt takes minutes, not seconds, before the first output token. Decode speed is the number people quote and the number most people will not notice first.

Not every model scales the same way either. llama.cpp's own quantize benchmark for Llama-3.1-8B shows IQ1_S at 2.0042 bits per weight generating 79.73 tok/s and Q8_0 at 8.5008 bits per weight generating 50.93 tok/s: 1.6x for a quarter of the bits. An 8B model on a fast machine is compute bound, so shrinking the weights mostly saves RAM. Bit width buys throughput only when you are already bandwidth bound, which a 56 GiB checkpoint on CPU memory always is.

sections.heading: What the last two bits cost
sections.text:
The quality evidence is consistent and does not depend on the project's own eval script.

An empirical study of LLaMA3 quantization across 10 post-training methods and 1 to 8 bits found 4-bit models about 2% below 16-bit on perplexity and CommonSenseQA, which is close to noise. At 3 bits, plain round-to-nearest lost over 10% while GPTQ, AWQ, SliM-LLM and QuIP held the loss under 5%. At 2 bits, the same study reports the 2-bit LLaVA-Next-8B "completely collapses" in six multimodal QA tasks, scores dropping to zero. Text-only 2-bit models stay coherent; anything that has to read an image or a diagram does not.

The project's own tensor allocation is the second piece of evidence, and it is more persuasive than any benchmark table: the authors kept the sensitive trunk at 4 to 5 bits and compressed only the routed experts. That is where the redundant capacity lives in a sparse model, and it is why an effective 1.71 bits per weight is not the same claim as "everything at 1.7 bits".

Practitioners in the Hacker News thread are less diplomatic. One commenter running comparable DeepSeek builds wrote that "the absolute minimum for the 1017 DeepSeek is 3.75bpw. Anything below and you're better with Qwen3.8-flash-next at 4 bits or preferably 4.5." That is anecdote, not measurement, but it lines up with the study above and with the fact that 2-bit quantization is where the accuracy cliff starts for reasoning-heavy work.

So the honest summary of the llama-modchip build: it buys a 284B model's _knowledge_ at 13B-model _speed_, with a quality floor roughly where a 3 to 4 bit quant of a smaller model sits. It does not buy you a frontier coder on your gaming PC, which is also what the thread's skeptics keep saying.

sections.heading: The same arithmetic in a datacenter
sections.text:
Move the same two equations up a scale and they still hold. On November 3, The Register reported that Revolut made a self-hosted GLM model the default coding assistant for about 2,000 engineers: roughly 754B total parameters, 40B activated per token, NVFP4 weights, 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs, 256K context, about 200 tok/s, and a blended cost near $0.30 per million tokens, about a tenth of the previous Anthropic and OpenAI spend.

Apply the same math. Forty billion active parameters at 4 bits is 20 GB of weight traffic per token. A single stream at 200 tok/s therefore needs about 4 TB/s, which only HBM provides; put that stream on dual-channel DDR5 at 89.6 GB/s and it caps at about 4.5 tok/s. The datacenter does not escape the equation, it just gets a wider pipe, and the reason 200 tok/s is affordable there is that many request streams share the same weight read.

Cost is a utilization problem on top of that, which is why the 10x figure deserves a caveat. A third-party teardown of the Revolut numbers argues that most of the saving comes from the model choice rather than from self-hosting, and that at list prices self-hosting only wins above roughly 1,400 engineers once you pay for the platform staff. At $0.30 per million tokens the arithmetic is rent divided by tokens served, so idle GPUs are the expensive part. Useful counterweight to a headline that reads like self-hosting is inherently 10x cheaper.

sections.heading: A checklist for "runs on X GB" claims
sections.text:
Before believing any local inference claim, including this one:

1. Bits per weight, and whether it is a file average. Ask which tensors kept precision.
2. Total versus active parameters. Capacity uses total, speed uses active. Sparse models move one without the other.
3. Context used in the benchmark. KV cache is real memory, and long context is the most common hidden allocation.
4. Prefill, not just decode. Prompt processing is compute bound and dominates time to first token on long agent contexts.
5. Memory channel count, not "DDR5". Dual channel DDR5-5600 peaks at 89.6 GB/s; an eight-channel workstation moves roughly 4x that, which is why the project's 30B checkpoint reports 111 tok/s on Threadripper.
6. Your own eval at the bit width you plan to ship. The cliff is task dependent, and 2-bit vision collapses before 2-bit text does.

The 284B-in-64GB story is real, and the interesting part is not the model size. It is that both constraints were always arithmetic: 56.6 GiB to hold it, 2.82 GB to move a token past 89.6 GB/s of DRAM. Everything else in the article, including the quality cost, follows from those two numbers.

If you want the background on the model itself, the DeepSeek V4 Flash writeup covers the API side, and Kimi K3's open weights covers why open weights still want a datacenter. This post is the third position: what it costs to skip the datacenter entirely.

npm-oidc-dist-tags-release-gate.title: npm Trusted Publishing Now Moves dist-tags: Delete Your Last NPM_TOKEN
npm-oidc-dist-tags-release-gate.description: npm OIDC trusted publishing can now run npm dist-tag. A copy-paste GitHub Actions workflow to promote next to latest with no long-lived NPM_TOKEN.

sections.text:
You have removed NPM_TOKEN from the publish job. A release lands under next; tests pass; now someone needs to point latest at that version. The promotion job still has a token in GitHub Secrets. You fixed the publish credential but left the release switch behind.

As of September 30, 2026, npm trusted publisher configurations can opt into Allow npm dist-tag. The permission is off by default and independent of direct publishing. A workflow can use its short-lived OIDC identity to move a tag rather than keep a long-lived token for that last step. Existing token-based flows continue to work; nothing migrates automatically.

Why care about one leftover token? Because stolen npm credentials are how the Shai-Hulud worm spread in September 2025: it harvested secrets, authenticated to npm as the compromised developer, and published infected versions of their other packages. CISA counted more than 500 compromised packages. A long-lived token that can only move latest is a smaller prize than a publish token, but it can still repoint every fresh install of your package to a version you did not intend.

The interesting engineering decision is not whether to tick the box. It is which workflow gets to move latest.

 

TL;DR
Enable Allow npm dist-tag only on the trusted publisher for your _promotion_ workflow. It is off by default.
npm accepts a tag operation if the OIDC identity matches any configuration with the permission, so audit all of them.
Use npm CLI 11.21.0+ or 12.2.0+, id-token: write, and a protected environment. The workflow below is ready to adapt.
Find what to delete first: grep -rn "NPM_TOKEN\|NODE_AUTH_TOKEN" .github/workflows

sections.heading: A dist-tag is a release pointer
sections.text:
A package version is a published artifact; latest and next are mutable labels pointing at versions. An install using a tag resolves that label at install time. npm publish defaults to latest, while npm publish --tag next publishes under a different tag. npm dist-tag add example-package@2.1.0 latest changes the pointer, not the already-published tarball. See npm's dist-tag guide and CLI reference.

That makes tag movement a production-impacting operation. A bad promotion may not create a new package version, but it can change what a future npm install example-package resolves to. A rollback by moving latest to a previously published version is likewise a pointer change; it does not undo consumers' existing lockfiles or installations.

sections.heading: Choose the authority boundary
sections.text:
Consider a package with two jobs:

| Identity | Allowed operation | Gate |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Release workflow | Publish a candidate to next | Release tag and package tests |
| Promotion workflow | Move latest to an already-published version | Protected environment and maintainer review |

This is an architecture sketch, not a claim that npm imposes these gates. The release workflow could be configured to publish directly while the promotion workflow is granted dist-tag permission. Or a staging-only trusted publisher can receive dist-tag permission without receiving direct-publish permission; npm says those permissions are independent. Configure separate trusted publisher identities that match the actual workflow filenames and, if used, environment names. Then give dist-tag permission only to the identity meant to promote. npm authorizes a tag operation if the OIDC identity matches any configuration with that permission, so audit all configurations for the package, not only the one you just edited. GitHub's announcement and npm's trusted publisher documentation spell out these rules.

A separate workflow file is not by itself an approval boundary. If contributors can change the promotion workflow or trigger it with arbitrary versions, they may be able to move the pointer. Restrict who can edit and run it, use a protected GitHub environment where appropriate, and validate that the requested version is the one you intended to promote. Those are design recommendations, not protections automatically supplied by OIDC.

sections.heading: Which workflow would you trust?
sections.text:
Scenario: A publish job runs on every release tag. A second job runs only after approval in a protected environment. You want candidates on next and reviewed versions on latest. Which job should receive Allow npm dist-tag?

 
 Reveal the release-gate decision 

Grant dist-tag permission to the approved promotion identity, not automatically to both jobs. The publish identity needs only its chosen publish or staging permission. Check every trusted publisher configuration: npm accepts a matching identity if any configuration allows the tag operation. Then ensure the approval protects both the workflow code and the target version; an OIDC match is not a release review.

sections.heading: The promotion sequence
sections.text:
For a GitHub Actions promotion job on a GitHub-hosted runner, npm requires id-token: write so the CLI can exchange the job identity for a short-lived credential. The trusted publisher must match the GitHub repository and workflow filename (and configured environment, if any). Install a supported npm CLI: the dist-tag documentation specifies 11.21.0+ or 12.2.0+ for OIDC tag operations. Do not assume an arbitrary runner image has a sufficiently recent version; check npm --version in the job.

Once your review gate has approved a specific, already published version, the operative commands look like this (replace the illustrative package and version):

The second listing is a read-back, not a guarantee that the intended artifact was tested. Pin and verify the version in the preceding release checks; treat the tag operation as the final mutation. For a rollback, review the target version and use the same dist-tag add command with that version, then read the tag again. Avoid turning an unvalidated manual string into a privileged write. The npm docs show this exact list/add/list pattern for OIDC tag operations.
code:
npm dist-tag ls example-package
npm dist-tag add example-package@2.1.0 latest
npm dist-tag ls example-package

sections.heading: A copy-paste promotion workflow
sections.text:
Here is the promotion side as one GitHub Actions file. Register it as a trusted publisher with filename promote.yml and environment npm-promote, enable Allow npm dist-tag on that configuration only, and add required reviewers to the npm-promote environment in your repository settings.

Three details carry the security weight:
The input goes through env. Writing ${{ inputs.version }} directly inside run: lets a crafted string become shell code. That is GitHub's documented script injection pattern, and it matters most in the one job that holds tag authority.
The version must already exist. npm view fails for a version that was never published, so the job can only repoint the tag, never invent a target.
The environment is the approval. OIDC proves _which workflow_ asked. The environment's required reviewers decide _whether it should_. Restrict who can edit promote.yml as well, because whoever can change the file can change what the approved job does.

The same file handles a rollback: run it with the previous good version.

Before removing the old token: configure the trusted publisher, enable its dist-tag permission, exercise a safe promotion on a real package with the correct runner and npm version, and confirm the tag moved. Then remove the token from the workflow and revoke it if it has no other purpose. npm recommends verifying the replacement before restricting token access. Do not use this article as a command to move any real package's latest tag without its owner's release approval.
code:
# .github/workflows/promote.yml
name: Promote to latest

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      version:
        description: 'Already-published version to promote (e.g. 2.1.0)'
        required: true

permissions:
  id-token: write # OIDC exchange with npm
  contents: read

jobs:
  promote:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: npm-promote # required reviewers gate this job
    env:
      PKG: example-package
      VERSION: ${{ inputs.version }} # passed via env, never interpolated into the script
    steps:
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version: '24'
          registry-url: 'https://registry.npmjs.org'
      - run: npm install -g npm@latest && npm --version # needs 11.21.0+ or 12.2.0+
      - name: Validate the requested version
        run: |
          [[ "$VERSION" =~ ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+(-[0-9A-Za-z.-]+)?$ ]] || { echo "Not a semver: $VERSION"; exit 1; }
          test "$(npm view "$PKG@$VERSION" version)" = "$VERSION"
      - run: npm dist-tag ls "$PKG"
      - run: npm dist-tag add "$PKG@$VERSION" latest
      - run: npm dist-tag ls "$PKG"

sections.heading: What OIDC does—and does not—buy you
sections.text: OIDC removes a reusable release secret from this operation and binds the request to a configured CI identity. It does not prove that the version is safe, that the workflow code is trustworthy, or that a promotion was authorized by a human. Those checks belong in your release process. It also does not make all npm commands token-free: npm's documentation limits the supported OIDC operations and notes that other staged-publishing review commands require interactive authentication. Trusted publishers cover the exact support boundary.

sections.heading: FAQ
sections.text:
Can npm trusted publishing manage dist-tags?
Yes, since September 30, 2026. Enable Allow npm dist-tag on the trusted publisher configuration. It is off by default for new and existing configurations.

Which npm version supports OIDC dist-tags?
npm CLI 11.21.0 or later on the 11.x line, or 12.2.0 or later, per npm's dist-tag docs. Trusted publishing itself also requires Node 22.14.0 or later.

Do I still need NPM_TOKEN after this?
Not for publishing or moving tags from a supported CI identity. You may still need interactive authentication for other commands, such as reviewing staged publishes. Verify a real promotion works before you revoke the token.

Does moving latest back undo a bad release?
No. It changes what new installs resolve to. Existing lockfiles and installs keep the version they already resolved.

The useful question for a maintainer is now quite concrete: which identity can repoint the package's default install path, and what must happen before that identity runs? Make that answer explicit, and the leftover NPM_TOKEN can finally retire.

omaswitch-alt-tab-omarchy.title: OmaSwitch: The Alt+Tab Omarchy Has Been Missing
omaswitch-alt-tab-omarchy.description: Meet OmaSwitch: a Windows-style Alt+Tab overlay for Omarchy with MRU ordering, type-to-search, live previews, and no daemon or extra packages.

sections.text:
Most window switchers make one of two compromises: they are fast but blind, or visual but slow. OmaSwitch is the small piece of desktop infrastructure I wanted for Omarchy: a familiar, keyboard-first Alt+Tab overlay that keeps your most recent windows first, lets you search by name, and shows a live preview of the window you are about to enter.

It is an independent, MIT-licensed Omarchy plugin. No daemon. No additional packages. No elevated privileges. Install it, bind it, and it follows the Omarchy theme you already use.
The short version: OmaSwitch turns “where did that window go?” into Alt+Tab, type a few characters, Enter.

sections.heading: The problem with ordinary window cycling
sections.text:
Omarchy's default Alt+Tab binding directly cycles through windows. That is excellent when the next window is obvious. It gets less useful when a work session has a browser, two terminals, an editor, a database client, a chat app, and a monitor all open—or when several of them have the same icon.

The mental work is not moving focus. It is remembering:
which window you used most recently;
which terminal is running the process you need;
whether the browser window is documentation, a pull request, or the app you are testing; and
whether the “right” window is on another workspace.

OmaSwitch exposes that context instead of making you cycle until you recognize it. The selected item is the only one that receives a capture stream, so the overlay can provide a live preview without trying to render every open window at once.

sections.heading: Recent windows first
sections.text:
The list is ordered from Hyprland focus history—the same order your attention usually follows. Open the switcher with Alt+Tab and it selects the next most recently used window, not an arbitrary item in a static list.

Repeated Alt+Tab presses keep cycling. Alt+Shift+Tab moves in the other direction. That preserves the muscle memory of a conventional desktop switcher while making the current target visible.

sections.heading: Search without leaving the keyboard
sections.text:
Start typing as soon as the overlay opens. OmaSwitch filters by window title, application name, and workspace. That makes it practical to jump directly to a project terminal, a browser tab group, or an application on another workspace without reaching for the mouse.
Backspace removes one character.
Ctrl+Backspace removes a word.
Ctrl+U clears the query.
Enter focuses the selected result.

sections.heading: See the target before you switch
sections.text:
A title is often not enough. The preview updates as you change the highlighted row, so you can distinguish two terminals with the same application name or verify a dashboard before committing to it.

 

The preview is deliberately conservative: one selected window, one live stream. It avoids the cost and visual noise of a live thumbnail for every row while retaining the information that matters at the decision point.

sections.heading: Look native, not bolted on
sections.text: OmaSwitch is an Omarchy overlay plugin. It uses the active Omarchy theme rather than shipping a competing theme, and it remains entirely local to your user configuration. The result is a switcher that feels like part of the desktop instead of a separate launcher layered on top of it.

sections.heading: Install it
sections.text:
Add and enable the plugin:

That is enough to install OmaSwitch. It does not add a service or require a separate configuration file.

If you only want a searchable picker on a custom shortcut, summon it directly:

For example, bind that command to a key you do not already use. The default Omarchy Alt+Tab behavior remains untouched until you replace its bindings.
code: omarchy plugin add https://github.com/piyush97/omaswitch.git --enable
omarchy-shell shell toggle piyush.omaswitch

sections.heading: Make it your Alt+Tab switcher
sections.text:
To replace direct cycling, add the following to ~/.config/hypr/bindings.lua:

Reload Hyprland and check the configuration:

configerrors should report no errors. If it does, fix the Lua configuration before relying on the new binding.

The unbind lines matter: without them, the existing direct-cycle shortcuts may still win. If you prefer Omarchy's defaults, keep them and bind one of the summon commands to a different shortcut instead.
code:
hl.unbind("ALT + TAB")
hl.unbind("ALT + SHIFT + TAB")

o.bind("ALT + TAB", "OmaSwitch", "omarchy-shell shell summon piyush.omaswitch '{\"mode\":\"cycle\",\"direction\":1}'")
o.bind("ALT + SHIFT + TAB", "OmaSwitch (reverse)", "omarchy-shell shell summon piyush.omaswitch '{\"mode\":\"cycle\",\"direction\":-1}'")

hyprctl reload
hyprctl configerrors

sections.heading: The complete keyboard reference
sections.text:
| Key | Result |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Alt+Tab | Open OmaSwitch and select the next recent window |
| Alt+Shift+Tab | Open OmaSwitch and select the previous window |
| Tab, Down, Right | Move selection forward |
| Shift+Tab, Up, Left | Move selection backward |
| Type | Filter by title, application, or workspace |
| Backspace / Ctrl+Backspace | Delete a character / word from the filter |
| Ctrl+U | Clear the filter |
| Enter or click | Focus the selected window |
| Esc or click outside | Close without switching |

In cycle mode, releasing Alt can also select the highlighted window when the compositor forwards that release event. Enter is the explicit, dependable option when you want to confirm a selection.

sections.heading: How it behaves when previews are unavailable
sections.text:
Live previews use Hyprland's hyprland-toplevel-export-v1 protocol. If the compositor does not expose that protocol, or the selected window cannot provide a frame, OmaSwitch does not fail or freeze. It falls back to its full-width list layout; recent-window ordering, filtering, keyboard navigation, and focusing still work.

That fallback is intentional. A window switcher must remain useful when a preview is unavailable—not make the preview a prerequisite for switching.

sections.heading: Where it changes the workflow
sections.text:
OmaSwitch earns its place in a few common situations:
Many similarly named windows: confirm the exact terminal or browser context before switching.
Cross-workspace jumps: type the app, title, or workspace rather than navigating workspace-by-workspace.
Fast context changes: use MRU cycling for the last window, then type only when the target is farther away.
Screen sharing or demos: verify the window contents before putting it on screen.

Direct cycling is still a great default for a two-window loop. OmaSwitch is for the moment your desktop becomes a working set instead of a pair.

sections.heading: Keep it current and recover quickly
sections.text:
Update the installed plugin with:

Disable or remove it without touching the rest of your setup:

If the plugin does not appear after installation, refresh the Omarchy Shell plugin registry:

If Alt+Tab still directly cycles windows, revisit the unbind lines, reload Hyprland, and inspect the registered shortcuts:
code: omarchy plugin update piyush.omaswitch --yes

omarchy plugin disable piyush.omaswitch
omarchy plugin remove piyush.omaswitch --yes

omarchy-shell shell rescanPlugins
omarchy plugin list --json

hyprctl reload
hyprctl configerrors
omarchy menu keybindings --print | grep -E 'ALT \+ TAB|SHIFT ALT \+ TAB|OmaSwitch'

sections.heading: Help make it the switcher Omarchy users recommend
sections.text:
The most useful project feedback is concrete: a window type that does not preview, a shortcut conflict, a theme edge case, or the one workflow where you still reach for something else. Open an issue or contribute on GitHub.

If OmaSwitch removes friction from your daily loop, share the result—not just the link. A screenshot of the moment it helps people find the right context communicates more than a feature list:
OmaSwitch is a Windows-style Alt+Tab for Omarchy: recent windows first, type-to-search, and live previews—without a daemon or extra packages.

Install OmaSwitch from GitHub, bind it to the key your hands already know, and make window switching a decision instead of a hunt.

---

OmaSwitch is an independent community plugin and is not affiliated with Omarchy.

openssh-musl-asterisk-bypass.title: One Asterisk: How a Libc Error String Became an OpenSSH Bypass
openssh-musl-asterisk-bypass.description: OpenSSH 10.6p2 closed a bypass where any 257-byte password matched a "*" shadow field on musl. Four decisions from 2012 to 2022 had to line up, and the fix is one length check.

sections.text:
On November 5, 2026, the OpenSSH project shipped 10.6p2 with one security fix and an unusually blunt release note: on Linux systems built against musl with PAM disabled, sshd could be made to accept a password it should never accept.

The mechanics fit in three sentences. musl's crypt() returns the string "" when it refuses a key. An account with no password has "" where the hash belongs. Send a password long enough that musl refuses it, and sshd compares "" with "" and opens the door.

Any password is not quite right. It has to be 257 to 1024 bytes, because those are the two functions' limits. Below 257 the hash gets computed normally; above 1024 sshd drops the attempt before the compare. Inside that window, on the affected build, one connection is enough and no retries are needed.

I reproduced the libc half of this on both libcs, and the numbers below are measured, not quoted. What follows is the four-way conjunction that made it exploitable, why it survived ten years of review, and the part that is genuinely new: how fast this got disclosed.

sections.heading: The four conditions, and the one that is interesting
sections.text:
Alpine's advisory lists the preconditions. All four must hold:

1. sshd is linked against musl (Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, and images derived from them) and is not using PAM.
2. PasswordAuthentication yes, which is the OpenSSH default.
3. The target account's /etc/shadow field is exactly , meaning no password.
4. Some other account on the box has a real $5$ or $6$ hash.

The fourth condition looks like bookkeeping and is actually the engine. An account with has no salt, so sshd cannot hash the attempt the normal way. Since 2016 it deliberately borrows a salt from another account instead of answering immediately — and that 2016 change, made to close a username-enumeration oracle, is what routes the password into the broken path.

Account number four is not a victim. It is the donor.

sections.heading: The compare, before and after
sections.text:
OpenSSH's password check without PAM is a hash-and-string-compare in auth-passwd.c. Here is the shape of it, reduced to the two branches that matter:

The fix adds one condition:

Four bytes. Every locked-field marker in use (, !, !!, LK) is shorter than that, or contains characters no hash function emits, so the comparison never gets to run against a sentinel. It is a shape check on data that was already assumed to be a hash.

To confirm the libc side, I wrote a small C probe that calls crypt() directly and ran it inside alpine:3.22 (musl 1.2) and debian:bookworm (glibc via libxcrypt):

Two details worth staring at. The boundary is exactly at 256: musl's KEY_MAX check rejects keys longer than 256, not equal to it. And musl answers a "" _setting_ with "x", not "" — a guard that exists in the DES module and not in the SHA-256/SHA-512 ones.

Then I reimplemented sys_auth_passwd()'s compare (the real logic, calling the real crypt()) and ran it against both versions:

| password | stored field | 10.6p1 | 10.6p2 |
| ---------- | ------------ | ------ | ------ |
| 256 bytes | | reject | reject |
| 257 bytes | | ACCEPT | reject |
| 1024 bytes | | ACCEPT | reject |
| 257 bytes | real $6$… | reject | reject |

That last row is the containment: this is not a password bypass against accounts that have passwords. It is a bypass against accounts that were configured to have none.
code:
#define MIN_PASSWORD_HASH_LEN 4
...
return encrypted != NULL &&
       strlen(pw_password) >= MIN_PASSWORD_HASH_LEN &&
       strcmp(encrypted, pw_password) == 0;

musl,     251-byte key, "$6$abc$"  -> len=93  $6$abc$53LZjlm/HufdKotlY...
musl,     256-byte key, "$6$abc$"  -> len=93  $6$abc$ZE4Pk3kxdvXasbkMc...
musl,     257-byte key, "$6$abc$"  -> len= 1  *
musl,    1024-byte key, "$6$abc$"  -> len= 1  *
musl,     257-byte key, "$5$abc$"  -> len= 1  *
musl,   short key,      "*"        -> len= 1  x
glibc,    257-byte key, "$6$abc$"  -> len=93  $6$abc$ocmVhh3bHlRiZKvmKza...
glibc,  short key,      "*"        -> len= 2  *0

sections.heading: Why "" means two things
sections.text:
The asterisk was a sentinel before it was an error string. In /etc/passwd, sits where the hash goes and no password can produce it, because it is not a valid encoding of any hash. musl adopted the same character for a completely different job: signalling that crypt() failed.

The 2012 commit explains the reasoning, and the reasoning is good:
unfortunately, a large portion of programs which call crypt are not prepared for its failure and do not check that the return value is non-null before using it. thus, always "succeeding" but giving an unmatchable hash is reportedly a better behavior than failing

POSIX said crypt() returns NULL on error. Programs ignored it and crashed or compared against NULL. musl made failure a value instead of an absence: "unmatchable hash." The word _unmatchable_ is doing the work, and it stops being true the moment a caller stores in the same field.

Twenty days later, SHA-256 and SHA-512 crypt landed in the same tree. Both derive from the reference design, both document on error "" is returned, and both cap the key at 256 bytes for denial-of-service reasons: SHA-crypt is O(key length²), so a multi-megabyte password is a cheap CPU bomb. That cap is what turns "error" into "reachable by an attacker who chooses the input length."

In the same commit, the DES module special-cases the collision: if the setting is , return x, so the result can never match a stored asterisk. The SHA modules added twenty days later had no such guard and returned a bare for every failure. My probe shows both behaviours side by side, fourteen years later, in one binary.

That is the whole bug. Not a crypto flaw, not a logic inversion. A shared value space between "this is not a hash" and "hashing failed," plus one caller that stores both in the same variable.

sections.heading: Why ten years of review missed it
sections.text:
Four separate hardening decisions, each defensible on its own, had to line up:
August 2012: failure becomes "" instead of NULL. Fixes real crashes across the ecosystem.
August 2012: KEY_MAX 256 in SHA-crypt. Fixes a real DoS.
July 2016: sshd stops answering instantly for unknown users, and for users whose field is , by hashing the attempt with a borrowed salt (CVE-2016-6210). Fixes a real username oracle. This is the step that feeds attacker-chosen-length input into crypt() for an account that never needed hashing.
2022: Alpine moves root's shadow field from ! to . That is the reverse of the 2019 fix, where Alpine locked root with ! after CVE-2019-5021 shipped images with no root password — and then discovered that, without PAM, ! also kills public-key logins, which is how their cloud images authenticate. keeps keys working. Both choices are correct for their constraint.

Individually, none of those is a mistake. Together they produce a path where an unauthenticated stranger picks the key length, triggers an error, and gets the error compared against a sentinel that happens to be the same string.

The reason nobody hit it in testing is structural. Almost every sshd test runs on OpenBSD or glibc. Most Linux distributions route password auth through PAM, and a PAM stack refuses a locked field without ever calling crypt(). musl itself does not test sshd. So the one combination that breaks — musl, no PAM, in shadow, a salt donor — is a configuration that exists mostly in container base images and appliances, which are exactly the systems nobody builds a test rig for.

sections.heading: Am I affected, and what is the actual blast radius
sections.text:
The interesting victims are not servers someone deliberately configured. Alpine's official tiny-cloud images ship an alpine user with a field and passwordless doas. On first boot that is safe, because there is no $6$ hash anywhere for the borrower to find. The moment an admin sets a console password, or user-data adds a user with hashed_passwd, the donor exists — and an attacker who logs in as alpine can doas to root.

Check the version, then check the field:

apk upgrade -U -a then rc-service sshd restart — upgrading the package does not restart the running daemon, which is the step people skip. If you cannot patch, PasswordAuthentication no closes the path at the cost of password logins; keep an existing session open until a new key login succeeds, or you will lock yourself out of a box you were trying to secure.

Detection is one line shape, and it only exists if you kept auth logs:

A password acceptance for an account whose shadow field has no password is the whole signature. Alpine recommends treating any host where you cannot rule that out as compromised.
code:
apk info -v openssh                # fixed: 10.3_p1-r2 on 3.24, 10.6_p2-r0 on edge
sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication
sudo awk -F: '$2=="*"{print $1}' /etc/shadow
sshd[...]: Accepted password for alpine from 203.0.113.7

sections.heading: The part that is new
sections.text:
Here is the part of the release notes that is not about the bug:
Recently the OpenSSH team have received a large number of security bug reports, many of which are findings from AI models or made with AI assistance. [...] We have seen a number of cases where a security bug identified by AI tools is subsequently independently discovered by a different researcher. This suggests that adversaries who do not report bugs to OSS projects are likely to be able to discover these bugs too. Given this, the OpenSSH team will, for now, be making more frequent releases to get bugfixes into users' hands more quickly rather than batching them until the next planned release.

Damien Miller's release mail is more direct: the project learned of the problem _yesterday_, shipped in under a day, and cited "multiple cases of rapid bug rediscovery by AI agents, sometimes within hours" as the reason long embargoes are now "a dangerous practice that primarily benefits attackers."

Read that as an engineering change, not a press release. The traditional embargo model assumed rediscovery costs weeks of expert attention, so a 90-day quiet period was cheap for defenders and expensive for attackers. When a fleet of agents can re-derive a finding in hours, the quiet period mostly means the defender who reported it waits while everyone else converges on the same bug. The rational response is the one OpenSSH chose: ship a workaround immediately, even a workaround the maintainers consider to be in someone else's code.

Which raises the uncomfortable question this bug is a good test case for. OpenSSH called the root cause "outside sshd"; Rich Felker called it "not a bug in musl just an erroneous use by the caller," while conceding the mechanism "very likely will be changed in the upcoming release cycle." Both statements are defensible, and the vulnerable window is the space between them. When a defect lives at a boundary, the party that ships the fix is the party whose users are exposed — not the party whose abstraction leaked.

sections.heading: What to change in your own code
sections.text:
The transferable rule is narrower than "validate your inputs," and it is worth stating precisely because this class of bug keeps landing:
Never let an error indicator share a value space with valid data. If a function's failure mode is a string, that string must be one that no legitimate value can hold. "" fails this test; "0" and "x!" pass it by accident, which is not a design.
Validate shape before comparing. The 10.6p2 fix does not attempt to detect the libc bug; it asserts that the thing it is about to compare is long enough to be a hash. Cheap, local, and it survives the next libc that invents a new sentinel.
When a fix closes a timing oracle by doing more work, ask what input you just accepted. The 2016 change was correct and it widened the input surface of a function that had previously been called with a fixed, safe argument.
Test the configuration nobody runs. The vulnerable combination was in the release notes of three projects and in no test matrix.

The bug is patched, and the window is closed. The reason it is worth writing down is that it took four good decisions, fourteen years, and one character to make an authentication check return true for a password nobody set.

sections.heading: Sources
sections.text:
OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes, 2026-11-05 — the fix, the AI-reporting paragraph, and the release-cadence change.
Commit 4353fdc — MIN_PASSWORD_HASH_LEN 4, the length check, and the pick_salt() memory handling changes.
Alpine Linux advisory, 2026-11-05 — preconditions, fixed versions per branch, tiny-cloud impact, detection guidance.
Damien Miller, "urgent security release: 10.6p2" — one-day turnaround and the embargo reasoning.
Rich Felker, "Advisory for OpenSSH+musl users" — musl's position and the planned change.
musl commit b3c4cc12, 2012-08-09 — "unmatchable hash rather than NULL", and the "x" guard for a setting in the DES module.
musl commit 88bf5a8a, 2012-08-29 — SHA-256/SHA-512 crypt, KEY_MAX 256, "on error is returned".
musl crypt_sha512.c — KEY_MAX, the O(klen²) comment, and crypt_sha512 returning "" on failure.

CVE-2019-5021 — Alpine images shipping root with no password, and the ! → history that followed.

SecurityWeek, OpenSSH rushes patches for "SSHole" — reports CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS 8.1); Alpine's advisory notes no CVE had been assigned when it published.
Measurements: my own probes, cryptprobe.c and sshd_compare.c, run in alpine:3.22 (musl 1.2, gcc from apk) and debian:bookworm (glibc via libxcrypt). The compare table reimplements sys_auth_passwd() and calls the real crypt(); it is not sshd itself. One image per libc, no kernel or build variation explored.

python-310-end-of-life-upgrade-guide.title: Python 3.10 End of Life: A Practical Upgrade Guide for 2026
python-310-end-of-life-upgrade-guide.description: Python 3.10 reached end of life on October 1, 2026. Check your runtime, choose a supported version, and plan a tested upgrade with an interactive quiz.

sections.text:
Your application still starts. Your tests still pass. The Docker image still builds. None of those things tell you whether the interpreter underneath it will receive another security fix.

Python 3.10 reached end of life on October 1, 2026. The official release announcement names 3.10.22 as its final release and says the series will receive no further security updates. Installing that final patch does not extend its support window.

This is the useful question behind the release news: which Python actually runs your application, who maintains it, and how do you replace it without guessing about compatibility?
The short answer: Inventory deployed interpreters, choose a supported target your dependencies can run on, recreate environments, then test and roll out a new artifact. Updating packages with pip does not update Python.

The support table below is a snapshot checked on October 5, 2026, not a permanent promise about which patch is latest.

sections.heading: What changed in the October Python releases?
sections.text:
The October 1 announcement covers five series: 3.10.22, 3.11.17, 3.12.15, 3.13.16, and 3.14.8. Their version numbers look like a routine patch sweep. Their support implications are different.

| Python series | Upstream status on October 5, 2026 | What that means for an upgrade |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 3.10 | End of life; 3.10.22 is the final release | Move off the series; a final patch is not continuing support |
| 3.11 | Security fixes only; scheduled EOL October 2027 | Still supported, but offers a shorter support runway |
| 3.12 | Security fixes only; scheduled EOL October 2028 | A possible compatibility-driven target, not the newest maintenance branch |
| 3.13 | Security fixes only; scheduled EOL October 2029 | 3.13.16 was the last full maintenance release, including binary installers |
| 3.14 | Bugfix maintenance; scheduled EOL October 2030 | A reasonable target to evaluate when dependencies and deployment tooling support it |

Sources: Python's version-status guide and the October release announcement. The future EOL months are scheduled dates and can change.

There is another distinction worth keeping straight: support status is not installer availability. Python 3.11 and 3.12 still receive upstream security fixes, but the announced 3.11.17 and 3.12.15 releases are source-only. Python 3.10.22 is also source-only, and that series is now unsupported.

A missing Windows or macOS installer does not mean every series in the announcement is EOL. An available installer does not guarantee years of full maintenance ahead.

sections.heading: Step 1: Find the Python you actually deploy
sections.text:
Do not stop at the version on your laptop. Check the application container, worker image, scheduled job, CI runner, and production process separately.

Run these commands inside the environment being inspected:

The executable path helps distinguish a system interpreter from a project environment. Using python -m pip associates the package tool with that interpreter instead of whichever standalone pip happens to be on your shell's path.

The standard library documents sys.executable, sys.version, and the -VV option. If your environment uses another executable name, substitute that interpreter explicitly.

Record three things for each deployed workload:
Interpreter and provenance: Python version, executable path, container base image or operating-system package.
Dependency contract: The project's lockfile or dependency manifest, including native extensions.
Owner and deployment path: Who can rebuild, test, and replace the running artifact.

The version in pyproject.toml describes a constraint. It does not prove what an already-deployed process is running. Likewise, upgrading a host's Python does not necessarily replace Python inside a container built months earlier.

 
 My Linux distribution still supports its Python 3.10 package. Am I unsupported? 

Upstream CPython support and distribution support are separate contracts. A vendor may backport fixes under its own policy. Check the exact distribution release, package, advisory history, and support entitlement.

The upstream EOL notice does not establish that your vendor has stopped maintaining its package. It also does not establish that your vendor is maintaining it. Record the evidence rather than inferring either answer from the minor version.
code:
python -VV
python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable); print(sys.version)"
python -m pip --version

sections.heading: Step 2: Choose a target your application can prove
sections.text:
Evaluate the latest supported maintenance series first. As of this snapshot, that is Python 3.14. Treat it as a candidate, not a compatibility guarantee.

Your framework, database driver, numerical stack, monitoring agent, and deployment platform may constrain the move. A package publishing a compatible wheel matters when your build environment cannot compile an extension. A successful install matters, but is not the same as a successful application test.

If a dependency prevents the preferred target, make the fallback explicit: a supported series, a reason, an owner, and a date to revisit it. Moving from 3.10 to 3.11 buys upstream support time; it does not buy the same runway as a later supported series.

Read the target's migration notes, including Python 3.14's porting section, alongside your dependencies' release notes. When crossing several versions, review the intervening changes too. Do not assume code that passed on 3.10 behaves identically after four minor-version changes.

 
 Should I jump through every Python version in production? 

Not necessarily. A direct move to a supported target can be reasonable when your dependencies support it and your tests cover the relevant behavior.

Testing an intermediate interpreter can help isolate a compatibility failure. That is a debugging technique, not a requirement to deploy each version along the way.

sections.heading: Step 3: Recreate the environment, then test the application
sections.text:
A virtual environment is based on the interpreter that created it. The venv documentation describes environments as disposable and explains why they should be recreated rather than moved or copied.

Build a separate target environment from the project's dependency contract. Keep the currently working deployment intact while you evaluate the replacement.

For a POSIX project that already uses requirements.txt and pytest, the shape is:

This is an illustrative workflow, not a universal installer. Use your repository's lockfile-aware installer and test command when they differ. Verify the chosen interpreter's patch version too; python3.14 alone does not establish that it is current.

 
 Show the equivalent PowerShell commands on Windows 

This example assumes the Python launcher can select an installed Python 3.14 interpreter, and the project has the same requirements.txt and pytest setup.

Calling the environment's interpreter directly avoids depending on shell activation. See the Windows launcher documentation for interpreter selection.

 

pip check checks installed dependency compatibility. It does not test application behavior, audit every vulnerability, or prove that a native extension works with your production data.

Put the old and candidate runtimes through the same meaningful checks: unit tests, integration tests, application startup, database connections, serialization boundaries, background jobs, and your critical request paths. During the migration, an old-runtime CI lane is a useful comparison. Once the migration is complete, remove it from the supported matrix rather than accidentally advertising ongoing 3.10 support.
code:
# Assumes Python 3.14 is installed and pytest is a declared test dependency.
python3.14 -m venv .venv-314
.venv-314/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv-314/bin/python -m pip check
.venv-314/bin/python -m pytest

py -3.14 -m venv .venv-314
.\.venv-314\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements.txt
.\.venv-314\Scripts\python.exe -m pip check
.\.venv-314\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest

sections.heading: Step 4: Roll out an artifact, not a version string
sections.text:
For containers, update the base image, rebuild dependencies, run checks against the resulting image, and deploy that image. Editing a Dockerfile without rebuilding does not change running containers.

For managed platforms, verify the runtime configured in the deployment system and the runtime reported by the deployed application. For operating-system packages, follow the platform's supported application deployment path; do not replace a system interpreter blindly.

A staged rollout needs a clear success signal: application health, error rates, worker failures, and whichever business operation the service exists to perform. Compare the candidate with your current behavior rather than accepting "the process started" as the finish line.

Keep a known-good artifact available during the transition. Code rollback does not automatically reverse a database or data-format change. If the runtime upgrade is bundled with a schema change, evaluate that compatibility separately; the zero-downtime database migration guide covers that adjacent deployment problem.

sections.heading: Interactive check: Can you spot the upgrade traps?
sections.text: These five scenarios test the distinctions that matter: upstream support, vendor maintenance, package updates, installer availability, and rollback. Choose an answer to reveal its explanation; complete the quiz or restart it to try another path.

sections.heading: Does end of life mean my application will stop working?
sections.text: No. It means upstream Python 3.10 maintenance has ended. Existing programs can continue running; that is not evidence that the runtime will receive future security fixes. Vendor-maintained packages need their own support-policy check.

sections.heading: Is Python 3.11 still supported?
sections.text: Yes, in security-fix-only mode as of this article's October 5 snapshot, with EOL scheduled for October 2027. The announced 3.11.17 patch is source-only. Support and official binary installers are separate questions.

sections.heading: Is updating to Python 3.10.22 enough?
sections.text: It gets you to the final upstream release. It does not remove the need to migrate to a supported interpreter or establish a separately maintained vendor package.

sections.heading: Which Python version should I upgrade to?
sections.text: Evaluate the current supported maintenance series, then verify your dependency and deployment compatibility. At this snapshot, Python 3.14 is the maintenance-series candidate. If it does not work for your application yet, document a supported fallback and a follow-up plan rather than declaring compatibility without tests.

sections.heading: The decision to make this week
sections.text:
The release announcement gives you a deadline fact, not an application migration result. Turn it into a small, owned piece of work: identify every deployed 3.10 interpreter, establish who maintains it, choose a supported target, and test the artifact you intend to ship.

A passing application is one signal. A maintained runtime is another. You need both.

sections.heading: Sources and freshness
sections.text:
Python's October 1, 2026 release announcement — final 3.10 release, five-series patch sweep, and installer distinctions.
Python 3.10.22 release page — release date and explicit end-of-life notice.
Status of Python versions — support phases and scheduled EOL dates.
Python 3.14 porting notes and venv documentation — compatibility review and environment recreation.

Support status and release availability were checked on October 5, 2026. Recheck the official version-status and download pages when following this guide later.
