tech-layoffs-economy-analysis.title: What Happens to the Economy When Tech Companies Mass Lay Off Workers?
tech-layoffs-economy-analysis.description: How mass tech layoffs ripple through housing markets, consumer spending, and startup funding, plus what they mean for your career as a developer.

sections.text:
Between 2022 and May 2026, public layoff trackers count more than 820,000 tech jobs cut across companies like Meta, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and hundreds of startups. The peak was 2023, with roughly 264,000 tracked layoffs. 2024 cooled but still saw about 153,000 cuts, 2025 added roughly 125,000, and 2026 had already crossed six figures by late May. This wasn't routine restructuring -- it was a sector-wide reset after a decade of overhiring fueled by near-zero interest rates.

If you're a developer, you felt it. Job postings dried up. Offer rescissions became normalized. Senior engineers competed for mid-level roles. But beyond the personal anxiety, what does this actually do to the broader economy?

sections.heading: Why Tech Layoffs Hit Differently
sections.text:
Not all layoffs are equal. A wave of retail layoffs affects the economy differently than a wave of tech layoffs. Here's why tech workers are economically disproportionate:

High income, high spending multiplier. The average software engineer in the US earns $130,000–$220,000. Economists use a concept called the local multiplier effect — each high-paying tech job creates an estimated 4–5 additional local service jobs (restaurants, childcare, construction, retail). When that tech job disappears, those 4–5 downstream jobs are at risk too.

Concentrated geography. Tech workers are clustered in San Francisco, Seattle, Austin, New York, and a handful of other metros. A national layoff wave of 100,000 engineers is effectively a localized economic shock to 6–8 cities, not a diffuse nationwide event. This concentration amplifies local impacts.

High equity exposure. Unlike most workers, many tech employees have significant wealth tied to stock options and RSUs. When layoffs happen alongside stock price drops — which is common since layoffs often signal broader company stress — employees lose both income and paper wealth simultaneously.

sections.heading: The Housing Market Effect
sections.text:
This is the most visible and measurable economic impact. Let's look at what happened in San Francisco after the 2022–2023 tech layoff wave:
Office vacancy rates in SF hit 36% in 2024 — the highest of any major US city
Median rents in SoMa and SOMA-adjacent neighborhoods fell 15–20% from 2022 peaks
Commercial real estate values in tech-heavy corridors dropped 40–60%

The mechanism: high-earning tech workers competed for premium housing and drove up prices. Their departure — or their employers' collapse — removes this demand. In cities where tech is the dominant employer, this can trigger a downward spiral: lower property values → lower property tax revenue → municipal budget cuts → degraded public services → further exodus.

 

Austin saw a softer version of this after the 2023 tech slowdown, with the condo market cooling sharply after years of price appreciation driven by the relocation of tech workers from California.

For context: the U.S. tech workforce is under 10 million people nationally, but the spending is highly concentrated in metro areas. Their layoffs don't just reduce aggregate demand -- they hollow out specific local economies.

sections.heading: Consumer Spending and the Confidence Effect
sections.text:
Aggregate demand drives economies. When thousands of $150K+ earners lose their jobs, the direct spending reduction is significant. But the indirect confidence effect is larger.

Economists distinguish between two types of consumer behavior:
Current income effect: you stop spending because you lost income
Permanent income hypothesis: you change spending based on expectations of future income

Tech workers who remain employed after rounds of layoffs often significantly reduce discretionary spending — not because they can't afford it, but because they're uncertain whether their job is next. This behavioral shift is hard to measure but matters enormously.

After large 2022-2024 layoff rounds, the pullback showed up in categories that depend on high-income confidence:
Restaurant and entertainment spending
Large discretionary purchases like cars, furniture, and travel
Home improvement and renovation work
Premium subscriptions and business software bought by small teams

Multiply this across hundreds of thousands of workers who survived layoffs but changed their behavior, and you get a measurable drag on consumer-driven economic sectors.

sections.heading: What Happens to Startups
sections.text:
The startup ecosystem is where the economy regenerates tech capacity. Layoffs affect it in complex, contradictory ways.

The talent availability paradox. On one hand, layoffs flood the market with experienced engineers, making talent more accessible and affordable for startups. Founders who had struggled to recruit senior engineers during the 2021 boom suddenly had more realistic hiring conversations. This is genuinely good for startups trying to build.

On the other hand, consumer-facing startups face destroyed demand. B2C startups targeting tech workers — fintech apps, premium productivity tools, high-end consumer software — see their addressable market shrink directly when their core customer base loses jobs or cuts spending.

The venture capital feedback loop. VC funding and tech employment are deeply correlated. When tech companies cut costs and signal market contraction, VCs tighten their own portfolios. Sequoia's famous "Adapt or Die" memo in 2022 explicitly told portfolio companies to cut burn rates, which cascaded into thousands of startup layoffs beyond the big-tech ones. Less VC funding → fewer new companies → fewer new jobs created to absorb laid-off workers.

The founder opportunity. There is a silver lining that economists and VCs frequently note: recessions and downturns create the best companies. Airbnb, Uber, Slack, WhatsApp, and Venmo were all founded during or immediately after the 2008 financial crisis. The reason: talent is available, office space is cheap, and necessity breeds innovation. The 2022–2024 layoff wave has already spawned thousands of new AI-focused startups, many founded by ex-FAANG engineers.

sections.heading: The Structural Shift: AI as the Real Variable
sections.text:
Here's what makes the current layoff cycle different from all previous ones: the stated reason for many cuts is AI-driven productivity gains, not just economic cycles.

When large tech companies cite AI investment, efficiency, and flatter organizations as reasons for headcount reductions, they're signaling something the 2008 or 2001 cycles didn't involve -- that some of these jobs may not come back, even during the next economic expansion.

The economic implications of this are significant and contested:

Scenario A: Augmentation (optimistic). AI tools make each developer 2–3x more productive. Companies need fewer developers for the same output, but the economy grows faster because software gets built cheaper and faster. GDP grows. Employment shifts — fewer developers, more AI trainers, more product managers, more security specialists.

Scenario B: Displacement (pessimistic). AI automates entire job categories faster than new categories emerge. Unlike previous technological shifts (the internet, mobile), AI substitution happens across white-collar work simultaneously. The transition period creates prolonged unemployment and economic dislocation.

The data from 2024–2026 suggests something between the two: AI tools have materially changed what a team of 5 developers can produce, but the productivity gains have primarily benefited companies (via cost reduction) rather than workers (via wage growth or job creation). This is a distributional problem — the economy may grow while tech employment stays flat or contracts.

sections.heading: The Government Revenue Problem
sections.text:
This is underappreciated in most layoff analyses. Tech workers pay significantly more in income tax than the average worker — not just because of salaries, but because of capital gains from RSU and stock option vesting.

During the 2020-2021 tech boom, California collected record income tax revenue, much of it from IPO-related capital gains and stock compensation. When financial markets cooled and layoffs began in 2022, California's revenue base weakened sharply. The Legislative Analyst's Office later estimated a $68 billion budget problem for 2024-25, with 2022-23 revenue coming in $26 billion below budget assumptions. The state is unusually exposed to tech cycles because income-tax receipts depend heavily on high earners and capital gains.

This creates a pro-cyclical government funding problem: when the economy is booming (and government spending is most needed for public goods), tech-driven tax revenue is high. When layoffs happen and unemployment services are most needed, that same tax base collapses. States with heavy tech sector dependency are essentially running a hidden leveraged bet on tech employment.

sections.heading: What This Means for Your Career as a Developer
sections.text:
If you're a software engineer reading this, here's the actionable picture:

The job market has structurally changed. The 2010s model of "become a developer, get multiple competing offers, negotiate aggressively" no longer universally applies. The direction changed: fewer openings, longer interview loops, more applicants per role, and less leverage for mid-level generalist engineers.

 

Specialization now matters more than generalism. AI can handle more generalist coding tasks. The engineers with strong job security are those with domain expertise that's hard to replicate: distributed systems at scale, security, ML infrastructure, regulatory-heavy domains (fintech/healthtech), and embedded/systems work.

Geographic diversification is real. The remote work normalization accelerated by COVID — and not reversed by layoffs — has genuinely distributed tech employment. Warsaw, Bangalore, São Paulo, and Toronto now compete in the same talent market as San Francisco. This is deflationary for US tech wages but inflationary for global economic opportunity.

Equity is not a salary substitute. The 2022 crash reminded thousands of engineers that unvested RSUs are not money. If you took a below-market salary for equity that never vested, that was a real economic loss. Cash compensation is worth more during uncertainty.

Build financial buffer, not lifestyle inflation. High income does not protect you if fixed costs expand to match it. Engineers who built 12-month emergency funds and avoided lifestyle inflation weathered layoffs dramatically better than those who expanded spending to match income.

sections.heading: The Macro Outlook
sections.text:
If mass layoffs continue at scale — particularly AI-driven cuts across not just tech but finance, legal, healthcare administration, and other white-collar sectors — the economic consequences are severe:

1. Consumer spending contracts across premium discretionary categories
2. Housing markets in tech hubs reprice significantly downward
3. Local governments face fiscal crises from reduced tax bases
4. Inequality widens as the gains from AI productivity accrue to capital, not labor
5. Social spending demands increase as retraining becomes necessary at scale

The countervailing forces are real too: new industries emerge, costs decrease for consumers, global productivity grows. But the transition is not smooth, not fast, and not evenly distributed.

For developers, the message is uncomfortable but clear: the era of unconditional demand for software engineers is over. What replaced it is an era where the best engineers — those who combine deep technical skill with business judgment, who can work alongside AI tools rather than be replaced by them — are more valuable than ever. And the rest of the market has thinned.

The economy will adapt. It always does. But this cycle is different enough in character — AI displacement, not just cyclical downturn — that treating it as a normal recession would be a mistake.

sections.heading: Data Notes and Sources
sections.text:
The numbers here are directional because layoff trackers, official labor data, venture funding reports, and local real estate reports measure different things. The layoff totals use Layoffs.fyi as a public tracker through May 26, 2026. Software compensation context uses the BLS software developer outlook. The local multiplier discussion follows Enrico Moretti's work and the Bay Area Council Economic Institute summary. San Francisco vacancy context comes from commercial real estate market reports such as Cushman & Wakefield Q2 2024 MarketBeat. California budget context comes from the Legislative Analyst's Office 2024-25 Fiscal Outlook.

---

_Views expressed are analytical perspectives based on publicly available economic data and industry reporting. This is not financial advice._

testing-ai-agent-actions.title: Testing AI Agent Actions: A Runnable Approval and Retry Harness
testing-ai-agent-actions.description: Twelve reproducible fixtures for an AI agent action gate: missing approvals, cross-project access, changed arguments, duplicate retries, conflicting keys.

sections.text:
An agent proposes a ticket. The application checks permission and approval, creates it, then loses the response. The agent retries. Does the second attempt create a second ticket?

That question is small enough to test without a model. It is also easy to miss if the only thing you inspect is the final chat response.

I built a small, local harness for the boundary between an agent proposing an action and an application executing it. It has twelve fixtures, a deliberately unsafe mode, and no API keys or external writes. You can download both files and run the same checks.

This is an educational experiment, not a report from a production deployment or a benchmark of an AI model. It tests a deterministic action gate. A passing result says that these particular fixtures behave as specified.

sections.heading: Run the example
sections.text:
Download the evaluation script and test fixtures into the same directory. Read the script, then run it with Node.js:

The first command should print 12/12 fixtures passed (guarded mode) and exit successfully. The second deliberately bypasses the gate. It should print 1/12 fixtures passed (unsafe mode) and exit with code 1. That failure is intentional: it demonstrates that the checks notice missing controls. Both modes write only to an in-memory array.

In this repository, the equivalent command is:
code:
node evaluate.mjs
node evaluate.mjs --unsafe
node public/examples/agent-action-evals/evaluate.mjs

sections.heading: Separate a proposal from permission
sections.text:
The demo accepts one tool: create_ticket. Its proposal contains a project, title, and request key. Those fields describe what the agent wants to do; they do not establish its authority to do it.

The application supplies a separate trusted context containing the user identity, allowed projects, and approved actions. In the fixtures, that context is test setup. In a real application, it must come from authenticated application state and the approval workflow, outside the model's control.

The ordering matters. A previously completed request does not bypass today's access or approval checks. Extra proposal fields, including approved: true, cannot change the trusted context and are never forwarded to the mock tool.
code:
Agent proposal
    → validate the tool and arguments
    → check project access
    → require approval for the exact action
    → check the request key
    → execute the permitted fields

sections.heading: The twelve fixtures
sections.text:
Each fixture starts with a fresh gate. A retry fixture contains multiple proposals so they share the same in-memory request history.

| Fixture | Expected outcome | Expected writes |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------- |
| Approved action | Executed | One ticket |
| Missing approval | Approval required | None |
| Proposal claims it is approved | Approval required | None |
| Retrieved text claims approval | Approval required | None |
| Different project, even with approval | Forbidden | None |
| Unknown tool | Unsupported tool | None |
| Blank title | Invalid | None |
| Title has the wrong type | Invalid | None |
| Null proposal | Invalid | None |
| Arguments changed after approval | Approval required | None |
| Same request retried | Executed, then duplicate | One ticket |
| Same key reused for different approved actions | Executed, then key conflict | First ticket only |

The harness checks both the returned outcomes and the exact writes. Checking only a response such as “approval required” would miss an implementation that rejects the request after it has already changed state.

The unsafe mode still passes the approved-action fixture. It fails the other eleven because it executes proposals without checking permission, approval, or request history. This is a useful negative control; a suite that also passed the unsafe version would deserve immediate suspicion.

sections.heading: Approval belongs to the exact action
sections.text:
“Allow this tool” and “approve this ticket” are different policies. This example chooses the narrower one: approval covers the tool, project, title, and request key together.

If a proposal changes after approval, it needs a new approval. The changed-arguments fixture proves that an approval for “Investigate timeout” cannot authorize “Delete the audit log,” even though both are merely ticket titles in this simulation.

The fixture that includes a forged instruction in a document field checks a similarly narrow property: extra text cannot grant approval through this interface. It does not prove a model resists prompt injection. No model reads the document here. Testing the upstream model requires supplying hostile documents to the real workflow and examining the resulting proposals.

sections.heading: A retry must preserve the identity of the work
sections.text:
The demo scopes its request key to the user and project. When the same key arrives again, it compares the approved action with the recorded one:
Same key and same action: report a duplicate without another write.
Same key and different action: report a conflict without another write.

The request key must remain stable across retries. If an agent invents a new key on every attempt, this mechanism cannot recognize duplicate work. A production application should own the logical request identity and carry it through retries.

An in-memory map is enough to demonstrate the policy, but it does not survive restarts or coordinate multiple processes. This example's execution is synchronous. It does not test concurrent requests, a crash between the external write and the local record, or the case where the downstream service succeeds but its response is lost. Those require durable coordination and a recovery design appropriate to the actual service. Do not copy this map into a production integration and call it exactly-once delivery.

sections.heading: Add the model evaluation as a separate layer
sections.text:
After testing the boundary, I would evaluate whether the real workflow proposes the right actions in the first place. Keep that experiment separate so a permission bug does not get confused with a planning error.

For each task, record the expected outcome, allowed actions, actual tool calls, unintended writes, latency, and cost. Include tasks that should finish without any write. Keep the model version, prompts, tool definitions, and test data fixed when comparing changes; run repeated trials to expose variability.

Report failures by category. A single overall pass rate hides the difference between an agent failing to create a ticket and creating a ticket in a project it should never access. Expand the dataset with independently designed cases and failures found in the real workflow. Twelve hand-written fixtures are a starting point, not a release criterion for every application.

sections.heading: Where this fits
sections.text:
If you are starting with tool calling, read the TypeScript MCP server walkthrough. For the broader security questions, continue with agent trust boundaries and MCP.

The useful artifact here is the executable contract: these proposals may create one ticket, and these proposals must create none. That gives the rest of the agent workflow a boundary you can inspect, break deliberately, and improve.

For a broader treatment of task design, graders, and repeated trials, see Anthropic's guide to agent evaluations.
Before we start to learn about what is HTTPS, let us first know the benefits:

sections.heading: 1. HTTPS makes your website less vulnerable to cybercrimes
sections.text: Let’s say you have a website that brings your customers to a third-party page where they make purchases using a credit card. If your site isn’t secured with HTTPS, or it is set up incorrectly, bad actors can intercept the content of your website, then easily create the exact same payment page they can control and allow them to see and capture each credit card number your customers submit. Having to resolve customer complaints due to lax site security resulting in credit card theft could be fatal to your business.

sections.heading: 2. Google tends to rank secure websites higher than websites without HTTPS
sections.text:
When Google changed its algorithm back in 2014, we saw a 60–70% increase in SSL update among millions of websites out there. Websites that become HTTPS secure got ranked higher, while the ranking of websites without HTTPS slightly dropped.

Sooner or later, HTTPS will become a standard consumers demand, and websites will need to have it in order to come across as trustworthy, reliable, and secure.

sections.heading: 3. A secure website gives you a better reputation
sections.text:
If visitors come to your website and can see your site information can be easily intercepted, it definitely does not give a good impression. If your website is not safe, secure, and reliable, what makes you think your customers would risk purchasing from you when they can purchase similar products/services from your competitors with more secure websites?

To ensure you maintain your company’s and brand’s good reputation, you should make a good first impression by showing that your site is HTTPS secured.

sections.heading: HTTPS (Secure Hypertext Transport Protocol)
sections.text:
HTTPS is a secure version of HTTP. This ensures that any communication sent online is secured by the SSL/TLS connection. Any ongoing communication between the server and browser will be encrypted for your safety. It allows you to evaluate how secure the environment is. If you are looking to establish an HTTPS connection, you will have to first purchase an SSL certificate from someone you can trust. You don’t want to purchase a certificate from just anyone. Look for trusted certificate authority. Then, you need to install it on the proper server.

HTTPS is the code-text that is written using standard HTTPS format and secured with SSL/TLS to encrypt the HTTP text and ensure the communication is protected at all times.

There are a number of reasons to use an HTTPS connection:
It helps to establish a secure communication between server and browser.
It secures websites against tampering activities or eavesdropping.
It protects users from man-in-the-middle attacks.
It is used worldwide by business of all sizes to process secure payment transactions.
It is used by banking, healthcare, eCommerce, social media, and government industries.

Regardless of what your situation might be, you need to look into the benefits of implementing SSL, HTTPS, and TLS secure connections in your business. You never know just how beneficial these secure methods are until you have to use them.

sections.heading: In HTTPS, how does TLS/SSL encrypt HTTP requests and responses?
sections.text:
TLS uses a technology called public key encryption: there are two keys, a public key and a private key, and the public key is shared with client devices via the server’s SSL certificate. When a client opens a connection with a server, the two devices use the public and private key to agree on new keys, called session keys, to encrypt further communications between them.

All HTTP requests and responses are then encrypted with these session keys (this takes place at layer 6 in the OSI model), so that anyone who intercepts communications can only see a random string of characters, not the plaintext.

## But HTTPS doesn’t always mean the site is safe

Let’s be honest, when most people see a little green lock with the word “Secure” to the left of a URL, they think the site is safe. Ditto for spotting the words “this site uses a secure connection” or a URL beginning with the letters “https.” More and more sites these days are switching to HTTPS. Most have no choice, in fact. So what’s the problem? The more secure sites there are, the better — right?

 

We’re about to let you in on a little secret: Those “Secure” symbols don’t guarantee a website is safe from all threats. A phishing site, for example, can legitimately display that comforting green lock next to its https address. So, what’s going on? Let’s find out.

sections.heading: A secure connection does not mean a secure site
sections.text:
The green lock means that the site has been issued a certificate and that a pair of cryptographic keys has been generated for it. Such sites encrypt information transmitted between you and the site. In this case, the page URLs begin with HTTPS, with the last “S” standing for “Secure.”

Sure, encrypting transmitted data is a good thing. It means that information exchanged between your browser and the site is not accessible to third parties — ISPs, network administrators, intruders, and so on. It lets you enter passwords or credit card details without worrying about prying eyes.

But the problem is that the green lock and the issued certificate say nothing about the site itself. A phishing page can just as readily get a certificate and encrypt all traffic that flows between you and it.

Put simply, all a green lock ensures is that no one _else_ can spy on the data you enter. But your password can still be stolen by the site itself, if it’s fake.

Phishers make active use of this: According to Phishlabs, a quarter of all phishing attacks today are carried out on HTTPS sites (two years ago it was less than 1 percent). Moreover, more than 80 percent of users believe that the mere presence of a little green lock and the word “Secure” next to the URL means the site is safe, and they don’t think too hard before entering their data.

sections.heading: How not to fall for the bait
sections.text:
To sum up, the presence of a certificate and the green lock means only that the data transmitted between you and the site is encrypted, and that the certificate was issued by a trusted certificate authority. But it doesn’t prevent an HTTPS site from being malicious, a fact that is most skillfully manipulated by phishing scammers.

So always be alert, no matter how safe the site seems at first glance.
Never enter logins, passwords, banking credentials, or any other personal information on the site unless you are sure of its authenticity. To do so, always check the domain name — and very carefully; the name of a fake site might differ by only one character. And ensure links are reliable before clicking.
Always consider what a particular site is offering, whether it looks suspicious, and whether you really need to register on it.

sections.heading: SSL (Secure Socket Layer)
sections.text:
SSL was created by Netscape Communications Corporation back in 1994. It was designed to create a secure internet communication via the Web. It is a standard protocol that encrypts communication between your browser and the server, and allows for private information like social security numbers, credit card details, and login credentials to be transferred easily over the Internet.

SSL utilizes two keys:
Public keys that are knowable by everyone.
Private keys known only by the person receiving the message.

The two keys work together to form an encrypted connection via the Web.

Being able to connect to a specific port requires a secure connection. As an example, you would use port 443 for HTTPS, 995 for secure POP3, 993 for secure IMAP, and so on. All of these ports are already set up on the server. They are ready to negotiate secure connections first, then they will proceed to do whatever else you need after that.

sections.heading: How does HTTPS help authenticate web servers?
sections.text:
Authentication means verifying that a person or machine is who they claim to be. In HTTP, there is no verification of identity — it’s based on a principle of trust. The architects of HTTP didn’t necessarily make a decision to implicitly trust all web servers; they simply had priorities other than security at the time. But on the modern Internet, authentication is essential.

Just like an ID card confirms a person’s identity, a private key confirms server identity. When a client opens a channel with an origin server (e.g. when a user navigates to a website), possession of the private key that matches with the public key in a website’s SSL certificate proves that the server is actually the legitimate host of the website. This prevents or helps block a number of attacks that are possible when there is no authentication, such as:
Man-in-the-middle attacks
DNS hijacking
BGP hijacking
Domain spoofing

sections.heading: HTTPS myth-conceptions (src: CloudFlare)
sections.text:
Many websites have been slow to adopt HTTPS. To explore why this is the case we have to look at the history.

When HTTPS initially began rolling out, proper implementation was hard, slow, and expensive; it was hard to implement properly, slowed down Internet requests, and increased costs by requiring expensive certificate services. None of these impediments remain true, but a lingering fear still exists for a lot of website owners, which has impeded some taking the leap into better security. Let’s explore some of the myths about HTTPS.

“I don’t handle sensitive information on my website so I don’t need HTTPS”

A common reason websites don’t implement security is because they think it’s overkill for their purposes. After all, if you’re not dealing with sensitive data, who cares if someone is snooping? There are a few reasons that this is an overly simplistic view on web security. For example, some Internet service providers will actually inject advertising into HTTP-served websites. These ads may or may not be in line with the content of the website, and can potentially be offensive, aside from the fact that the website provider has no creative input or share of the revenue. These injected ads are no longer feasible once a site is secured.

Modern web browsers now limit functionality for sites that are not secure. Important features that improve the quality of the website now require HTTPS. Geolocation, push notifications and the service workers needed to run progressive web applications (PWAs) all require heightened security. This makes sense; data such as a user’s location is sensitive and can be used for nefarious purposes.

“I don’t want to damage my website’s performance by increasing my page load times”

Performance is an important factor in both user experience and how Google returns results in search. Understandably, increasing latency is something to take seriously. Luckily, over time improvements have been made to HTTPS to reduce the performance overhead required to set up a encrypted connection.

When an HTTP connection occurs, there are a number of trips the connection needs to make between the client requesting the webpage and the server. Aside from the normal latency associated with a TCP handshake (shown in blue below), an additional TLS/SSL handshake (shown in yellow) must occur to use HTTPS.

 _src: CloudFlare_

Improvements can be implemented to reduce the total latency of creating a SSL connection, including TLS session resumption and TLS false start.

By using session resumption a server can keep a connection alive for longer by resuming the same session for additional requests. Keeping the connection alive saves time spent renegotiating the connection when the client requires an uncached origin fetch, reducing the total RTT by 50%.

Another improvement to the speed at which an encrypted channel can be created is to implement a process called TLS false start, which cuts down on the latency by sending the encrypted data before the client has finished authentication.

Last but not least, HTTPS unlocks performance enhancements using HTTP/2 that let you do cool things like server pushing and multiplexing which can greatly optimize performance for HTTP requests. In total there is a significant performance benefit for making the switch.

“It’s too expensive for me to implement HTTPS”

At one point this may have been true, but now the cost is no longer a concern.

“I’m going to lose search ranking while migrating my site to HTTPS”

There are risks associated with website migration, and done improperly a negative SEO impact is possible. Potential pitfalls include website downtime, uncrawled webpages, and penalization for content duplication when two copies of the site exist at the same time. That said, websites can be migrated safely to HTTPS by following best practices.

Two of the most important migration practices are:

1. using 301 redirects and 2) the proper placement of canonical tags. By using server 301 redirects on the HTTP site to point to the HTTPS version, a website tells Google to move to the new location for all search and indexing purposes. By placing canonical tags on the HTTPS site only, crawlers such as Googlebot will know that the new secure content should be considered canonical going forward.

If you have a large number of pages and are concerned that the recrawl will take too long, reach out to Google and tell them how much traffic you’re willing to put through your website. The network engineers will then crank up the crawl rate to help parse your site quickly and get it indexed.
## Stay Curious!

understory-engineering-blogs-explained.title: Understory: Engineering Blogs, Explained, With Receipts
understory-engineering-blogs-explained.description: Why I built Understory, a reading layer that turns new engineering blog posts into reviewed explainers with diagrams, an ELI5, trade-offs, and a citation behind every claim. Runs entirely on the Cloudflare free tier.

sections.text:
I read a lot of engineering blogs. Most weeks I open more posts than I finish, and the ones I do finish often leave me with the announcement and not the mechanism. A post says "we cut p99 latency by 40%" and I spend the next twenty minutes reading three other articles to work out what they actually changed.

So I built Understory. It watches the posts that engineeringblogs.xyz already aggregates, and when one looks worth the time it produces an explainer: context, how the thing works, a diagram, an ELI5, the trade-offs the announcement leaves out, and a source behind every substantive claim. A person reviews each one before it goes live.
Try it: understory.piyushmehta.com. Source on GitHub, code under MIT and content under CC BY 4.0.

The name is the layer of a forest that sits under the canopy. The headline is the canopy. The interesting part is underneath it.

sections.heading: What a reader gets
The pipeline is deliberately boring
sections.text:
I wanted something I could leave running without worrying about it. Every step is a separate job with its own row in the database, so a failure stops at the step that failed and nothing half-finished leaks onto the site.

 

1. Discover. A cron trigger runs every 15 minutes, reads the engineeringblogs.xyz listing, and records new links. It takes at most six new posts per run, ignores anything older than four days, and skips sources under 220 words.
2. Extract. A queue job fetches the article and runs it through Cloudflare's HTMLRewriter. It strips navigation, share bars, comments, and ads, finds the main content, and stores a snapshot of up to 220 blocks with a content hash. Each block keeps its heading path, which makes citations precise later.
3. Draft. A second job asks Workers AI (@cf/qwen/qwen3-30b-a3b-fp8) for a structured explanation using response_format: json_schema.
4. Validate. The draft must pass a Zod schema and a second round of semantic checks before it can enter the review queue.
5. Review. I read the draft against the snapshot and approve or reject it, with a note.
6. Publish. Approval writes an immutable revision. Fixing a published explainer means publishing a new revision; the old one never changes in place.

sections.heading: Two Workers, one database, zero dollars
sections.text:
The whole thing runs on Cloudflare's free plan. That was a hard constraint from the start, and it shaped most of the design.

 

understory-web is a Hono app with server-rendered JSX. It serves the public pages, a JSON API, RSS and a sitemap, and the private editorial desk. understory-pipeline handles the cron, the queue consumer, extraction, generation, and validation. They share one D1 database that holds articles, snapshots, revisions, reviews, jobs, and the AI budget.

The repo also has an interactive version of that diagram, built with Archify, with route focus and source links.

sections.heading: What validation checks
Diagrams come from data
sections.text:
I didn't want the model drawing SVG. It returns a small graph (two to ten nodes, up to sixteen edges, flow or sequence) and a deterministic renderer in src/domain/diagram.ts does the layout.

Flow diagrams get a topological sort into columns. If a cycle slips through, the leftover nodes go into a final column instead of crashing. Nodes have fixed sizes and coordinates are rounded. Element ids come from an FNV-1a hash of the title and description, so the same input always produces byte-identical SVG. Each figure ships with role="group", a , and a so screen readers get the same explanation as everyone else.

Each node and edge can also carry its own citation, which is why the figures on Understory show small s1 markers. You can trace a box in the diagram back to the paragraph in the original post that justifies it.

sections.heading: Spending a free AI budget without overspending it
sections.text:
Workers AI's free tier gives you 10,000 neurons a day. Understory budgets 8,000 by default and caps the setting at 9,000, so there's always headroom.

Every generation attempt reserves an estimated 500 neurons before calling the model, in a single atomic statement:

If the row would go over budget, nothing changes and the job is deferred to the next UTC midnight. If the call fails because of a network or binding error, the reservation is released, because a transport failure shouldn't eat the day's budget. The API doesn't report exact neuron usage, so a completed attempt is recorded at the conservative estimate.

Reading the site never touches this path. If the budget runs out, the index keeps serving; it just stops growing until tomorrow.
code:
INSERT INTO ai_budget (day, reserved_neurons, used_neurons, generations, updated_at)
SELECT ?, ?, 0, 1, ? WHERE ? <= ?
ON CONFLICT (day) DO UPDATE SET
  reserved_neurons = reserved_neurons + excluded.reserved_neurons,
  generations = generations + 1,
  updated_at = excluded.updated_at
WHERE ai_budget.reserved_neurons + ai_budget.used_neurons + excluded.reserved_neurons <= ?

sections.heading: Leases, so a retry can't overwrite newer work
sections.text:
Queues retry. Workers get evicted. On the free tier you assume both will happen. Every pipeline job holds a lease token, and every write the pipeline makes is conditional on still holding that lease. Generation renews its lease before each attempt and quits with "Job lease lost." if another worker has taken over.

State transitions go through db.batch, so a job is never half-moved.

sections.heading: Caching without purges
sections.text:
Pages are cached with the Cache API, using TTLs from 120 seconds for the index up to 900 seconds for topics, sources, and about. The cache key includes v= .

Approving a draft increments that publication version in the same batch that writes the revision. Every cached page is now addressed by a key that doesn't exist yet, so the next request renders fresh. There's no purge API call to forget and no partial invalidation to debug.

sections.heading: Being a good citizen to publishers
sections.text:
Understory reads other people's work, so it needed to be careful about it:
Outbound fetches block private and reserved IP ranges and local-style hostnames, follow redirects manually with a cap, and enforce a timeout and a byte limit. There's no arbitrary URL ingestion and no open proxy.
The bot identifies itself as UnderstoryBot with a link back to the about page.
Original publishers and authors are linked prominently on every explainer, and "Read original" is the primary button.
Public snapshots keep only two or three short quotations per source.

sections.heading: The editorial desk
sections.text:
Every draft passes a person before it's published. The desk shows the draft as a reader would see it, next to a record of the article, the snapshot id, the model, the prompt version, and the schema version.

 

Access is a bearer token compared via SHA-256 digests, and optionally a Cloudflare Access JWT that the Worker verifies itself: RS256 keys fetched from the team's certs endpoint, with issuer, audience, exp, and nbf checked. The Worker doesn't trust that the edge did it.

sections.heading: The drawing-sheet design
sections.text:
The visual design borrows from technical drawing sheets: paper-coloured background, a faint grid, red-pen accents, figures presented as numbered plates. Barlow Condensed for display, Source Serif 4 for reading, Spline Sans Mono for metadata, all self-hosted. Dark mode follows your system.

I wanted the index to be dense, like Hacker News, and the article page to read like a teaching document. Topic filters and a publisher index cover browsing; everything else stays out of the way.

sections.heading: What I'd tell you if you built one
sections.text:
Make the model decide less. It writes prose and returns a small graph. Ordinary code does layout, linking, validation, and publishing.
Check references as well as shape. Zod tells you the JSON is well formed. Your own checks tell you it's true to itself.
Put the budget in the database. A conditional insert is a perfectly good rate limiter.
Keep a person in the loop where it's cheap. Reading a draft that already passed validation is quick. Retracting a wrong explanation is not.

sections.heading: Go read something
sections.text:
Understory launched today with eleven explainers across AI infrastructure, networking, databases, security, observability, and more. New ones show up as the pipeline finds posts worth explaining and I approve them.
Read it at understory.piyushmehta.com
Follow the RSS feed like any other blog.
Fork it from github.com/piyush97/understory. It deploys to a free Cloudflare account.

If a post you care about deserves an explainer, or one gets something wrong, open an issue on the repo. I'd much rather fix a revision than leave a bad one up.

uptime-monitor-ci.title: Monitor Website Uptime using GitHub Actions
uptime-monitor-ci.description: How to Monitor any website uptime using GitHub Actions for free

sections.text: Create your own website monitor in seconds!

sections.heading: Step 1
sections.text: Create a new repository, I'll name it piyushmehta.com

sections.heading: Step 2
sections.text: Create a directory named and workflows inside it .github/workflows

sections.heading: Step 3
sections.text: Create a file with any name, I'll name is uptime-monitor.yml

sections.heading: Step 4
sections.text:
Write the following in uptime-monitor.yaml
Whenever your website is down, you'll get a notification from GitHub.

Fin!
code:
name: Uptime Monitor

on:
  schedule:
    # Run every hour, You can choose your custom time
    - cron: '*/60 *  * * *'

jobs:
  ping_site:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    name: Uptime Check
    steps:
      - name: Ping Site
        uses: srt32/uptime@v0.2
        with:
          url-to-hit: 'https://piyushmehta.com/' # Website whose uptime you want to track
          expected-statuses: '200'

vercel-to-cloudflare-migration.title: I Moved This Site From Vercel to Cloudflare. Here Is What Broke.
vercel-to-cloudflare-migration.description: Migrating this site from Vercel to Cloudflare Workers: the adapter swap, the Redis client fix, the native binary that broke, and the blank social-card bug.

sections.text:
This site ran on Vercel for years without much drama. Then I moved it to Cloudflare Workers, and for about a day, every link I shared to a new post rendered as a blank blue rectangle. Not broken in an obvious way: the request came back 200 OK, the content type was image/png, the dimensions were exactly right. There was just nothing on it. No title, no text, nothing.

That single bug turned into the best possible tour of what actually changes when you move a site off a Node.js serverless platform and onto a V8 isolate. This is the record of what moved, what broke, and why.
The short version: the adapter swap was the easy part. The hard part was a native Rust binary that only works at build time now, and a caching layer that kept an old broken image alive long after the underlying bug was fixed.

sections.heading: Why leave Vercel at all
sections.text: Nothing was on fire. The honest reason is that I wanted one platform instead of two: Cloudflare already sat in front of DNS and a couple of other side projects, and running the actual site somewhere else meant a second dashboard, a second set of environment variables, and a second mental model for "how does a request get served." Workers also don't have the cold-start-after-idle behavior that Vercel's regional functions do, and I liked the idea of the site living on Cloudflare's edge network instead of one region. None of that is a knock on Vercel. It's a genuinely good platform, and this migration was about consolidation, not escaping something broken.

sections.heading: The adapter swap
sections.text:
The actual config change is small. astro.config.mjs went from the Vercel adapter to the Cloudflare one:

Vercel's ISR (incremental static regeneration) doesn't have a Cloudflare equivalent, so that config just disappears: pages are either prerendered at build time or served on demand from the Worker, with no middle ground where a page gets cached and silently regenerated later. A new wrangler.jsonc shows up alongside it, describing the Worker itself: the entrypoint, the assets binding, and (this detail mattered more than it looked like it would) where the static output actually lives.

Where Vercel produced one build output, Cloudflare produces two: dist/client for everything Workers Assets serves directly, and dist/server for the actual Worker script. The CI build-verification step had to change to match, because checking for a single dist directory was no longer enough to know the build actually worked:

sections.heading: Redis had to get edge-native too
sections.text:
The post-reactions endpoint uses Upstash Redis, and the default @upstash/redis client assumes a Node.js runtime; it isn't guaranteed to work inside a Worker's fetch-based environment. Upstash ships a dedicated entrypoint for exactly this:

I also added an explicit timeout and a single retry. Vercel's regional functions had generous defaults that papered over slow Redis round-trips; a Worker doesn't, so an unbounded request is a much easier way to leave a user staring at a spinner.

The rate limiter's IP detection flipped order too. On Vercel, clientAddress was the trustworthy source. On Cloudflare, it's cf-connecting-ip, set by Cloudflare's own edge and not forwardable by the client, with x-forwarded-for kept only as a last-resort fallback:

Get this ordering wrong on a rate limiter and it isn't a cosmetic bug. It's a rate limiter a client can bypass by setting its own x-forwarded-for header.

sections.heading: The bug that actually cost me a day
sections.text:
This site generates its own Open Graph images (the cards you see when a link gets shared on LinkedIn or X) using Satori to lay out a React-ish element tree as SVG, then @resvg/resvg-js to rasterize that SVG to a PNG. resvg-js is a Rust library exposed to Node through a native addon. That's fine in a Node.js serverless function. It is not fine in a Worker: a V8 isolate has no filesystem and can't load a compiled native binary.

 

So every OG-image route had to move from generating an image per request (prerender = false, fine on Vercel) to generating every possible image once, at build time, via getStaticPaths (prerender = true, the only thing that works on Workers). That's the right fix, and by itself it's not even a hard one.

The actual bug was subtler, and it's the reason this took a day instead of an hour. The font file was being resolved with path.join(process.cwd(), 'InterVariable.ttf'), a path that happens to work when you run node from the project root and does not reliably resolve to the same place inside a build runner's working directory. When the font failed to load, the code didn't throw. It fell through to a fallback renderer that draws the card with plain SVG and no font attached, which resvg silently renders as nothing. Correct dimensions, correct content type, 200 OK, and zero visible pixels of text: a blank blue card that looks, to any monitoring you might have, like a complete success.

The fix was to resolve the font relative to the module's own file instead of the process's working directory, and to give the fallback path an explicit, always-available font so it can never again silently render invisible text. But by the time that shipped, the damage was already cached: LinkedIn, Slack, and Discord had all fetched the blank version and stored it under an image URL that never changes. Fixing the renderer doesn't un-cache anything on someone else's server. I ended up building a whole second layer on top of the fix just for that: a content-hash query parameter on every card URL so the URL itself changes when the card does, plus a manifest so a page can never again advertise a card that was never actually generated, plus a build step that walks every rendered HTML page and fails the build if a single og:image doesn't resolve to a real, correctly sized PNG.

sections.heading: What I'd do differently
sections.text:
Two things, if I were starting this migration over.

First, I'd audit every dependency for native bindings before touching the adapter, not after the blank cards showed up. @resvg/resvg-js was the only one in this codebase, and it's exactly the kind of dependency that keeps working right up until the moment your architecture changes underneath it. Nothing about "it built successfully in CI" tells you whether it'll run in the target runtime.

Second, I'd write the build-time coverage check first, not as a response to a production bug. It's about forty lines of Node that walk the built output and confirm every generated asset a page claims to have actually exists on disk. It would have caught the missing-card class of bug on the very first build, instead of after a report from someone whose link preview looked broken.

If you're mid-migration on something similar, this is the pattern I'd watch for: it's rarely the framework config that bites you. It's the dependency you forgot was doing something clever behind a "just works" abstraction.

what-is-event-loop-in-javascript.title: What is Event Loop in JavaScript
what-is-event-loop-in-javascript.description: JavaScript Event Loop explained via the call stack, task queue, and microtasks: the concept behind every async interview question.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
JavaScript Event Loop is one of the most fundamental concepts that every developer must aspire to understand. It is also one of the most frequently asked interview questions.

JavaScript essentially is Single-threaded, i.e., it can only execute one task at a time. So, what happens if one request takes more than 2 minutes to execute? Will the user be kept waiting for ever? It certainly not an ideal situation. Thankfully, JavaScript’s Event loop architecture comes to the rescue, as it provides the ability to process multiple requests asynchronously.

We will first look at the following components that constitute Event Loop Architecture.

The Call Stack

Web API

Event Queue

Once we try and understand how they work together, then explaining Event Loop becomes very simple.

sections.heading: Call Stack
sections.text:
The Call Stack is a part of the JavaScript Engine and it is simply a stack in which you can add an item and the item added first is processed last. In other words, it follows the FILO - ‘First In Last Out’ principle.

A Call Stack acts as a placeholder or a holding area for all the JavaScript functions that have been fired for execution.

Let us look at the below code sample and understand how the function ‘sayHello’ gets added to the Call Stack.

sections.heading: Step 1 - sayHello Function gets added to the Call Stack
sections.text: From the illustration below, you can see once the function sayHello() is invoked, it is added to the call stack.

sections.heading: Step 2 & 3 - Function returns a value & gets popped from the Call Stack
sections.text:
Once the function returns a value, the output ‘Hello from Skay’ gets displayed on the console. As soon as the function returns, almost immediately, the function is also popped off from the call stack.

 

Now, let’s look at the below code example, with two functions and understand how the JavaScript Engine executes it.

As discussed previously, the two functions are added to the Call Stack as shown below. And the function sayHello() is popped off the stack once the function execution completes.

 

However, as for the second function ‘timeoutFunction’, it returns a setTimeout function which is a part of the Web API. Let us look at what Web API is first.

sections.heading: Web API
sections.text:
Web APIs are built into your web browser and they are able to process data from the browser to do complex useful things. The main thing to understand is that, they are not a part of the JavaScript language, but, they are built on top of the core JS language and provide much more capabilities such as Geolocation, localstorage, etc.

So, coming back to our code example, when the function ‘timeoutFunction’ is executed, it returns the ‘setTimeout’ function and is popped off the stack.

Since the ‘setTimeout’ function is part of the Web API, it gets moved to the Web API as shown below. Along with that, the timer function in Web API is set to 1 second (1000 ms) based on the argument we had passed to the ‘setTimeout’ function as shown in the illustration below.

 

So, what happens after one second? Ideally, you would have anticipated that the function is returned back to the Call Stack for execution. However, instead, it adds it to the Event Queue.

sections.heading: Event Queue
sections.text:
Event Queue is a data structure similar to Stack, which holds the data temporarily and the important thing to note is that the data added first is processed first. In other words, it follows the FIFO -> ‘First in First out’ principle.

So after one second, the ‘setTimeout’ function from Web API is added to the Queue as shown below.

sections.heading: Event Loop
sections.text:
Finally, the ‘Event Loop’ we’ve been waiting for. The function of Event Loop can simply be explained as connecting the Event Queue to the Call Stack.

 

Event Loop does the following:

Checks if the Call Stack is empty, i.e., if all the functions have completed their execution and they have been popped off the Call Stack.

Once the Call Stack is empty, it moves the first item from the Event Queue to the Call Stack.

When the setTimeout function gets added to the Call Stack, the function simply returns the output ‘Hello from Timeout Function’ on the console and is popped out of the Stack.

 

That’s all there is to know about Event Loop. Hope the explanation with illustrations provided a way to understand Event Loop in a simple manner.

In fact, there’s a tool to visualize the Even Loop in real time built by Philip Roberts, which you can access from this link.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text:
To summarize, in this article, we learnt about how JavaScript is Single-Threaded in nature and using Event Loop, it supports processing multiple-requests with the help of a Call Stack, Web API and Event Queue.

Event Loop is basically the way where JavaScript engine looks at the queue to find out if there are any immediate functions to run and picks the one added first and moves it to the Call Stack.

We demonstrated the above concept using the asynchronous setTimeout function which is a part of the Web API.

Fin!

zero-downtime-database-migration-at-scal.title: Zero-Downtime Database Migration: Scaling from 10M to 100M Users
zero-downtime-database-migration-at-scal.description: A comprehensive case study of migrating a 50TB PostgreSQL database to support 10x user growth with zero downtime, improved performance, and 40% cost reduction.

sections.text: When your startup grows from 10 million to 100 million users in 18 months, your database becomes both your greatest asset and your biggest bottleneck. This is the story of how we successfully migrated a 50TB PostgreSQL database with zero downtime, improved performance by 300%, and reduced costs by 40% — all while maintaining business continuity during our most critical growth period.

sections.heading: The Challenge: When Success Becomes a Problem
sections.text: Picture this: It's 3 AM, and you're woken by alerts. Database response times have spiked to 8 seconds. Users are abandoning transactions. Your database, which handled 10 million users gracefully, is choking on 40 million. The business team needs an answer by morning.

sections.heading: The Numbers That Kept Me Awake
sections.text:
50TB of production data across 200+ tables
100,000+ QPS at peak traffic
$180,000/month in database infrastructure costs
99.99% uptime SLA with zero tolerance for maintenance windows
48-hour revenue impact window (our weekend sale period)

The existing PostgreSQL 12 cluster was showing clear signs of strain:
code:
-- Query performance had degraded significantly
SELECT
  query,
  calls,
  mean_time,
  max_time
FROM pg_stat_statements
WHERE mean_time > 1000
ORDER BY mean_time DESC;

-- Results showing queries that once took 200ms now taking 3-5 seconds

sections.heading: Deep Dive Analysis
sections.text:
My first step wasn't jumping into solutions — it was understanding the problem completely. I spent two weeks analyzing every aspect of our system:

Database Performance Audit:

Key Findings:
60% of queries hitting unindexed columns
Table bloat reaching 40% on core user tables
Connection pool exhaustion during peak hours
Read replicas 2-3 seconds behind primary
code:
-- Analyzed connection patterns
SELECT datname, numbackends, xact_commit, xact_rollback
FROM pg_stat_database;

-- Identified table bloat and index efficiency
SELECT schemaname, tablename,
       n_tup_ins, n_tup_upd, n_tup_del,
       last_vacuum, last_autovacuum
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_tup_upd + n_tup_del DESC;

sections.heading: The Migration Strategy
sections.text:
After extensive analysis, I proposed a multi-phase approach:

 

Phase 1: Infrastructure preparation and replication setup
Phase 2: Data synchronization and testing
Phase 3: Application layer preparation 
Phase 4: Cutover execution
Phase 5: Validation and optimization

sections.heading: Risk Assessment and Mitigation
sections.text: The risk matrix above shows how we categorized and planned for potential issues. Each high-risk item had multiple mitigation strategies and rollback plans.

sections.heading: Building the New Environment
sections.text: We chose PostgreSQL 14 with a completely redesigned architecture:
code:
# Terraform configuration for new database infrastructure
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "primary" {
  cluster_identifier = "app-primary-v2"
  engine            = "aurora-postgresql"
  engine_version    = "14.6"

  database_name = var.database_name
  master_username = var.master_username
  master_password = var.master_password

  # Performance optimizations
  db_cluster_parameter_group_name = aws_rds_cluster_parameter_group.optimized.name

  # High availability
  backup_retention_period = 7
  preferred_backup_window = "03:00-04:00"
  preferred_maintenance_window = "sun:04:00-sun:05:00"

  # Monitoring
  enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports = ["postgresql"]

  # Security
  storage_encrypted = true
  kms_key_id       = aws_kms_key.rds.arn

  tags = {
    Environment = "production"
    Purpose     = "migration-target"
  }
}

sections.heading: Lessons Learned: Beyond the Technical Implementation
1. Communication is as Critical as Code
sections.text:
One of the most important lessons was the importance of stakeholder communication. I created a daily migration status email that included:
Current replication lag and data consistency percentages
Risk assessment updates
Timeline adjustments with clear reasoning
Success metrics and business impact projections

Template I used:

### Current Status: GREEN 🟢

- Replication lag: 0.8 seconds (target: <2 seconds)
- Data consistency: 99.97% (target: >99.9%)
- Application compatibility tests: 47/50 passed

### Today's Accomplishments:

- Completed connection pool optimization
- Resolved index creation performance issue
- Validated rollback procedures

### Tomorrow's Focus:

- Pre-cutover checklist validation
- Team coordination dry run

### Risks and Mitigations:

  - Mitigation: Emergency scaling procedures tested and ready

sections.heading: 2. Building Trust Through Transparency
sections.text:
During the planning phase, I encountered resistance from the product team who were concerned about potential downtime affecting our weekend sale. Instead of dismissing their concerns, I:

1. Created a visual risk dashboard showing real-time migration health
2. Provided detailed rollback timelines (< 15 minutes to previous state)
3. Offered incremental validation by migrating non-critical services first
4. Established clear success criteria that the business team helped define

This approach transformed skeptics into advocates and ensured business buy-in for the technical approach.

sections.heading: 3. Automation Prevents Human Error
sections.text: I automated every possible aspect of the migration:
code:
#!/bin/bash
# migration-cutover.sh - Automated cutover script

set -euo pipefail

log() {
  echo "[$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] $1" | tee -a migration.log
}

validate_prerequisites() {
  log "Validating prerequisites..."

  # Check replication lag
  LAG=$(psql -h target-db -t -c "SELECT EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (now() - latest_end_time)) FROM pg_stat_subscription WHERE subname = 'migration_sub';")
  if (( $(echo "$LAG > 2" | bc -l) )); then
    log "ERROR: Replication lag too high: ${LAG}s"
    exit 1
  fi

  # Validate application health
  if ! curl -f http://localhost:3000/health; then
    log "ERROR: Application not healthy"
    exit 1
  fi

  log "Prerequisites validated successfully"
}

perform_cutover() {
  log "Starting cutover process..."

  # Stop replication
  psql -h target-db -c "ALTER SUBSCRIPTION migration_sub DISABLE;"

  # Update feature flags
  redis-cli hset migration:feature_flags new_db_writes '{"percentage": 100}'

  # Wait for application restarts
  sleep 30

  # Validate new connections
  validate_new_database_connections

  log "Cutover completed successfully"
}

rollback() {
  log "ROLLBACK: Reverting to original database..."
  redis-cli hset migration:feature_flags new_db_writes '{"percentage": 0}'
  log "ROLLBACK: Completed"
}

# Main execution
trap rollback ERR
validate_prerequisites
perform_cutover

zfs-saved-my-data-seagate-warranty.title: My 12TB Drive Failed. ZFS Saved 3.4TB of Data
zfs-saved-my-data-seagate-warranty.description: A Seagate IronWolf developed 52 bad sectors. Here is how a Proxmox ZFS mirror kept my homelab online and rebuilt onto a 16TB warranty replacement.

sections.text:
One of my 12TB Seagate IronWolf drives developed 52 bad sectors. At that point, about 3.4TB of homelab data was depending on the surviving half of my ZFS mirror.

The Proxmox server stayed online. My media and application data remained available, Seagate replaced the failed drive without hassle, and ZFS rebuilt the mirror onto a new 16TB IronWolf.

This is the sequence I followed, including the USB enclosure reset that briefly suspended the pool and the checksum errors ZFS caught after a later reboot.

ZFS could not stop the drive from failing. It did stop that failure from deleting my data.

sections.heading: TL;DR: the recovery in numbers
sections.text:
Failed disk: 12TB Seagate IronWolf with 52 bad sectors
Data at risk: 3.37TiB allocated on a degraded ZFS mirror
Warranty replacement: new 16TB Seagate IronWolf
Resilver: 3.38TiB in 5 hours 30 minutes
Resilver result: zero errors and the mirror returned ONLINE
Usable capacity: still 10.9TiB because the other mirror member is 12TB

The mirror supplied another copy, ZFS checked the blocks, and Seagate supplied the replacement drive.

sections.heading: My Proxmox ZFS mirror before the failure
sections.text:
My vault pool lives on a Proxmox server. It stores media, application configuration, and other homelab data. I built it as a two-drive ZFS mirror:

Both drives sit in a TerraMaster USB DAS. The enclosure exposes each disk to ZFS instead of hiding them behind hardware RAID. ZFS needs that direct access to manage the mirror and verify checksums.

The pool held about 3.37TiB of allocated data when I replaced the drive. A mirror gets the capacity of its smallest member, with another copy of each block on the other disk. When one drive started failing, that second copy kept the pool alive.
code:
vault
└── mirror-0
    ├── 12TB IronWolf
    └── 12TB IronWolf

sections.heading: The 12TB IronWolf had 52 bad sectors
sections.text:
SMART showed 52 bad sectors on one of the 12TB drives. I was not going to clear the warning and keep using it. Once a disk cannot reliably read its own sectors, I do not want it holding the only copy of anything.

I removed it from service and opened a Seagate warranty claim. The process was painless, and Seagate honored the warranty. They sent a 16TB Seagate IronWolf to replace the failed 12TB drive.

The replacement arrived with the clean baseline I wanted:

Its short SMART self-test also completed without error.

The Seagate part was refreshingly easy. A failed drive already gives you enough to worry about. I did not have to fight the warranty process too.
code:
SMART overall health:       PASSED
Power-on hours:             0
Reallocated sectors:        0
Current pending sectors:    0
Offline uncorrectable:      0
Reported uncorrectable:     0
Command timeouts:           0
Interface CRC errors:       0

sections.heading: The degraded mirror kept serving data
sections.text:
After I removed the failed disk, ZFS showed the pool as DEGRADED:

The warning was serious. The pool had no redundancy left, so another disk failure would have meant data loss. The datasets were still available from the surviving member.

The disk had failed, the mirror had lost redundancy, and ZFS made both facts obvious without taking my data offline.
code:
pool: vault
state: DEGRADED

mirror-0
  missing  UNAVAIL
  survivor ONLINE

sections.heading: Hot-plugging the replacement reset the USB enclosure
sections.text:
The recovery got more stressful when I inserted the 16TB drive. The TerraMaster enclosure reset its shared USB connection, and the surviving 12TB disk disappeared for a moment.

ZFS suspended the pool:

That was the right response. With its only available member temporarily gone, ZFS stopped accepting I/O rather than claiming that writes had succeeded.

Once both disks were visible again, I checked their model, serial, WWN, SMART state, and partition signatures. Then I resumed the pool:

The pool returned to DEGRADED with the surviving member online. zpool clear removed the suspended state. It did not restore redundancy.

This incident also exposed a weakness in my setup. Both mirrored disks share the same enclosure, cable, controller, and power supply. The mirror protects against one disk failing, but those shared components can still affect both drives at once.
code:
pool: vault
state: SUSPENDED
zpool clear vault

sections.heading: The replacement command was zpool replace
sections.text:
The 16TB disk had to replace the missing mirror member. Adding it as another top-level vdev would have changed the pool topology instead of repairing the mirror. zpool add was the wrong command for this job.

I used:

The WWN path under /dev/disk/by-id/ identifies the physical disk. I did not use /dev/sdc because Linux can assign a different device letter after a reboot or USB reconnect.

ZFS partitioned the blank replacement and started resilvering it.
code:
zpool replace vault \
  <missing-vdev-guid> \
  /dev/disk/by-id/wwn-<replacement-disk>

sections.heading: ZFS resilvered 3.38TiB with zero errors
sections.text:
The resilver copied the allocated data from the surviving 12TB drive to the new 16TB drive:

 

Both drives finished online. ZFS recorded zero read, write, and checksum errors during the resilver. The datasets mounted normally, Proxmox reported the storage entries as active, and the pool had redundancy again.

Usable capacity remains about 10.9TiB. The smaller member limits a mirror, so the extra space on the 16TB disk cannot be used yet. If I eventually replace the remaining 12TB drive with another 16TB or larger disk, the mirror can expand.

I would rather have redundancy now than extra capacity I cannot safely use.
code:
scan: resilvered 3.38T in 05:30:27 with 0 errors
state: ONLINE
errors: No known data errors

sections.heading: ZFS caught 11 checksum mismatches after reboot
sections.text:
A later Proxmox reboot imported the pool and recorded 11 checksum mismatches on the new member. The pool remained ONLINE, and applications were unaffected because the other mirror member had a valid copy.

ZFS compared the data with its stored checksum, rejected the incorrect bytes, and read the correct copy from the other disk.

The surrounding hardware evidence remained clean. SMART passed, the reallocated, pending, and uncorrectable sector counts stayed at zero, and the interface CRC count did not increase. The kernel showed no new USB reset or I/O failure, and ZFS reported no known data errors.

A full scrub began checking every allocated block. I am keeping the checksum counters until it finishes because clearing them now would discard useful evidence. If the scrub finishes cleanly and the count stays at 11, I can clear the historical device errors. If the count keeps rising, I will investigate the TerraMaster bay, USB bridge, cable, power delivery, and the replacement drive.

I liked seeing ZFS do what I had set it up to do. A successful read was not enough. The bytes also had to match.

sections.heading: What ZFS and the mirror each did
sections.text: The mirror and ZFS handled different parts of the failure.

sections.heading: The mirror kept another copy
sections.text:
The surviving disk still contained the pool after the first drive became untrustworthy. Later, when one copy failed a checksum, the mirror gave ZFS another copy to read.

Checksums can detect bad data, but they cannot recreate the correct bytes. That requires redundancy or a backup.

sections.heading: ZFS checked the data
sections.text: ZFS checksums data and metadata. It can tell the difference between a drive returning data and a drive returning the correct data. During a scrub, ZFS checks allocated blocks and repairs a bad copy when another valid copy exists.

sections.heading: ZFS made the failures visible
sections.text: DEGRADED told me the pool had lost redundancy. SUSPENDED stopped I/O when the only available member vanished during the USB reset. Neither state was pleasant, but neither hid the problem.

sections.heading: Stable disk IDs kept me on the right drive
sections.text:
The WWN path kept pointing to the replacement even when /dev/sda, /dev/sdb, and /dev/sdc changed after reconnects and reboots.

A filesystem cannot protect you if you run the right command against the wrong disk.

sections.heading: RAID is not a backup
sections.text:
The mirror protected me from one disk failure. It would not protect me from accidental deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, a destructive command, or corruption copied to both members.

Anything irreplaceable still needs an independent backup.

sections.heading: Run scrubs and read the result
sections.text: A scrub verifies data while another copy is available for repair. I care whether it repaired anything, found permanent errors, or caused a device counter to increase, not only whether the scheduled job ran.

sections.heading: Use SMART and ZFS together
sections.text: SMART identified the original failing drive and gave me a hardware baseline for the replacement. The later checksum events showed why filesystem checks still matter. A drive can report healthy while ZFS detects incorrect data.

sections.heading: Use /dev/disk/by-id/
sections.text: Device letters are convenient labels, not stable identities. Replacement commands should use persistent disk IDs.

sections.heading: Treat the enclosure as shared hardware
sections.text: Hot-plugging one bay reset the USB path for both disks. The enclosure, USB controller, cable, and power supply need the same attention as the drives.

sections.heading: Check the pool topology before changing it
sections.text: zpool replace repairs a missing mirror member. zpool add changes the topology. I checked the command and target before pressing Enter.

sections.heading: Can ZFS recover from a failed drive?
sections.text:
Yes, if the pool still has a valid copy. One member of my two-disk mirror failed, while the other kept the pool available. I replaced the missing member and ZFS resilvered the allocated data onto it.

A single-disk ZFS pool can detect corruption with checksums, but it has no second copy to repair from.

sections.heading: Is a ZFS mirror the same as RAID 1?
sections.text: Both provide two-copy redundancy. ZFS also manages the filesystem, block checksums, scrubs, repairs, snapshots, and the pool itself. When two copies disagree, ZFS can verify which one matches the stored checksum and repair the other.

sections.heading: Does a 12TB + 16TB ZFS mirror provide 28TB?
sections.text: No. The smallest member limits the mirror. My 12TB + 16TB mirror remains about 10.9TiB usable. Replacing the remaining 12TB disk with another 16TB or larger drive will allow the mirror to expand.

sections.heading: Does ZFS or RAID replace a backup?
sections.text: No. My mirror handled one disk failure. It cannot protect both copies from deletion, ransomware, theft, fire, or a destructive command. Irreplaceable data still needs an independent backup.

sections.heading: Should I use zpool add when replacing a failed mirror disk?
sections.text: No. zpool add changes the pool topology. Use zpool replace with the missing vdev and the replacement disk's stable /dev/disk/by-id/ path.

sections.heading: The recovery was boring, which is what I wanted
